- - WHO WAS BABY BUNTING! Of Baby Bunting ip the book I often love to read: . Her father and her mother dear • Were very poor indeed, With nothing but a rabbit-skin To wrap poor Baby Bunting in. Her father would arhunting go, And stop out all day long; Her mother sat at home to sew, And sang a little song, And rocked the cradle, filed with hay On which poor Baby Bunting lay. I wonder where the Buntings lived ? I often wish to know If all these things are happening now, Or happened long ago. It would have been so nice to take Poor Baby Bunting, clothes and cake! --Tram Little Folks Haftecine for April.

- _ Furi,of import—A custom house. Self-possession in a young woman is well' enough for a while, but she shouldn't keep it up too long. . If Jay Gould visits Austria, the Emperor can do no less, in recognition of his merits, than make hint a Knight of the Golden Fleece. As a fleece, Jay has always been „

a great success.—Satracuse Herald. On one occasion, when a new serjeant had been created, and it became his duty. according to custom, to present rings to the Judges, inscribed with the usual brief "posy" in Latin, Sir George Rose indicated his appreciation of the then existing company of serjeants by suggesting for the motto in question, "Scilicet" (Silly set). A CosrmoN CCSTO3I. An English gentleman who passed his winters abroad was in the habit of making purchases of cutlery in Paris "because the knives and forks of France were trinch• more elegant and durable than those made in his native country." Last year he sent his butler to make the annual bargains in the Rue de Rivoli, and received an apology to the effect that the articles could not be delivered for a few days, as they had not arrived from Sheffield! Whether, the death ef this cherished illusion had a patriotic effect upon our countryman is not known!. So uncertain are the affet- tions of many "citizens of the world" thot it is not un- likely he discovered in his basket of cutle-- f!neve deformities that aoassed for perfections and beauties when stamped with the fair name of France.—Casselrs "Saturday Journal. THE /JAUNTED GlN.—That is the way that a cotton- gin, near my father's plantation in Tennessee, was known. It was necessary one time torrequest the field hands to get up about dawn in order to gather sufficient cotton to be shipped•the next day. The darkies objected , to this, and )n order TO show some good reason why they should not go to work so early, told the following story: "Ole massa, wet own'd de plantation 'fore .de wah, neber'd wuk at dat time of ae mawnin', 'kase de ghosses don' like it. Oar wuz once a man wot owned dat gin up yonder, an' he useter pit up ter wuk mighty early. So one mawnin' as he was a-ginnin' dar, an' de niggers wuz wukin' down-sters, a ghos' come up an' catched him, an' he whopped him fearful, an' he whopped an' he -whopped, an' he whopped an' he whopped, an' de man I hollered an' he hollered an' he hollered, an' de ghos' kep' cryin' all de time, 'Dar's a time fee me an' a time for you. der's a time fer mean' a time fer you, dar's a time .fer me an' a time fer you'; an' de ghos' whopped, dat man till sunup, an' den de ghos' went 'way. Pat man neber would wuk no mo"fore de Sunup, an' clat's de reason de niggers don' like ter, 'kase dey's 'feared ob de ghosses." And •the story gained the coveted rest.—Herper's Afartazine. WHILE TRIR EAsT WINDS Btow.—ln spring-time it is the custom in this country to blame all' trifling ailments, depression of spirits, temporary colds, and aches, and biliousness, on the east wind, if it dares to blow at all. Now. I do not allege that exposure for a long time to the wind will not give colds and other troubles; but it is a very much-belied wind, nevertheless, aad if people would only eat in reason, and clothe rationally, the east wind would have a better time of it during its visit to these islands than it has. In spring, if we would be well. we , can hardly take too much exercise, especially long walks, and we ought to dress lightly but warmly. The clogging, 1 cumbersome topcoat, the india-rubber mantle, the mack- intosh, the heavy muffler, and deadly galosh, should all be left indoors when we go out to walk. Gloves should be worn, warm thick stockings, and easy soft shoes: a light silk scarf may be taken—and put on if required— and also an umkrella; but these are all the arms which one should carry against the weather if he or she valises health. Verily, prevention is better than cure. But if, we cuddle ourselves up in-doors in badly-ventilated, overheated rooms, and take-our exercise abroad, laden to the earth with extra clothing, we cannot be well either in body or in mind. We shall be peevish all day, destitute of spirit and ambition; we shall have wretched appetites. sluggish livers, and restless nights.—Cassell's Family Magazin.e. Soars MiSTRANSLATIONS.—The works of various English prose writers have, in some places, been incorrectly translated owing to the fact that in the original a phrase or word has been tred in a purely technical sense. An English historian, referring to an incident in the -Seven Years' War, said that Lord George Sackville was "broken" for cowardice at the battle of Minden, em- ploying this expression 'as a synonym for cashiered. A Freneh writer, quoting this paragraph, translated the word ".bmken " as "roue," which means broken on the wheel; and he appended a note to the statement, in which he corriMented strongly upon the barbarity of inflicting—for a purely military offence—a punishment which, in France, was reserved for crimes of the deepest dye. Miss Cooper, a daughter of the American novelist, Stales that, when in Paris, she saw a French translation of her father's tale, "The Spy," in which there were several mistakes; but one of them was such that it was almost incredible that any one could possibly have been guilty of it. The residence of Mr. Wharton, one of the characters who figure in the story, is spoken of by the author as "The Locusts." Now, the translator had been evidently ignorant of the circumstance of there being any species of trees bearing this name. Having, there- fore, looked out the word in his dictionary, and finding the definition to be given as "Les Sauterelles "—grass- hoppers—thus he rendered it in the text. Presently, however, he came across a paragraph in the novel in which it was stated that a visitor to the house of Mr. , Wharton had tied his horse to a locust. Then it might • be naturally supposed that the translator would at once have discovered his error. Not a bit of it His reason- ing would appear to have been somewhat on a parity with that of a celebrated countryman of his, when he declared that "if the facts do not agree with the theory, so much the worse for the facts." Nevertheless, the writer seems to have been conscious that some explana- tion was due of so extraordinary a statement as that a horseman had secured his steed to a grasshopper. Con- sequently he went on to gravely inform his readers that in America these insects grow to an enormous size -, and that, in this ease, one of these—dead and stuffed, of course—had been stationed at the door of the mansion for the convenience of visitors on horseback !—Cornhill Magazine for April. • THE PROS AND CONS OF MARRIAGE.—Money, no doubt, is the root of much that is evil. but a little of it is a great convenience when shopping, as it also is when marrying; unless, indeed, mortality is one of the effects of marry- ing, as a servant girl seems to have thought- The lady with whom she last lived, meeting her, said : " Well. Mary, where do you live now?" "Please, ma'am, I don't live now; Pm married." Those of us who are married know that we do live, and that we cannot live on nothing, so we appreciate the Scotch girl's common sense who said that" a kiss and a tinful of cold water make but a poor breakfast." I quite believe in marrying for gold and working for silver, but there should be a reasonable chance of getting work to do, for it is nothing less than criminal folly to marry on nothing a week, and that uncertain—very. On the other hand, there is some truth in the saying that what will keep one will keep two. Show me one couple unhappy merely on ac- count Of their limited circumstances, and I will show you ten who are wretched from other circumstances. There are bachelors who are so ultra-prudent, and who hold such absurd opinions as to the expense of matri- mony, that, although they have enough money, they have not enough courage to enter the state. Pitt used to say that he could not afford to marry, yet his butcher's bill was so enormous 'that some one has calculated it as affording his servants about fourteen pounds of meat a day each man and woman ! For the more economical regulation of his household, if for no other reason, lie should have taken to himself a wife. Of course a young man with a small income cannot afford to marry if he smokes big cigars, and gives expensive drinks to every /y fool who claps him on the back and calls him "old man.'" He must be particular, too, in choosing a wife, to select one with a slender waste (not one who has made her -waist slender with health-destroying corsets, but one -who is economical and who can keep house with the least amount of waste). Swift's saying about nets and cages is well known. He thought that one reason why many marri...g,,es are unhappy is because women spend their time in making nets to catch husbands rather than in making cages to keep them in when caught. True, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, and we see no reason why a girl should not do all that is consistent with self- respect and modesty to obtain a husband. She should remember, however, that conquests have to be kept as well as made, and that for a woman to fail to make and keep her home happy is to be a " failure " in a more real sense than to have failed in getting a husband. "Why don't the men propose, mamma?" One reason is because they are afraid. that the girls of the period will make ex- travagant wives. The other day a girl was talking with a middle-aged bachelor: the girl was ofaby no means shy disposition, so she began to " chaff" him about his wretchedly unmarried condition. "Why don't you marry? Can't you afford to keep awife?" "My innocent young friend," was the reply, •„I can afford to support heal a dozen wives, but I can't afford to pay the rnillinerla bills of one." And you Mothers. think not always about getting good husbands for your daughters, but think sometimes how to make your daughters tit to be rood wives.— Author of How to be Happy though. }cave seen an open-air dentist draw alooth out of a man as easily as you or I would draw a bulldog out of a barrel, even though a good portion of the gum had to come with the topth, but whether the man' could fairly be considered as having been gulled or not I won't venture to say. There are a few of these operatOrlf Who; give (or take) more than you have paid for, in which: case it wouldn't be right to say they gulled you. . If the EngliShman won't acknowledge his gullibirit3i, it is, of course, useless to expect the Englishwoman to own that, she is gullible. If, therefore you wish .tct,, gently demonstrate that the fair sex.also cave. an innate desire to be gulled, you will have to pose as a prevaricator in their estimation. While I don't mind posing as a prevaricator, I have no particular ambition to pose as a misanthropist, but I honestly believe that. every Englishman delights in seeing his Wife gulled.. This statement might be twisted into a compliment to the fair sex by saying that, if true, it proves they are gulled so seldom that the male rejoices to realise that, his wife is human, at least human to the English failing. He sacs, "Sarah. is this tea from that confounded present Shop again ?" "Yes," she answers. "Why ?" Then he sorts out, from a series of grunts and mumblings, the information that he could tell she had either bought it there, or smoked the water in the kettle. .ould

I consider it rather a rich joke for the average man to talk about bad tea. His wife buys some at 3. 4d. a pound, and he simply uses it to wash his daily bread down with, but makes no comment. She next buys some at is. 6d. the pound, which runs over the same palate, but without eliciting any remark. There is something here off the hinges. If one slice of bread was spread with butter at Is. sd. a pound, and another with palm oil and company at 7d., the chief subject of con- versation between a man and his wife for a week or so would be butter. lam glad I haven't the job of buying tea. I think I could easily manage to buy all the other groceries, but to buy tea would be too much; it would unnerve me altogether. - On a big advertising wall you see the names of some fifteen firms, each of which sells a better tea at 2s. than the others. Now, where should I select? I know. I should have an uncontrollable desire to be gulled, and I should see a placard announcing that the North Pole Tea Company gave a silk hat or a pair of clogs with a pound of tea. I don't think I should ask how they managed to do it, because, as I said before, a gull isn't worth anything unless it is involved in mystery. A man may be gulled without being suspected of having lost his wits but he cannot go into a losing transaction and know beforehand to a fraction, how much he is going to lose without being an idiot. This is the dif- ference between a gull and a dead swindle. I never like to tax anybody's imagination, but sup- pose for a moment a tea firm to be candid, and this to be their advertisement :—" One pound of our famous tea costs us sd. We pay duty on it at the rate of Sd. per pound. We average the cost of blending, packing, paper, printing, &c., at 3d.; total cost to us, Is. 2d. per pound. If you pay us 2s. Bd., we will let you have a pound full weight, and present you with a large washing mug worth 6d., which will only leave us the modest profit of is. on the transaction." N.B.—You can have the same tea at 3s. 6d. or 4s. if you want a "superior quality." Why, even the Englishwoman would despise the firm who exhibited such candour, and look upon the notice as an infringement upon her right to be gulled. I must acknowledge that, personally. I am above the average in gullibility In the tea line, as I take six lumps of sugar in each cup, and I'm afraid I shall not detect any dif- ference in the quality of the tea even when some arm presents a public-house to each customer with every ,p lund of tea. The strongest evidence of fho Englishmen's gullibility is the very existence of advertisements that ask for a certain number of stamps to be sent, and in return the advertiser will tell you " how to make a rapid fortune," or will send you a" recipe for producing whiskers," and many other advertisements which we might fairly designate "English Blarney Stones." 1 I once forwarded the six stamps to an advertiser who knew the secret of getting rich (no mistake about that, , and he advised me to " sell hot coffee in some busy street from five to six o'clock in the morning." Understand, I don't exactly acknowledge that I was , gulled, because I haven't tried it. When I have tried it, I will write you a full detailed account, that is if you haven't grown too old by that time to take an interest in it.

I kvew a young man who vainly tried to focus the ' light upon the down on his upper lip, who sent twelve stamps to an advertiser who prepared a decoction that would produce hair on a marble slab. The advice of the marble slabbist to the twelve stampist was briefly " Wait till they grow." I once despatched twelve stamps by persuasion of Mrs—Bette to the advertiser of a certain "knitting machine," which "turned out at great speed scarf s, jerseys, Tam o' Shanter hats. Bz.c." Mrs. Bette knew it couldn't be worth anything at that price (she said this after it came), and she didn't expect it would take us a couple of hours to unpack it. Well, this "knitting machine" was nothing more nor less than a special edition of the cork with a hole through, and four pins round the top, upon which children do wool work, only the ." knitter" was made of wood instead of cork. Mrs. B. said the advertiser ought to be locked up, but, as I pointed out toter, he wasn't there to show us at what speed the thing really could be worked. He might certainly have referred us to some of his customers who were making their independency with the knitter, but possibly he didn't think of it. You see, having had a hand in the affair, I didn't care to own that we had been gulled. Those who have already "increased their income by ES per week" through the medium of such advertise- ments, will probably not stand up to say that they haven't been gulled, as they will doubtless be dead, owing to having lived too luxuriously on the surplus I income.

I should say that the easiest way to add £5 or £l.O per week to your income is to advertise for stamps iii exchange for some gigantic gull. • PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HUGH BETTE. X.—GULLIBILITY. No one can conceive the pride I feel when 1 donsider
that lam one atom of the Great British Public. 4ts consider its place among nations, however, and realise -
that that place is maintained by its industry *and astute- ness, I cannot reconcile the character of the nation with that of the individual Briton. I make the painful

admission that the component parts of the 01'. are guillible. Although the dictionary denounces the word gullible as vulgar, I know of no other word that will fill the bill. I don't suppose that every Englishman will own to it, but he knows that in his inmost soul he has a craving to be gulled. We all know how well the English- man keeps his own council. When he has been gulled, he doesn't tell anybody; he either laughs to himself or curses in solitude, and then he is quite ready to tie gulled

again. , - • , Although he knows very well that a swindle is a swindle, no amount of example will prevent him from being gulled. In fact, being gulled once or twice only whets his appetite more. Make him believe that there is something to be almost given away, and surround the transaction with a little mystery, and you have him at
witidle,

your mercy. Now, after making these allegations against the charac- ter of the Englishman, there ought to be some proofs advanced to support them. The market-place supplies a few. Here is the king of quacks, whu wears a massive gold albert and a sleeve hat, and has an assistant. He is no common pill-seller. He tells you that his whole life has been devoted to_ the study of the human ear.

Some man who has caught cold in one ear, and been I rendered a little deaf in that organ, steps up to the plat- form, and the aurist (?) digs an instrument into his ear. We cannot follow that deaf ear through the many hospital' wards which it will most probably enter, but we can ask why that man didn't take it in the first instance to be operated upon by one of the oyster stall men. The fact is, he knew that the oyster man wouldn't have, gulled him.

You have the same result from the quack who buys, three pounds of soap for 101 d., and retails it in the shape of pills at about 700 per cent. profit; and even in the antediluvian looking quack whose stall consists 'of small box on three legs, and who' vends a patent corn solvent made of anything that will melt in the flame of candje. The small change teems in and the great British public shatters its ear drum, its stomach with suds, drops molten shellac on its corns, and is happy.

div.p: OUR LONDON LETfER.

'LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT. The attendance at the House of Commons this afternoon was, as usual, on the resumption &busi- ness after holidays, comparatively small. There was on the paper no business more urgent than Supply, and the opportunity of voting a million or two of public money does not draw members with anything like the irresistible force of the prospect of a personal squabble. The fullest bench, in the House was that on which Ministers sit. It is a point of honour for occupants of the Treasury I Bench, from the highest to the lowest grade, to be in their places on. sueh occasions as to-day. If the Leader of the House is there it would ill become the most junior Lord of the Treasury to extend his holiday. So they all show themselves at question time, after which the strain on the bridle is lost, and they are at liberty to do what they pleas, so that they remain within sound of the division bell. As the pressure of attendance is the most strong upon members of the Ministry, so have they benefited to the fullest degree by the early closing movement. One of them tells me he would have been obliged to resign this session had the old order of things gone forward. He found it -physically impossible to go the pace demadded by former cir- cumstances. Next to Ministers I fancy the I'arner-T, lites are the most pleased with the reform. As- long as it was possible to keep the House sitting all night or far into the night it had occassionally to be done. BLit the pleasure is one which, after some- thing like thirteen years of steady practice, palls upon the appetite, and Mr. Biggar is as glad to go home to bsd at mid-night as is Mr. W. H. Smith. Mr. John Morley's speech, delivered at Newcastle last night, is worth close study for something more than the ordinary reasons which make his public utterances attractive. Referring last week to the report current of the business which occupied Mr. Gladstone and his friends in the private meeting at Earl Spencer's house. I stated that only one-half, and that the least important part, of the business was disclosed. It was stated that the Local Go- vernment Bill had engrossed the attention of the Leaders of the Opposition, and no reference was made to discussion of the Budget. But the Budget , was, after all, the critical topic of discussion, and Mr. Morley last night set forth at length, and with his usual force and clearness, the ground which Mr: Gladstone will take up in opposing Mr. Goschen's measure. That schetne is so cunningly concocted and draped that at the time of exposition it gained almost 'universal acceptance even among Liberal critics. It was noticed at the time that Mr.'Gladstone was ' significantly silerit, • handing over to Mr. Childers the duty which habitually devolves upon the Leader, of the Opposition of saying a few words upon the Budget Scheme. He wanted to have opportunity to think the matter over, and he has, I believe, availed himself 'of the opportunity with conse- quences that Mr. Goschen cannot regard without apprehension. Mr. Gladstone will undertake to show that the Budget, so far from dealing fairly with all classes with some tendency towards ade- quately taxing the rich, is a rich man's, or at least a landowner's, Budget. Ido not suppose he will upset the scheme, 'the -Government being impreg- nable in their position, fortified by the alliance with the'Dissentient Liberals. But when the Budget comes up again in committee theremill be arnarked variation from that attitude of benevolent neutra- lity which Mr. , Gladstone has through the session displayed towards right hon. gentlemen on the opposite bench. • 'Next Sunday is likely to be a critical day in Ire- land, and its events, are awaited with grave anxiety. The crisis arises out of one of those boast- fully flippant things which Mr. Balfour would do so mach better to leave unsaid. Defending his policy in the Howie of Commons he declared that in certain parts of Ireland, notably County Clare, where the Coercion Act had been vigorously en- forced, the power of the Nltional League was shat- tered.' His object in thus dragging his coat tail be- fore the Irish benches was unmistakeable. It was a clear invitation to the representatives of national opinion to tread on it, and they promptly j duped upon it. • With the intention of testing the accur- acy of the Chief. Secretary's declaraticm, the National League have summoned for Sunday IV series of meetings in the specified districts. Of course, if Mr. Balfour is well informed, and accurate in his statement, the result of this movement can only be to justify him. If the, power of the National League is, as he says, shattered, the meet- ings will be a failure. But .Mr. Balfour has not the courage of his opinion. He shrinks from the test, and invoking the militaiy and police forces at his disposal has proclaimed the meetings. The Irish members, of course cannot retire from their posi- tion. The members for County Clare claim the right, in common with the members for Lancashire, Yorkshire, or Staffordshire, to meet their consti- tuents when and where it may be mutually agree- able and convenient. The meetings will certainly be held, the soldiers with fixed bayonets and the police with drawn batons will as certainly appear on the scene, and nothing short of a miracle can prevent lamentable and criminal bloodshed. On the eve of the muster for the Easter review a wild whisper went round the camps that the Duke of Cambridge would find it convenient not to put in an appearance. It was alleged that his Royal high- ness would shirk the ordeal of facing the massed volunteers a day or two after the promulgation of what was practically a writ of eviction from Wim- bledon Common. The report was, of course, falsi- fied, the duke turning up as rotund and rubicund as ever, to all appearances absolutely unmoved by the storm of obloquy which his action in respect of Wimbledon Common has drawn upon him. It is certainly unfortunate that the duke's private in- terest as a landed proprietor should clash with his duty and inclination as head of the British army, including the reserve forces. To have preserved Wimbledon for the use of the volunteers would have cost the duke some hundreds a year. But, under the circumstances it really seemed worth while to 1 face the sacrifice. It would not have left his Royal ' Highness altogether penniless. In addition to his annuity of £12,000 a year as a member of the Royal Family, he draws a salary' of .£6,6.32 per annum as Commander-in-Chief, with an additional .C6OO se- , ured for his son Colonel Fitz George, who acts as i rivate secretary. It is out of this splendid income, ayable through many years, that the duke was able to Make a favourable investment in building land on the edge of Wimbledon Common. Some of his tenants threatened to leave if the canny was re- tained. If they carried out their threat the houses might remain empty . or • leasable only at reduced rents. That was more than the gallant soldier could face with equanimity, and sothe volunteers are dis- possessed. It is a pitiful story, so little calculated to strengthen the position of royalty that it would have been werth the while of other members of the Royal Family to have made a jornt subscription and guaranteed the Duke of Cambridge against any monetary loss, if he had left the volunteers undis- turbed. , There has been, a great deal'of gossip about Mr. Tadema's picture. which will be seen at the artist's reception on Sunday. He has been at work on it for more than a year, and has sold it for .46,000. The sum seams enormous. But Tadema got £6,000 for his last year's picture as well, and this one has certainly a great deal more work in it. The subject. is a banquet given by the Emperor Heliogabolus at. which, by a sudden dropping of the awning, the guests were nearly smothered in rose leaves. They are seen in the' picture emerging froixt the pink petals that have come down upon them like an avalanche. The owner celebrated the-completion of this picture by a banquet, to which many eminent lutists wete bidden. The table was strewn with roses, and a chaplet was reserved for the painter, who wets the guest of the evening, ' I hear two per-,
E EAMINER, SATITIMA?, APRIL 7,

• traits painted in America will divide with Mr. Roll's portrait of Mr. Gladstone the public interest at the forthcoming exhibition. I have seen the i latter picture. It s very remarkable in many respects, the head very large, a great look of power, and that peculiar gleam in the eye which seems to strike every painter to Ivhom th 9 ex-Premier has "Aid. (line of the most striking things is the treat- ment of the hands. They are qrong and large, and rather coarse. Other painters, Millais and Rich- mond, have given: Mr. Gladstone the delicate hands of an author or thinker, but these *Mr. Roll has painte I look as if they were wont to grasp the axe.

It is ainong the things noegenerally known that the State keeps One citizen out of the ranks of the unemployed by commending to his care the winding "up of Big Ben, the great four-faced clock flint looks out all over London'frOm the tower that flanks the Houses of Parliament... Not less than 100 guineas a year is paid to an able-bodied man for winding and regulating the clock. The pay is-considerable, but , then, the clock is large. How targe can only be guessed at by persons privileged to climb the tower' and stand face to faCeisliftli, the-Miglifylimekeeper.l .It ia'sorne years sincel idits there. But to this day distinctly remember :the cariousgnovement of the minute hand. as seen from the inside. Its shadow, reflected on the face of the clock, is the size of a, young sapling, and it ' marks the accumulating secofids with a distinct movemelit as if it were, a member of the Irish police bludgeoning a sympa- thiser with an evicted tenant.. • This anonymous gentleman who draws over £2 a week froin the Consolidated Fund for winding, up Big Ben is not nearly as curious' an institution as the Rat Catcher at Buckingham Palace, or his fel- low labourer at Windsor Castle. The Windsor Castle Rat Cateher is ditt cheap. drawing only £lO a year,. a sum so trifling that it might almost be included in the ordinary Civil List: But when that was drawn up, and all the various offices carefully sche- duled, the Rat Catcher as unhappily • forgotten. The Queen's annhal income from the State amounts to £385,000. Of this, the greater part is allotted for the salaries and expenses of the Household. To be precise the Queen's Household expenses amount every year to £303,760, or to be more precise, that. ie the sum that is drawn on this account. If the Rat Catcher at. Windsor „Castle was to 4:paid- by the Queen, clearly this sum 'should bave been £303,770. It was too late to make,the alteration, and accordingly the salary of the Rat Catcher is every year solemnly voted by the House of Com- mons under "Sub Head,A. " of the vote for "Salar- ies, wages, and,allowanees provided for in connec- tion with the Royal Palaces." It is the Rat Catcher at'Buckingliam Palace. ho*ever, whose place, dig- nity, and emolumnts are sufficieqt to make many a mouth water. "It is true that as a Rat Catcher his pay is only .E 8 per annum. But then, he is also Turncabk, for which: he receites £73 a yeari'tci- gether with a residence,. rent free, situated in the very centre of the fashionable; part of .London, in close proximity to the parks, the Houses of Parlia- 'tient, Trafalgar Square, and• the iresidences of the other nobility and gentry..

TITF, LATE RECTOR OF WAR RINGTOg. THE FUNERAL. The- remains of the late Rev. William Quekett, Rector of Warrington. were on Tuesday Interred in the Cemetery. At one o'clock there was a choral service in the Parish church; conducted by Canon Lefroy, Archdeadon of Warrington. Who afterwards read the burial service at the, side a the grave. The, sacred edifice was crowded, many of those Present; being deeply affected. The coffin had been placed' in the chancel on the previous night, and, at the commencement of the solemn service, it was carried to the'ehurch gates, where a procession of surpliced clergy and choristers was formed. The procession, which was headed by the Archdeacon of Warring- ton, was joined by the mourners from the Rectory, then slowly entered the church, the choir singing the hymn commencing,'" When our heads are bowed with woe," The coffin was again placed in the chancel, knd the service was then proceeded with. At its' conclusion t,he " Deed Mareh " in "Saul" was played by the organist, Mr. W. S. Woods. ' The funeral profession was afterwards re-formed out. side the church gates in the' following order :—Messrs- N. B. Percival (rector's warden), R. W. Francomb (people's warden), John Dewhurst and S. Davies (sides. men), and Reid (parish clerk) ; the choir; local and other clergy, including the Revs. Canon Green- all, S. Wilkinson (St. Paul's), W. J. ,Melville (Ashton-iii-Makerfield), H. Monk (Newton-le-Wil- lows), W. H. Williams (radgate), F. Slater (St. James', Latchford), E. Q. E. Carleton (Holy Trinity), G. F. Roberts (18ollinfare), J. G. Richards, (St. Anne's), G. Allton (St. Barnabas') G. D. Wray (St. Peter's), J. Carson (Winwick), G. Feather (vicar of Glazebury, Manchester), J. A. Drummond (curate-in.' charge, St. Elphin's), and the Archdeacon of.Warrifigton; thc hearse bearers who walked three on each side of the hearse; Colonel Greenall, Captain Ridgway, Captain Baynes, and other officers of , the local volunteer corps, who also walked beside the coffin; the late Rector's car- riage • • carriages containing the following mourners Mr. iiiekett (nephew of the deceased), Mr. H. W. Long- den, Bev. W. G. Longden, Mr. R. G. Webster, M.P. (step-son), General Fooks, the Rev.. T. H. Twist, Dr. White (the deceased's medical attendant), Dr. Adams (who had also attended the deceased), and Dr. McFall; the_following members of the Corporation and the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Aldermen Webster; Burgess, and Pickmere,.. And Councillors Greening, Edward Greenall, John Wright T. Litton, U. Dakin, R. W. Marsh, Joseph Taylor, J. Ashton, G. Blackhurst, W. Tinsley, and R. Heaton; the scholars from the Sun- day schools, headed by the following teachers :--Mesfirs. Scotson, Coates, Scarisbrick, Heron, Brookes, John Tay- lor, and R. Lee. There were also a number of private caxrages. Amongst the general public who either walked in procession, attended service in church, or attended at the graveside were :—The Revs. Canon Dodd (vicar of Stretton), T. P. Williamson, H. G. Smith, Canon Hopwood (Rector of Winviick), J. Llewellyn, E. Bigot (a former curate of the Parish Church, but now Rector of the Bishop Lee Memorial Church, Manchester), the Rev, O. E. Young (superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit) ; Messrs. Peter Stubs, John Tinsley, 11. Greenall (who represented the trustees of the Blue Coat School), Alderman Harrison, T. H. Lyon, J. R. Ruckton, E. C. Cooper (Winwick), Edward Rose, Wm. Dooley, Dr. Connell, Wm. Fairhurst, S. Hunt (chief con- stable of Warrington), Charles Hindley (Eccles), Thomas , Robinson, John Walton, F. Taylor, T. Longdin (Borough Surveyor, of Warrington), H. B. White (clerk to the Borough Magistrates), .J. J. . Sanderson, J. Whittle, W. Price, Robert Garnett, George Powlson, James Smet- hurst, R. W. Brundrett, T. Moores, J. Gaskell, John Hat- ton, and many others. At the gates by which the Cemetery is entered detach- ments of the Warrington Volunteer Corps., and of the South Lancashire and /4.h Queen's Own Regiments, of which the deceased Rector had been chaplain, were drawn up as a guard of honour. As the procession entered the cemetery, the choir sang the hymn commenc- ing "Through the night of death and sorrow," and after the by had been lowered into the vault another hymn was sung. On the conclusion of the service, the Archdeacon of Warrington said that it would ill become them to separ- ate on an occasion like that without a few observations, spoken in all humility and sincerity, but yet in weakness. They were gathered together by the open grave of one whom to know was to love. They should miss him in the diocese of Liverpool; they should miss him in War- rington ; and they should miss him in thavarious educa- tional, moral, and religious enterprises in which, so far as his strength permitted, he was up to the last enabled to take a part. But those who knew him in his earlier days would miss him still more. For well-nigh half the allotted period of human life he had laboured in the church. For many of these years he was content to spend and be spent in the service of the Master whose commission he held. Men were asking now, even in the presence of the dead, as well as in the presence of the living, "Is life worthy, or is life worthless ? " As they stand by the grave of him they left in the keeping of our Eternal Father, they were prepared as Christian men to give an answer to these questions, and the answer come from the voice of the Church of Christ. "Life is worthy, and life is worth living." During the service a large concourst of people assem- bled in the cemetery: but the police, under the charge of the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) and inspectqrs Cox and Spinks, kept good order, both in the cemetery and on the route taken by the precession after it left the church. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, of Saukey-street, by whom the coffin .was supplied. It was qf fumed oak, panelled, with brass mountings, and on a massive plate of brass bore the inscription Quekett, Rector of Warring- ton. Died Good Friday, 11Iarch 30th, 1888. Aged 85 years." The vault in which the remains of the deceased- gentleman were interred is situated in a :central 'and con- spicuous position; a few yards behind the fountain. Over it is a monument in early English style. It is 18 feet in height, and is made of • the best Bolton Wend stone. In depth it is 8 feet. , The Monument is a' very handsome one, and is to be enclosed by cast-iron pah- sades. It is the work of Messrs. Essenhigh Bros., of Manchester-road. The following is a list of those who forwarded wreaths, -crosses, or anchors, with which the coffin was covered: Mrs. Quekett, Rev. W. G. and Mrs. Longden andfamily, Mr. R. G. Webster, M.P., Mrs. Peter Rylands, Mrs. Bur- ton, the Rev. G. and Mrs. Feather, Miss Gaskell• Mrs. Woods; Clergy Daughters; Siniday , School Teachers; the Rev. W. Charlton, Mr. and Mrs. Dew- hurst, Mrs. Bolton, Miss Shaw, Miss Crebbin, Mrs. Lyon; Adult members of the choir; Mr. Quekett's old servant, William Hignett ; Scholars of Girls' Sunday School; Miss Slater, Training College; Mrs. Jones, Miss E. Jones (the Elms) ; Superintendent Teachers; Young Men's Class of

Harrison, Miss Malley, Miss liebbington, Major and Mrs. Pickmere, Mr. John Crosfield, MAW Keith, Kirkside, N. 8.; Lady Greenall, Mrs. Hamilton, Mrs. Warrington Wood, Mr. Mr. George Milne, and the Misses Milne. Contributions of flowers were sent by many other parishioners. PUBLIC REFERENCES.

Speaking at the Parish Church on Sunday morning, the Rev. A. Mays, M,A., L.L.8., of Withington, made a brief reference to the'death of the Rector, and preaching at the same church in the evening, the Rev. J. A. Drum- mond, curate in charge, said that though their Rector was dead his works still remained, and his name would ever be remembered in the scene of his early labours, that densely populated part of the Metropolis. . Here, 'too ,the would be remembered as tfieir parish priest, and his venerable form could never fade from their memory. The Rev. J. J. Richards, vicar of St. Anne's, preach- ing on Sunday eVening,. said. that the incalculable amount of goad the late Rector did in his time, the un- conquerable energy he displayed in promoting the in- tertsts of religion and education in spite of well-nigh insurmountable difficulties, the spiritual activity, +which he communicated to dead-alive pardchial organisations. and many other good points, entitled him to respect and admiration

On Easter Day, the Vica; of St. Baxnabas, the Rev. G. Anton made special mention of the death of his aged friend, the Rector of Warrington, :referring tkthe large store of knowledge he possessed, and to his liberal kind- ness and Christian character. . .

At St. Paul's Church on Sunday, at the conclusion of the service in the evening, the Dead March in "Saul" was played on the organ by Alr..l.4ythgoe, and the hell- ringers rang a muffled .peal as a'mark of respect to the rector before and after`the service.

' The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, preaching at iHoly Trinity Church, on Sunday,morning, said the late recto; had been practically laid aside for some time from active work, but his mental faculties remained in unimpaired vigour to the last. The younger generation, of course, could not know what manner of man he was in the days ot his earlier activity and energy, but he had left sub- stantial records behind him; both here and elsewhere, which would speak of his usefulness in life to future enerations: ~g

At a meeting of the parishioners of Christ Church, Padgate, held on Easter Monday, resolution'was,adopted tendering sympathy with the bereaved wife and family of the late rector, and their cordial sympathy in them hour of trial and affliction. • • At the Parish Church vestry meeting, held on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. N. B. Percival, Rector's warden, proposed ," That:this vestry meethrg expresses its heartfelt sorrow at the death of the late Rector, the Rev. Wm.Quekett, and sympathizes with his widow and family in their loss, and assures them that they deeply deplore the decease of their worthy and retected pastor, who had served the church and parish for 34 ,years.”—Alderman Webster, in seconding the proposition, said that there could be no doubt that the Rector as a man who would be very

much missed throughout the diocese. In 'eductional and other institutions he always took the greatest interest; indeed, they knew that he was a man of singular energy and determination.—Mr. J. E Wright supported the resolution, which • was carried unanimously. The fol- Flowing letter has been received by Mr. H. B. White; ivestry clerk, in reply to the foregoing .resolution "Rectory, Warrington, sth April, 1888. Dear' sir,—On behalf of Mrs. Quekett and Mr. Longden, I beg to thank you very much for your not-of yesterday, enclosing the resolution which the vestry were so kind as to pass oh • Tuesday. I,can assure you that such public expression of sympathy is highly appreciated and valued by Mrs. Quekett and also by my wife.--Believe me to remain, dear sir, yours very faithfully, W. G. LONGDEN. H. B. White, Esq." • ' •

• - . HUSBAND AND WIFE. "Why have you drawn all the blinds down, and made sr naturally gloom room look ten times gloomier? There is no sun,' said Lady Vedora, as she came into the Eaton Square library one morning. Amor ma FUNNY BONE.—Is there a single reader of "Little Folks" who does not know what the "funny • bone" is? But why is this bone at the elbow-joint called "funny ?" Those who are learning Latin will find it easy to understand the reason, for they will remember', that huinerus is Latin for ",shoulder." Now, humorous is' English for "funny," and it was out of a play on the two words—which, when pronounced; are almost alike • in sound—that the elbow-bone was named the " funny " bone. Some of you may have heard the conundrum whose answer explains the whole thing. •• Why is the 'funny' bone so called ?" "Because it borders on the " humorous (humerus)."—Little Folks Magazine.

PRANCE.—ANOTHER POLITICAL CRISIS.• Paws MONDAY.—The Ministerial crisis is over, and M. floqq_ct hA9 succeeded in getting together a working dSbinei, three of whose members held office under the late Tirard Ministry. These are Admiral Krantz, who 'remains at the head of the Ministry of Marine, and .eesrs. Loubet and Viette, who maintain respectively 'meat portfolios as Ministers of Public Works and Agri- „selliture. The complete list is as follows: M. Floquet, 1.4-resident of the Council and Minister of the Interior; de Freycinet, Minister of War; M. Goblet, Minister of , L'oreign Affairs: M. Lockroy, Minister of Public Instruc- tion; Admiral Krantz, Minister of Marine; M. Peytzal, , _minister of Finance; M. Loubet, Minister of Public Works; M. Viette, Minister of Agriculture ; M. Richard, t ulster of Justice: M. Legfand, Minister of Commerce; N. Ploquet's present Government is the 24th Ministry Mhich has been formed since the fall of the Empire in 1870. The Parisian public are completely indifferent to the Ministerial crisis. •

GERMANY—THE WititOrt.—AN AMNESTY. , EttuAir, gOND- AY.—The Emperor attended Easter ser- !rice this morning at Charlottenburg, and then drove '•.• Into Berlin with the Empress and the Princesses inclosed •flarriages, the weather being less genial than on FridaY. Majesty first visited the Exnpress Augusta, and then PreeeMed to his own palace, where the rest of the Royal Family. assembled atjunch. On his return to Chattotten- • ,' bitrg the Emperor slept for some time. The amnesty, which appeared late last night, has given great satisfac- tion. The document, which .bas reference only to the Prussian dominions, extends the Royal pardon to offences such as insulting the King or one of the• Royal Family, menacing or using force to members of the legislative bodies to prevent them from diecharginge their duties, tampering with voting papers, accepting bribes, inciting t;o breaches of the law, inciting to mutiny, insult- nag magistrates br ecclesiastics in the performance rif their duty, and offences against the press laws tead the right of assembly. Further, all sentences of im- prisonment for periods of six weeks and under and all ms of 150 marks and under are cancelled, and the con- /acted persons are at once restored to their civil rights. Prince Bismarck to-day celebrated the seventy-third anniversary of his birthday. From an early hour tele- aranhic and epistolary congratulations and gifts of Li °seers have been pouring into the Chancellor's palace. 13 leas than 500 telegrams had arrived by noon. In the • Morning a selection of sacred music was played, before the Prince's residence by a Madgeburg infantry regiment 'Which had been specially sent here for the purpose. The 'Emperor despatched Colonel Broesigke, one of his aides- de-camp, to offer his congratulations to the Chancellor, 'Who was also waited upon by Count Seekendorff, the Chief master of the Household, delegated by the Emperor and Empress conjointly. The Crown Price ' Personally presented his congratulations to Prince Bis- , Merck. CAMPAIGN TN ABYSSINIA. div.head: QUEEN IN 'FLORENCE.
div.p: THE QUEEN IN 'FLORENCE.

s Her Majesty Queen Victoria, with the Prince and Princess Henry of Eattenberg. the Duke of Edin- f.iurgh, Prince Alfred of Edinburgh, the Queen of Servia, and the Grand Duke of Letichtenberg went on Saturday at noon to the Bienllo Institute, and from the windows witnessed the ancient ceremony of the "pp ael Carro." The square of the Duomo in front of the r'st thed ral, where the Bigallo Institute is situated, was iiscorated with rich carpets, which hung from the bal. ,onies, and with a profusion of beautiful flowers. The Marquis Torrigiano' Syndic of Florence, stood by Queen Victoria, and explained the traditional festivity, which interested her Majesty not a little. The cere- mony dates from the time of the Crusades, and the fire which WEIS then used to ignite the powder that in those days destroyed a living dove was always brought from the Holy Sepulchre by a nobleman of the Pazvi family, who were founders of the ceremony, and who left a revenue to maintain it. In the present day a pyrotechnic dove has been substituted for the living bird, and this machine whirrs from the higher altar of the cathedral through the door to the " carro" outside, creating an explosion. It is supposed to be a celebra- tion of the resurrection, and the Florentine peasants have been wont to found upon the success or failure of the explosion their augury of good or bad harvests. The scjuare was on Saturday unusually, crowded, this being the first time that the ceremony has been observed since the new facade of the cathedral was completed. Fresh proofs of the anxiety of the Italians to show every courtesy to the Queen are continually being evinced. Among the bouquets which have been presented was one from the Horticultural Society of Tuscany, corn- Posed exclusively. of flowers grown in the open* air in various parts of the Queen's dominions. The Hima- layas, the plains of India. Burmah, the Cape, and Australasia were all represented. For this attention the Queen, through Sir Henry Ponsonby; signified to the President of the society her gratification. An address has been forwarded through Sir Henry Ponsonby, em- bodying a format expression of respectful homage towards the Queen on the part of the municipal council, speaking in the 'name of the cititsens of Florence, and ex- pressing the pride and honour it is to them to have her in their midst.

div.p: EXTRAORDINARY CAREER OF A • WOMAN.'

About three weeks ago notice was given at the West„ North, and Central Station at Chicago that a detective was wanted immediately at No. 72, Rosebud-street. Officers Kelley and Spierling were summoned, and after some search they found the right number in the little back alley which is named so inappropriately. In a bare rear room on the second floor they found a strange woman. She WAS seated in a broken rocking chair, with a scantily clothed baby in her arms, and a little boy about four years old, with a very ragged jacket on, standing by her side. The womati was very good looking, and chose her words as carefully as a college professor. In a few words she explained that there existed in Chicago an organised band of male and female thieves which confined its operations to the large hotels. Her husband, she discovered months before, WRS a member of such a gang, Elle said, and she then determined to take the first opportunity to notify the police. The officers listened in astonishment while she told the details of her story. She then uncovered a pile of goods in the corner of the room. There-were fine camel's hair blankets, costly linen shirts, empty purses, -a sealskin cap, heavy overcoats, bedspreads, fine soaps, valises, &c. The officers were convinced, and on Mon- day night arrested Frank Emmett, the trusted watch- man at the Sherman House, together with James Boylan and Patrick Needham, an sexel'al ohm <404 Tnen t.sal vmmw'who f4OtiPPrad utTitifiifutecl. sl of the tber big hotels have been systematically robbed by Qevnn of their employes, and the police ,have eecured several waggon loads of goods taken from hotels. The woman, who gave the name of Mrs. James Murray, told the detectives the following story : __ . _

"My maiden name WAS Lizzie JOsqliehine Kerns. My father was Jelin Kerns, who, many years before my birth, was Lord Mayor of Dublin City. I WM born in Dublin, and lived there until I was sent away 14 go_ 2n ;with Tv education. Father was wealthy, and we w 4.0 liappf family. There were six sisters of us. and I was the beauty, and WAS spoiled. In the Ursuuline Convent ef 'Antra I regciyed my instruction in the higher branches in music and painting. Then I was sent to Boulogne, France, where I finished my education. Shortly after my return to Dublin, when I was going out in society a great deal, my father died. While we were all still in mournifig, my mother fell heir to another fortune by the death of a relative in Birmingham. England, Part of the property was a villa and grounds at Aston Park, Birmingham. We moved there the next year. It was a deligloftil place, and my mother still lives there with my sister Beatrice. In that villa I was introduced to James Murray, who was then a wealthy shoe manu- facturer in Limerick. We were married in 1869, by the Right Rev. O'Sullivan, in the Birmingham chapel. We were not very happy together. Two years after our marriage we moved to Philadelphia. My husband is still in that city, a member of the shoe manufacturing firm Of Hayes, Murray, and Co.. located at the corner of Ninth and Market streets. We quarrelled a good deal about. trivial matters. Finally he sent back to Ireland for some of his poor relatives, and they came to live with him. I left the house and went to New York. He 'commenced divorce proceedings on the ground of desertion, and was granted a bill. In New York I was without a friend, and was soon out of money, and was forced to go to a cheap hotel, and I went to the St. Omer. Frank Emmett was a porter in the hotel. When I was taken sick be be- friended me. When I recovered my health I commenced living with him. That was four years ago. • Wail we moved to Chicago I belimd him to be strictly honest. We w_oq,l:4 irlabek but that as a Catholic I Fait the wife of James Murray, the millionaire, to this day, in spite of the decree." nult et:Beers who have investigated the case have found many corioacing t 4 circumstances which convince theta) of the truth of Nu 1 urray's story.

A large gang of masked alio armed "Moonlighters" visited, on Sunday night, the house of a dairyman named Thornton, at Ballyhootoilet); Cork. They fired into the house, and, bursting the door, savagely assaulted Thorn- ton and his son, at the same time extorting a promise from Thornton to give no the dairy to another man. , WM. O'BRIEN, Mr., ATMITCHRLSTOWN. ' Mr. Wm. O'Brien, M.P., accompanied by Mr. T. M Healy, M.P.; on Monday addressed a meeting of his con- stituents at Mitehelstown. Several thousand persons attended, most of whom wore League cards in their hats. . A Government reporter and District Inspector were allowed seats on the car. No police force was present, and there was no disturbance. The Rev. Father d'l),,er,gliue presided. Mr. O'Brien said if the right of ,publin meeting were asserted everywhere in lrelsnd with the same determination as at Youghal they would soon cure stipendiary magistrates of their theory that they could suppress whole communities it the instigation of secret societies. He reviewed the position of the tenants, and said in Mitchelstown they, had got relief without Mr. Balfour's mid, and in spite of Mr. Balfour. Referring to Mr. Balfour's statement that • the League was a thing of the past in proclaimed dis- tricts, he said the Chief tieeretary was either the most audacious liar that ever swore the lid off a pot, or else he was the "roost arrant donkey that ever floundered up to his neck in any Irish bog.

Ta Wzran GOLD DISCOVERT.—Mr. Morgan, of the Dolgelly gold workings, states that on Monday he ob- tained 628 ounces of gold from 334 tons of quartz, being the cleaning up of the last fortnight. This result is highly satisfactory, as it equals those of the best gold mines in the world, the average being nearly two ounces to the ton, and less than a quarter of an ounce paying the cost of production. ALARMING FIRE IN A DEAF AND DUMB INSTITUTION.-- ATI alarming fire occurred on Saturday night in the pre- mises of the Deaf and Dumb Institution at Langside, Glasgow. About 100 inmates were in the institution at the time. These were all removed to a place of safety amid a scene of great excitement. Happily, the flames were prevented from spreading, although a considerable portion of the roof had fallen in before the arrival of the Glasgow Fire Brigade. ' MURDER OF A FOREMAN AT BARNSTET.—On the 21st ult. a foreman at. the brickworks of Messrs. Chamberlain at Barnsley, named Burrage, had occasion to discharge a labourer named Richardson. The man went home, and after a time returned to the works and shot Burra,,..oe in the head and the abdomen with a revolver. He then walked to the police station in company with one of his emmoiers and gave himself into custody. From the first there was no exception that Burrage would recover, hut though shot in such a vital part he did not die till Sunday afternoon. Richardson now stands charged with murder.

A Summons Doo.—A striking instance of the instinct or sagacity in a dog was exemplified at the close of last week, when an animal returned from Manchester to its former home at Staveley; near Kendal. About a fort- night ago a farmer living at Staveley sold a collie to a Manchester butcher, and the dog was forwarded by train. It was observed, however that the collie was un- easy and dissatisfied with its new home, and one morn- ing it was missed. The animal had made the whole of the journey, about 76 miles, on foot, snd was lying on the doorstep when the farmer opened the door in the morning. . .

SAD DROWNING CASE: Two LIVES Lost —A distressing fatality occurred on Monday at Upper Caterham. A party, consisiing of Mr. Burt, picture frame maker, Croydon, his wife, his son (aged 12 years), and his niece (aged 18) were driving hotne,through Upper Caterham, when they came to a very large pond. Mr. Burt let the horse go towards the pond for a drink. The bank at the spot is very steep, and a man seeing their danger shouted to them, but was too late. The horse slid down the bank, pulling the vehicle and its occupants into 20ft. of water. Mrs. Burt and her son at once sank and were &owned. Mr. Burt and his niece were rescued, in an exhausted state, the latter being for some time unconscious. .-- DISF:4IItaNG A 1 ACTRESS.—Screams from a carriage driven ,at furious rate of speed. startled punplelir Springfield, Missouri, recently. , The re! kle • was pur- Ailed by the, poiice and citizens, and, when stopped, a young woman was found with blood streaming from her head and face, groping blindly for the door. The other occupant was Pr. 'George M. Cox, a United States pinkion examiner for that district. •He stepped 1 out of the Carriage, and gave himself up to • the : police. A year ago Dr. Cox's son becarne infatuated ,with the young woman, Miss Effiie Ellis, of St. Louis, and declared he would marry her in spite of his family'w strenuous opposition. She was an actress of great beauty, and he followed her about the country, spending a great deal of money. She went to Springfield in response to repeated telegrams signed in young Cot's name, but sent by the father, who met her with a carriage. As they drove along he seized her, and when she begged him not to kill her he said, "I'll not kill you. I'll do worse. I'll disfigure the beauty that led my son s way ! " Iler eyes are burned out, and she will probably die. The mob would have lynched the doctor but for t lie intervention of the police.

AND me Maas.—Writing in reference to the fund being raised to'wards defraying the damages and costs in which Mr. Pickard, M.P., was recently •mulcted at the Yorkshire Assizes, in an action for. libel, Mr. Samuel Plimsoll, ex-M.P. for • Derby, says t•-•-•'! I re- member the time, years ago now, when I had received notices of 12 actions for libel—three of whicl . were in lull swing in tile courts, and which were, no doubt, intended to ruin me. At that time of anxiety the working men came to -my ald with wonderful liberality, and the colliers with what may truly be called munificence, especially when it is borne in mind that every shilling they contributed represented from an hour to Om hour and a half's downright hard labour. I bee your acceptance of the enclosed cheque for £2OO. I also enclose a second cheque for £2OO, to he used either wholly or in part, in case your subscriptimis should fall short of the needs of the ease. The colliers stood by me in the hour,of need, and I with to stand by them now in the person of their worting representative, Mr. Pickard. They are noble Seßows, the colliers—a•full third of them at this moment :ire uncomplainingly supporting aged parents or orphaned brothers and sisters, as would be proved again next week in case of the occurrence of an explosion.'

Tns GOOD TEsrerAsts.—The nineteenth annual session of the Grand Lodge of the Independent Order of Good Templars was commenced at Sunderland on Mornip.y a We- . noon. There was a large attendance of delegates from all parts of England. 'Mr. Malins, the president. in his report on the. state of the Order, said that £7,000 had been promised tovvargs the fund of £lO,OOO being raised for special mission work. At the last annual session a serious decrease of lodges and members as shown, but now the tide had turned.' With regard to the County' Government Bill, he protested against the proposal to tax the people to compensate publicans whose licenses Were ' not again issued. The proposal was most startling, and was based upon the assumption that license-holders already had a vested interest in their licenses. The annual balance-sheet showed a small excess of income over expenditure.—The session was resumed on Tuesday, and among the distinguished visitors present were Bro. W. W. Turnbull, Chief Officer of the International Court; and the officers'of the Grand Lodge of Scotland. The report a the G.W.C.T., dealing with the state of the Order in several districts, was considered and adopted, and a discussion on the political action of the Order occupied the remainder of the morning sitting. At the afternoon sitting a protest was, submitted by Bro. Boyd (Sheffield) from 200 Grand Lodge members, against one of the terms of reunion of the Order, which provides for dual Grand Lodges where difficulties of ram prevent united working. The protestors prayed the Grand Lodge to retrace its steps, and hold firm. to the principle of the brotherhood of man. Consideration of the protest was deferred. The officers' reports were considered, and generally adopted. '

THE LATE RECTOR.
