THE WATCH COMMITTER.-DHLININNNESS IN THE

.. .....-.......—.. . The Watch Committees minutes mentioned the fact that a deputation, consisting of the Rev. John Yonge, Messrs. E. 'rwiss, J. H. Gornall. J. Walker, and ri.. Roberts, had waited upon it and presented a memorial calling attention to the words of Mr. Justice Grantham, at Liverpool, and expressing a hope that the Committee would impress upon the police the importance of endea- vouring to trace each case of drunkenness to its source, and of prosecuting, whenever possible, the publican who serves drunken people with intoxicating liquor. It may be lidded that the full text of the memorial was given in our columns two or three weeks ago. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor JOLLEY seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON said it was shown in the minutes that the Chairman of the Committee had saidlthat he "quite agreed with the deputation that while drunken- ness amongst men was diminishing, the same vice amongst females was increasing, which would probably be accounted for by the alleged facilities afforded by the holders of ' off-licenses ' to their female customers in supplying them with beer and charging for the same to their husbands under the head of provisions, &c." He differed from this statement, and he pointed out that in the statistics presented by the Chief Constable for 1880-88 the number of females proceeded against during the present year was very much below the average. For the last year 204 females had been proceeded against, in 1885, 240, and in 1883, 238. ,He should like to know how the conclusion was arrived at that drunkenness amongst females was on the increase. There was a mean and dirty insinuation that this drunkenness was probably to be accounted for by the alleged facilities "afforded by the holders Of off-licenses," but there was no proof of this insinuation because the class of Peopld who were repeatedly convicted ta?ore the magistrates were not people to get bqeS Which was charged to their husbands .711 rider the head ef provisions, becyjuse a..,.Ertt,.m...aig of itiratill4illa OaNduSed Ictrgesizlo.e.f vtlt i-i-rifar gego"t"oTePUlnlo-- lic, for they all knew the unscrupulous manner of the teetotallers In using statements of this kind. (Hear, hear, and "question.") They would gladly ignore the word " probably," and use it as a direct assertion that this drunkenness had been caused by the off-licenses. Then with regard to the statement of the Chairman of the Committee "that the Watch Committee in the ap- pointment of new police officers usually inquire from the appliCants if they were total abstainers always com- , Mending those that were," he (Councillor .Bolton) , thought that instead of having a teetotal police Ante I 1 there were only one or two professedteetotallers amongst' ' the policemen. That also was a statement which, he thought, had no right to be put on the minutes. As the minutes of the Watch Committee were not open to the discussion of the Council, he did not know what to do with them—(laughter)—but he thought that on the Whole it was a very discreditable report. , Ho left it to the honour and integrity of the Council not to let that thing go to the general public without a .ffistinct denial. Alderfnan CROSFINLD was very much pleased to see that the Watch Committee received the deputation with such courtesy and consideration. He had sat on the bench of magistrates, and he knew the difficulty there was in convicting publicans of breaking the law. Of course, the matter was beyond the power of the Watch Committee, as it was the law of the land that a license must be endorsed three times before it could be forfeited. They drove a coach and six through that Act of, rarlia- menV without any difficulty, because if a publican had his license endorsed he had to walk the plank the net day; a fresh man was put in his place, and he had to be- gin with a clean sheet. The Council would see, there- fore, that it was perfectly impossible to get a license en- dorsed three times over. He Could understand Mr. Bolton speaking feelingly about the matter, but he must tell him that he thought the general public considered that there were sadly too many cases of drunkenness in the town, both amongst men and women, and that the number of prosecutions of publicans, in proportion to the ' number of people brought up for drunkenness, was re- -1 markably small. The Watch Committee said Warring- ton appeared third on the list of all the towns they men- -1 ttpned in Lancashire, but he did not think that it was any credit that it appeared third on the list. He thought it a disgrace to all the towns in Lancashire, because the' were quite certain that if there were 12'- -00 e ..., cakii oi drunkenness in Liverpool,' there must linve been more than fve cases where publican!: 'dad disobeyed the law in giving n'z_4lk l 0 . a man already under its influence. He was talking oil Meriday to an American who had lived in New York a great many years, and he told him that if a publican there was in the habit of giving drink to a ma,n who was intoxicated, in the leltst degree, the wife of that man could go to the publican tiod say, "If ' you give my husband any more drink I will report you ;" and so strong was the law that if the man did so after the wacning he lost his licens(il voice : Drunk or m.iber ?)—No, if it was gi,ipri to the husband when he We under the influence of licmOr or approaching a state of intoxication, the publican would lose his license, and the evidence of any one in the bar would be taken as suffi- cient.. The law of this country was very loose in com- parisan to the American law. They were all anxious for the respectability of the town and that there should bei less drunkenness both amongst the men and the women,' and he thought most of them-would agree with him that the Act which was passed for giving licenses to grocers had been proved to be mostrhischievous and injurious to the nation at lArge. He hoped that when the Local Go- vernmentlffil was passed they would see the abolition of grocers' licenses. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then passed. STREET LILPROVEHISNT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. •

_ ' , Th.is committee recommended the approval of the fol- lowing plans :—Three cottages in Gaskell-street, for Mrs Porter ; three houses in Latchford-road for Mr. J. Leigh. Also that the sum of £lO-be paid to the Warrington Co-operative Society for a strip of land containing 10 8-9 yards in Winwick-street. Councillor GREENINO moved the adoption of the minutes. Councillor DixoN asked when they could have the coat of lighting the streets reduced from £2,859. Alderman lltzaoxss said if he was rightly informed they paid the same price per street lamp to-thy as they 'paid in 1847 when the town was incorporated, while the price charged to private consumers was, he believed, just half what it was in 1847. He thought there was some- thing that wanted looking into in the matter and he was not sorry that Councillor Dixon had called atten- tion to it.

Councillor GREENING in replying, said the price of street lighting would be reduced as soon as it was pos- sible to reduce it. They had considered that matter in committee and ,they had had a report as to the cost of .lighting various towns in Lancashire and Cheshire and elsewhere, and this showed that the cost in Warrington was lower than in most and a very great deal lower than., in some. Mr. Paterson had also always assured them that the price paid per lamp, although it was the same as in 1847, was less than the cost. The minutes were then confirmed. SANITARY COMMITTEE. ESTIMATE OF EXPENDITURE, LONDFORD DEPOT, Sze.• The minutes of this committee contained the following items :—That the tender of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, and Co., be accepted for the repairs of the dryer at Longford. That the following letter from the Wa ring- ton Slate Co., Limited, be entered on the minutes, and that it be recorded that the ,statement made by Mr. Councillor Dixon therein contained is absolutely Un- true—

Warrington, March 12th r 1888. Alderman John Bur- gess, J.P., chairman of the Sanitary Committee. Dear sir,—At a meeting of the Ratepayers' Association, held ongliursday evening last, Councillor F. Dixon is repor- ted in the "Warrington Examiner" of Saturday, the 10th inst., to have made the following statement Councillor Dixon complained that when he made his proposition in the Council with regard to the sale of manure to the Warrington Slate Company, he could get no one to second it. In his calculation, from the way the markets had turned the Slate Company would clear from £6OO to £1,000." We shall be glad if you will take such steps as are necessary to refute this grossly untrue and • mischievous statement. —Yours truly, for the Warrington Slate Company, Limited, HENRY Roamers, Managing Director. 21st March, 1888. The fol- lowing is a summary of the estimated expenditure of the committee for the twelve months commencing 26th March, 1888, viz.:—Scavenging department, £2,792 14s; nightsoil departinent, £3,014 Ss 6d; Longford depot department; £1,762 14s 6d; intercepting depots department, £546 *los ; hospital, £1,136 12.;; total, £9,252 165.--This committee having had under their consideration the representations of their Medical Officer

of Health on the subject of the registration of disease, are of opinion that a system of central registratlon of in- fectious disease is desirable, similar to that of the Regis- trar General in respect of deaths, whereby sanitary authorities of one "notification town" may be warned in time of the• approach of any infectious dis.gee from other towns. And this committee therefore respectfully I urges the Local Government Board to undertake the I collection and publicalion of weekly returns of infectious disease for all the toUns which are provided with legal powers for the compulsory notification of infectious dis- ease.—The Town Clerk having reported that the order of tho Town Council under the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879, extending the powers of that Act with reference to the compulsory notification of infectious disease to meo.sles and whoop- ing cough, would expire on the 31st March, 1888, it was resolved that the order be not renewed, and that the Town Clerk give notice to that effect to the medical practioners in the town. Alderman Boaanss, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Committee, said he Wished first of all to make an announcement, namely, that at an early period —it might be before the next meeting ot the Council or it•might be after—when their arrangements had • been completed, a sanitary scheme would be brought before the Council that would relieve the town of some danger and the committee of some difficulty. The matter could then be discussed and dealt with thoroughly, 'and, he hoped a correct decision would .be arrived at. (Hear, hew.) The Mayor had given a promise to the effect that a special meeting pf the Council should be called. He did not think a qttestion of the magnitude of the expen- diture oh sanitary matters could be properly dealt with at an ordinary meeting of the Council, when other busi- ness had to be transacted. , (Hear, hear.) He congratu- lated the Council on the fact that there was a reduction this year in the rate of 6d in the pound. He held in his hand a list which had been prepared by Mr. Chorley—a very valuable list—of the rates that had been required I from the ratepayers of Warrington for the past 30 years, commencing in 1857, and finishing in 1886. He found that during the 30 years there were only four When the rate was less than it was this year, 1888-9. There was only one year in which the rate was precisely the same, and for 25 years out of the 30 the rate had been higher than they were having this year ; in some instances it had been very much higher. In 1858 the rate was 6s 4d, in 1881 6s Bd, and in 1882 6s 6d, so that.the rates had been heavier a great deal than they were now. H. begged to congratulate the Town Council and the ratepayers that so much less money would be required this year, and he hoped. he might indulge in a little pardonable pride in believing that the Sanitary Committee werecon- tributors to the reduction of the rate. (Hear hear.) It was a justifiable bit of pride. Aid. Burgess then referred in detail to the estimate of expenditure. With refer- ence to the Longford depOt they orpended more last year than they estimated for by, he thought, about 000. The machinery at Longford haddone its work admirably, and it had not failed them in one point, and the result of their labours, taken altogether, was very satisfactory. But he was free to admit that while the machinery had done its work the results were somewhat disappointing. (Hear, bear.) ' there were two things' he had to admit to the Council. In the first &ice, they did not get as much finished material as they were entitled to; and in the second place, the cost at which they werp made to work was more than they ought to pay. They had found during the present year a leakage, which applied, he believed, to every,works of the kind in the kingdom. They knew where it was, and they knew how it was brought about, and having that lznowledge—well, it Would be very hard indeed if they did not rectify it with the concurrence of the Council. He was as though they were, • ' . opeaking now They to deni With the matter. t °Ale 4') ; Ito could het tell. Evil might weiipon the way, but if they were intrusted with the carrying out of the work the Council might expect— and they had a right to do so—that there should be a larger production and a somewhat diminished cost. Mr. Pierpoint had asked him about a statement he proposed to make. They had been preparing it for a long time; or rather he should say it was not a preparation of their own. The work was in other hands; and they did not intend to come iq an unprepared state to the Council. Mr. Pierpoint, he was afraid, took Umbrage at one meet- ing at what he thought was a curt observation of his— that he (Alderman Burgess) Would supply the informa- tion asked for when it suited his convenience. He though p Mr. Pierpoint had known him long enough to believe that that was i simply a joke; but he was sorry to find that he gave a vote n consequence which was prejudicial to a very worthy man. Alderman Burgess.l next referred to the dryer for the repair of which they had accepted a tender. It was a Firman's dryer I and they .invited tenders from Warrington firms, Man- I love, Aloft and Co. also tendering, for the repairs. One, of three Warrington firms did not reply at all; the DaUa.m Forge people declined to undertake the work, and Jones and Co. tendered at £55. The tender of Messrs. Manlove and Co. was £49 10s, and as it was the lowest the work was given to them. It was gratifying to them as a committee to know that the work at Long- ford was so satisfactory. The resolution of the 14th March, he thought, explained itself. They had a letter addressed to them by the managing director of the Slate Company/in which he complained of what Mr. Councillor Dixon had said at a public meeting in the town— Councillor :J. PIEIZPOINT : Of the Ratepayers' Associa- tion. . . . . .

Alderman BURGESS: Well, it might be a meeting of that magnificent association. (Laughter.) He knew something about them; he wanted to see their balance sheet, and it would comesome day he supposed. (Laugh- ter.) He was told that the subscriptions were falling I off. But all that went for nothing, but still he should like to see their balance sheet. (Laughter and hear, hear.) The 'Slate Company might have transactiTas with the Corporation, but it they made £6OO, or pi ,000 profit out of a £1,200 or £1,300 cont- little for the members of the C 0..- with ard odi -met 't said very tnanner in which th-- ' ;eg to the their bus . trarigacted iness and parted wi+' Ho- .•4.1 their property. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) wever, the fact was, that the Slate Company, instead of making a profit of £6OO or £l,OOO, found that the sum of £4O was the outside of all the profit they could have.; but if they Made a bad debt on five tons Of manure their profit Was gone. (Hear, hear.) ' Alderman Ceosner.P, in seconding the adoption, re- minded the Council that the Sanitary Committee had been carrying out what they might call a new experi- ment, and when a man.was in a manufacturiog business and tried something new which nobody, had ever tried before, he would find out very often that if he had estimated the cost at about £5OO or £l,OOO, it would cost him about £3,000. He might tell them, as a case in point, that his firm had been trying a new pr. es. 4 which had never before beenused in thiskmgdom. He estimated that the cost would not be more than £5OO. but he found to his sorrow that it cost exactly £3,000. Whether they would get any benefit trona it or riot remained to be seen. Be wanted, therefore, the Council to give the Sanitary Committee as much credit as they could for being actuated simply by a desire to imprtrve the - town and save the ratepayers expense. (Hear, hear.) He had always said of that committee thee .they were bound, as rduch as any pri- vate individual, not to create any nuisance. However, he must admit that the Longford works were for a long time a nuisance. His friend, Mr. Worsley, had complained of it to him many a time, and he always admitted that he had a right to complain. At that time, he supposed, there were a thousand tons of raw refuse Mixed with cinders in the yard at Longford. There it was seething and making a most abominable'stench, which was carried by the wind right across Winwie-k-road. That state of things had now Ipeen changed. Everythingthat went to kLongford now was kept -away from the atmosphere, and was not allowed to come into contact with it until con- verted into a dry manure fit to go Out. Therefore he said that no one now had any: reason to complain that the Longford depot was a nuisance. _ There had, how- ever, been some complaints made within the last two or three weeks, and very properly made too, that the nuis- ance had arisen again. That was owing to the dryer having broken down. In consequence of that mishap. a lot of the raw excreta had to be sold to the farmers direct, without its being manufactured into manure. The consequence was that the farmers came and took it away, and one of them actually stored a lot in a field by the side of the Winwick-road, and naturally, as Mr. Worsley termed it, "it was something awful." That, as he had said, was-brought about by the breaking of the machinery, and that was a point which Alderman Bur- gess would bring before them at the special meeting to which reference had been made • and lie should be very much surprised if, after they had heard a full statement of the matter, they did not see the necessity of duplica- ting some portion of the machinery. He felt sure that their own sense would tell them that it was the right thing to do. (Hear, hear.) He was reading on Monday a report by Mr. Taylor, whb was the father of the pail system at Rochdale, and, without boasting at all, or pro- fessing that they knew more than anyone else, any un- prejudiced person would admit that they in Warrington had succeeded better than the people at Rochdale had. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Taylor contended that the decrease in the death-rate owing to the adoption of their system was equal in money value, in life alone, irrespective of the saving of expense, to £36,000. Well, if it was £36,000 in Rochdale, the saving in Warrington must be at least £50,000. (Hear, hear.) That was entirely outside the saving they effected in the collection of the excreta. He simply told them those facts in order that they might consider the matter further, and he hoped that whenever the special meeting of the Council was held they would all come prepared to go into the question with an un- biased and fair judgment. (Applause.) Councillor F. A. Ronstrrswas anxious t,oknow whether Alderman Burgess considered that the sunis put down in the estimates for repairs at Longford and the intercepp- ing depots were sufficient in amount to put that ma- chinery, at the end of the financial year, in the same state of preservation as it was to-day? He believed it was false economy on the part of the Corporation to al- low their Machinery to get into insufficient repair be- cause of the expense it would entail in the ratepayer of the day. (Hear, hear.) Couneillor Bot Torr objected to having the rates raised. They were doing enough for posterity already. They were buying the gas works for them. (Laughter.) Alderman Burgess had said that the rates were so very easy to pay, and were so much less than they were 30 years ago, but he forgot the rateable value was perhaps

double what it was in years past. Let them have both sides of the question. Councillor MONKS remarked that there was no one who knew the difficulties which the Sanitary Committee had to grasp better than he did ; and he gave them every credit for doing the work which they had. (Hear, hear.) It had beena very king and arduous task, and one whichliad caused the expenditure of a great deal of time and thought; and he had been very, glad to hear the Chairman that night express the conclusion of his own mind, They were the conclusions at which he (Council- lor Monks) had arrived four or five years ago, namely, that the results were disappointing, and the cost greatly 'in excess of what was anticipated. That was the key of the whole matter. (Hear, hear.) Their first estimate was very disappointing, and he had thought that the Committee would have profited by that experience in submitting the estimates in 1884 for the extension of the depot. He hoped that in the forthcoming report the Chairman would give the results of the work which was being done, that was the quantity of stuff delivered and the quantity of material manufactured from it, and if he did, then he should not move the resolutioni of which he had given notice. He was sorry that the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee took credit for any reduction in the rate, for facts would not bear out the statement. In- stead of the estimates of the Sanitaryrommittee decreas- ing, they s'ere constantly increasing. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Wm. PIERPOINT said with regard to the letter from tne Warrington Slate Company, Limited, he said he did not quite see what the Council had to do with a matter which occurred outside. (Hear, hear.) It *as he must admit, connected with them in some measure, but still he thought if they allowed the matter to pass in the minutes of the dommittee such expressions as "grossly untrue" applied to a member of thh Council were not quite what he oouid ' agree with. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that Councillor Dixon would be able to give them some explanation which would enable the Council either to alter those words or to expunge the letter altogether. (Hear, hear.) Councillor DIXON said that since the contract was entered into between the• Sanitary Committee and the State Company the market rate of sulphate of ammonia had gone up £2 per ton. Therefore if the Warrington Slate Company got 500 tons, which he supposed was a 'year's make, and the difference was £2 a ton, did not that come-to very nearly £1,000? (Laughter.) Councillor HENRY ROBERTS remarked that the chair- man of the committee had told them that any member of the Council could ascertain for himself at what price the contract was let. Many members of the Council had done so, and if Councillor Dixon had been at all anxious to have obtained the same information he could have ob- tained it, and he would not then have made the ridicu- lous statements which he had. It was also stated at the time that the contract was not for /2 months, but for a. period of four months only. Councillqr Dixon's explana- tion was about on a par with the usuid style of explana- tion he made in that Council when he was challenged to give a reply to statements he had prhyiously made. Alderman Braeass having replied, the minutes were confirmed,
•A
PAVING AND SENCEOADE COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this Committee contained a recom- mendation that a fresh agreement be entered into be- tween the Corporation and the Clerk of the Pear:. of Lancashire for the repair of the lower street from the centre of Warr;- of three years at a sum of ' .-Eogtfin tridge for a period of condolence on the . leis per annum; also a vote whose"'- -. cleft% bf the late councillor Brown, • . engem on the Committee Councilor Monks .had liven elected to fill. The yearly estimate of expenditure ' of the Committee (24,950) contained £5O for' the remo- val froth Friaee-green yard to Howley, and £3OO for preparing the land at Howley, with fence. Councillor WRIGHT proposed the adoption 'of the minutes, and, referring to the vote of condolence passed to the family of the late Councillor Brown said that Mr. Brown had been a most attentive and useful member of the Committee. With regard to the estimates he re- marked that the Committee were only £5O in excess of last year in what they required. They expended £450 last year on a steam roller, but notwithstanding that had undersvent their estimate. Councillor MARSH having seconded the proposition, the minutes were confirmed.
TOWN HALL, PARK, AND. BATHS CONHITTEN.

This -committee recornmended that the baths be re- opened forthwith, and that the alterations • be deferred until the end of the bathing season The minutes were confirmed on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor .1. PIERPOINT.

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that a suitable address be presented to Mr. Gilbert Greenall on his coming of age, and that the Mayor and Aldermen Webster ad Burgess be appointed a committee to arrange for the pfe- paration of the address. • , The minutes were adopted, on the proposition of the MAyon, seconded by Councillor FRANCOMB.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTER.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTER.

The Finance Committee, recommended that Councillor Monks be one of its members in place of the late Coun- cillor Brown. Its minutes also contained the following *commendations :—That calls be made on the overseers of he townships of Warrington and Latchford, on borough rate account, for the sum of £9,331 Os ld, pay- able by two half-yearly instalments. That the loinance Committee be authprised to make an improvement rate for the year commencing 26th March, 1888, at 2a 6d in the pound, to be collected by two half-yearly instal- ments, which is estimated to produce about £14,400. That a sewers rate be made for the year commencing 26th March, 1888$ at 4d inthe wound, to be Collected by two le-yearly instalments, which is estimated to pro- ce about £1,984. The adoption of the minutes having been proposed by Alderman HOLMES, and duly seconded, Councillor F. A. ROBERTS asked how it was that in the estimate given in the committee's minutes the sum of 1E2,268, for the purchase of land in Howley, was put down as last year's revenue. It appeared in the ininutee as a credit for the corning year. Alderman HOLMES, in reply, ssid that it was the inten- tion of the Finance COMMittee to borrow the money. It was expenditure on capital account, which , it was thought theyatepayers at present should not bear out of their wa pocket, and it was therefore agreed to boy- row the miney. hoped, however, that it would not be necessary to borrow, the whole a The minutes were then confirmed. THE SSTISIATES. The estimates of expenditure of the various committeei for the year commencing 26th March, 1880, were as 'fol- lows :—Watch Committee, £2,329 14s; Street Improve- ment and Lighting Committee, £3,290; Sanitary Com- mittee, £92g2165 Paving and Sewerage Committee, £4,950; School Attendance Committee, £345; Ceme- tery Committee, £531 ; Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee, £1,929 17s 9d (inchiding £4OO for taking down of wall in front•of Town Hall) ; Markets Commit- tee, £1,131 us; Fire Engine, £243; General Purposes Committee, £1,120 7s 4.d; Finance Committee, £5,609 Os 2d. They were all adopted. Formal resolutions empowering the levying of borough, improvement, and general sewers rates having been passed, the Council rose.

div.head: JOKE WIIICH BROUGHT TEARS TO HIS EitS.
div.p: A JOKE WIIICH BROUGHT TEARS TO HIS EitS.

Tlwee commercial travellers sat over their wine and cigars. one day after dinner, in a comfortable inn in Devonshire.. They were "jolly good fellows," knowing each other as Tom, Dick, and Harry. After comparing notes on the state of trade, etc., jokes and stories went around, till, at last, Tom and Dick began chaffing Harry on the shabby condition, of his head, for his hair was fast falling Out, and the sparse quantity he still retained was rutite gray; and both de- clared he had deceived them concerning his age, for his scanty gray hairs proved that he had already "fallen into the sear— the yellow leaf.' Dick declared that ise.knew of a sureremedy. Harry innocently and anxiously inquired what It was. Dick told him, Cut half a dozen red .onions into thick ;Rees; rub your head thoroughly with them, and--leaving the Brims on your head—sit in the hot sun for three hours l' "Nonsense!" Harry objected. "Well, if you don't choose to try it, go bald I " Harry secretly resolved to try it. and did. The next day his mischtevous friends spied him sitting in the sun, in the stable yard, his head plastered with onions, his eyes full of their juice, and streaming with tears. The shout they set up told Harry that he was sold, and but for Tom's interfeeence Dick's head would have stood in need of a plaster. Dick apologised, and made amends by informing Harry of the ' admirable qualities of Mrs. S. A. Allen's Wprld's Hair Re- storer, which never fails to restore the hair to its natural oolour, prevents it from falling out, and gives it the luxuri- ance and silken glossiness of youth. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the world. It should always be kept on the toilet table for dressing the hair. It is delicate and agreeable. • .

A New York Correspondent telegraPhs that the strikes on the lines 'connected with the Burlington Rail- way have collapsed, the men having returned to work unconditionally. In the French Clamber, on Wednesday, DI. Maine, an Opportunist, was elected Speaker. There was a tie be- tween him and M. Clemenceau each obtaining 168 votes. F. Moline was declared elected by seniority. it was resolved at the resumed Conference of elernen-1 •tary teachers at !Cheltenham on Wednesday that , the subscriptions to the Union should be increased, in order to raise a fund for securing the return to Parliament of a practical teacher. Speaking •at a Liberal meeting at Nottingham, on Wednesday,. Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P. pointed out how, in relation to Parliamentary Procedure and the Oaths BiU, the Conservatives had lately supported what they formerly opposed. The Liverpool carriers met on Tuesday, and pasped a resolution protesting against the proposed wheel tax as an impost on trade commerce, and locomotion, and con- trary to all principles on which recent legislation had 'been based, and as a retrograde movement. By the burning of a barn and granary, at Long Mars- ton, near York, on Tuesday mowing, a man unknown was burnt to death. Three cows and a calf were also ' destroyed by the flames, which are suppcsed to have been accidentally caused by the man who lost his life. MR. GILBERT GREENALL'S BIRTHDAY. A WEEK OF REJOICING.

The week that is just closing has been one of great rejoicing in the villages that owe allegiance to the residents at Walton Hall, and the tenantry •of the Walton estates have been, making merry in a vigorous fashion. As most -people' in this neigh- bourhood are by this time aware, the eldest and only son of the member for Warrington attaiked his majority nn Good Friday, and in celebration of the auspicious occasion, festivities on an extensive scale have taken place. The unfortunate accident that Sir Gilbert Greenall met with on the very day on which his son came of age prevented his much- desired presence at them, but Lady Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, and the other members of the family have been kepi pretty busy receiving the congratulations of their friends, and various sub- stantial tokens of regard in addition.

TREAT TO COTTAGERS. The festivities commenced in good earnest on Monday,pn the eveniag of which day a tea add enter- tainment were giyen to the cottagers and their wives at Sessions House, Daresbury. Nearly eighty cottagers • from Daresbury, Newton-by-Daresbury, and Hatton, were present, and amongst them was a man who, locally, is considered of some note. This was Mr. Thos. Houghton, who, during a forty-five years' service as parish clerk, has never one,e been absent from his duty. It is also claimed as a distinction that the office of sex- ton has been retained in his family for several genera- tions. Hqst Philips. of the Ring o' Bells Inn, Daresbury. I set a good -knife and York tea on the tables, and assistance ws rendered in the way of helping the guests by Mr. I John White, Mr. T. Smith Burgess, Mr. John Cooper, I and others. Later on, after the creature wants had been attended to, there was the entertainment, at which Mr. John White was in the position of chair- man, and duly submitted the loyal toast of "The Queen." Songs and sperwles, intermixed, followed and soon after the proceedings commenced the Misses Greenall, Mrs Whitley, Miss Cunliffe, Mr. Gilbert Green- all, and Mr. John Whitley, graced the gathering by their presence. The Rev. Thomas Whitley was also there. After Mr. J. Mercer (Warrington), and Mr. E. A. Wal. lington (Sutton), had contributed songs, Mr. Jolts Funs- STON, an inhabitant of Daresbury for over thirty years, proposed the health of "Mr. Gilbert Greenall." • In doss mg so he expressed the hope that Mr. Gilbert would be a better man than his father—s sentiment that may be taken in more ways than one, but was evidently not meant to be uncomplimentary to Sir Gilbert. Mr. Furm- ston added that he had always held the Greenall family in the highest esteem and respect, and said that the best wish that he could express was that Mr. Gilbert Green- all might follow in the footsteps of his respected and be- loved father. When the toast had been honoured, the cheering had subsided, and Mr. Mercer had introduced a topical song, Mr. GILBERT GREENALL made a few, re-. marks in reply. The next toast—tbat of the health of "Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall "—was proposed by the Rev. T. Wnrruer, and Mr. Join; WRITE follows:xl by toasting the health,s clreenahl and bliss Cunliffe." The only otbes. tS c t•he ffeelitlE was that .;,"‘ ths health of the "Jac, T. Whithi" ' posed by was pro- _ SMITH BURGESS: The subsequent pro- ceeding s were convivial, and, in addition to Messrs. Mercer and Wallington, Messrs. John Cooper, Philips, &sc., gave songs.

div.head: -PRESENTATION'S, DINNERS, SCC,
div.p: -PRESENTATION'S, DINNERS, SCC,

The celebrations were in great force on Tuesday. In the morning a deputation of the tenantry visited Walton Hall for the purpose of presenting an illuminated address to Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, and a silver- gilt cup and salver to the heir. The address, which was executed by Mr. Macgregor, of Liverpool, was enclosed in a red-morroco case, and the cup and salver bore,the family crest, and the motto, "Alta peto," which, being interpreted, means "I seek the heights." The presenta- tions were made in the library, where there were present Lady Greenall, her two daughters. Mr. G. Greenall, Miss Cunliffe, Mr. Robert Davies, and Mr. John White. Sir Gilbert, in consequence of his accident, was not able to bettresent.—Mr. Robert Devres introduced the depu- tation, which consisted of Messrs. Joseph Elland, Apple- ton; John Weir, Walton; Peter Percival, Daresbury ; Henry Percival, Newton • • Henry Whitlow, Halton; Alfred Broady, Higher Walton; T. Smith Burgess, chair- man of the Presentation Committee; and John Cooper, secretary and treasurer.—Mr. WEIR, on behalf pf the tenantry, then .presented the address, which was read by Mr. Joint Wang. It expressed the congratulations of the tenantry of the estates in Higher and Lower Walton, Hatton, Daresbury, and Newton, to Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, on the occasion of their heir attain- ing his majority.—ln acknowledging its receipt, Lady Gamest" said a few suitable words, and remarked that Sir Gilbert had expressed his deep regret at not being able to be with them. The silver cup and salver were then presented to Mr. Greenall, the duty being entrusted to Mr. BURGESS, who made it known that the testimonial had been subscribed to by ever tenant on the estate.—After Mr. Gilbert GREENALL had replied, the deputation withdrew. In the evening of the same day the workmen connected with the brewery at Wilderspool were entertained in the huge " loading ' warehouse, where about 150 persons at down to dinner, Mr. and Mrs. Speakman, of the Saracen's Head, catered for them. The chair was taken by Mr. Down, managing director of the Wilderspool Brewery Company, and amongst those also present were —Messrs. Gilbert Greenall, Wynn Jones, and Brooke Cunliffe ; Messrs. H. Clarke, James Henry, John Whitley, Walter Young, T. Howard, W. Howard, and W. Green- house (staff) ; Messrs. W. B. Roberts and Geo. Wallace. —The CUAIRMAN, who proposed the health of Mr. Green- all, in the course of a neat speech asked Mr., Gilbert to convey to his father the svmpathy that those present felt for hint in his present misfortune, and their earnest wish that Soon he would be completely restored to health, When the toast had been honoured, the company gang " For he's a‘jolly good fellow," gave cheers for Mr. (treenail, and one cheer more for" Mrs. Greenan that is to be." On behalf of the employes at WiMerspool Brewery, and as a mark of their esteem and reg.' e't fee him, Mr. W. B. ROBERTS then asked kr. Greenall's eeeeeeeire of a silver claret jug. They welcotned, he said lMr. Geeenall's coming 'of age, ad trusted that his , life might be extended so that their friendship might continue for years to come, and that he might follow in the footsteps of his honoured father. Other toasts and several songs were given during the evening, but Mr Greenall, after acknowledging the presentation, left to ader a second carnival gathering that was being held eel at Walton. A dinner was given at the iCalton Arms, under the superintendence of Mr. and Mrs. Broady, to between sixty and seventy of the cottagers and workmen on the estate, including the members of the Walton Brass hand, who are under the leadership of Mr. 0. Lane, and several of the tenants. The chair was taken by tile Rev. Leicester J. T. Harwell, vicar of St. John's, Walton, and there were also present, in addition toMr. Gilbert,Green- all, Miss Brookes Cunliffe, and the Misses (treenail, Messrs. John White, TeSmith 'Burgess, William Turner, William Weir, William G. Shearn, Beswick, John Cooper, Joseph Whitfield, Joseph Muskett, med James Dooley. Among the workmen were several who had been on the estate for over 20 years, one of whom, Mr. Charles Tur- ner, has been in the service of Sir Gilbert for a period Of 45 years, and who, although he is in his 85th year, looks well and hearty. The loyal toasts having ,been given from the chair, Mr. T. LANE read an addreseMtich had been prepared by Mr. C. J. Calvert. It offered to Mr. Greenall the sincere congratulations on his coming of age of the household and outdoor servants, gardeners, and gamekeepers, and was accompanied by a present of a dressing bag and set of silver studs.—Mr. G. Simmer, on behalf of the members of the Walton Brass Band, then presented a yeomanry bugle to Ile. Gilbert Greenak, along with a congratulatory address thanking him for the interest he has taken in the band, and in doing's') he assured the recipient that should he ever have occasion to sound the -bugle the members of the band would readily respond to the cal'. The toast—" Health and I long life to Mr. Gilbert Greene% the heir of Walton "—leaving been honoured, Mr. Grantereet thanked all who had interested themselves in connection with the presentation., that had just been made.—Mr. Jens WHITE, in proposing the health of "Sit Gilbert and Lady Greenall," remarked that he felt sure that from the good example their son had had set before him all his life, and with the valuable assistance he still /oohed forward to receive from those connected with the estatie Mr. Greenall would discharge the social and domestic ' duties which attached to his position in a most exemplary man- ner.—Other toasts were also given, and songs were sung by Messrs. Mercer Allen, and others. Amongst other Mercer, is one that also took place on Tuesday, when a deputation from the employes at the ' firm's breweries at St. Helens went to Walton Hall to preeent a solid silver inkstand bearing the crest and monogram of the- Greenall family- hi the, evening the employes were entertained to dinner at the instance (if Sir Gilbert at the Fleece Hotel; St. Helens, where, after the repast, varicus toasts were honoured. There were about 150 persons present, amongst them being Mr. Jos 'Robinson, manager of the St. Helens breweries, who pre- sided, and Messrs. S. Robinson; VV: Leither, J. Willace, J. C. Harvey, J. Harley, W. P. Harris, J. Valentine, J. Turten, T. Blisrp, 11.-Bermard, J. Wood, J. Holt, T. Nay- lor, J. Taylor, and G. Ripley. Th.? servants at Walton Hall have presented to Mr. Greenall a se,t of silver studs and two cases of brushes. On Thursday eventng a very successful ball was held at Walton Hall, and last evening a ball was given to the tenantry.

Mr. Hulbert, of London, died at Gat ?shoed, on Wed- nesday, from injuries received during the recent snow- storm. Mr. Chambelain, addressing a private meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Radical Union at Birmingham on Thursday night, said the Liberal Asso- ciation was no longer representative of the party in Bir- mingham, and he recommended that a new association. be formed.

-- --- STOPPAGE OF A Bt.—Great excitement has been caused at Deal by the sudden closing of the Deal Trading Bank, the manager of which has been missing from the neighbourhood since Monday. Besides the money be- longing to the bank proprietors, the money paid in on the Star-Bowkett shares and on the shares in the new Jam Factory Company is all missing, to the amount of • about .22,000.

The School contains two divisions. The work of the Lower. div.head: . EXAMINER,
div.p: THE . EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, APRIL 7, 1888.

-- THE Warrington ;Town Council had a great' . amount of business to transact on Tuesday, hav- ing to aeal with, amongst other ,things, the esti- mates for the ensuing year. It is gratifying to observe that there is to be a reduction in the ratqs of no less than sixpence in the pound. The average for the past twenty years has, we understand, been tis• 101 d. in the pound. Last year the rates were 68. ; this yeat they are to be ss. 6d. There is a bonsensus of Opinion amongst the rate- payers that ss. 101 d. in the pound is too much to Pay, one year with another, and it is therefore to be hoped that, during the ensuing decade, the average will be considerably reduced. There can • be no question that the fact of rates in a town ' being high or low has domething to do with its trade development. People who are wise count the cost when they embark in a new enterprise; alad that the difference between high and low rates sometimes a determining factor is indicated by the fact that iieveral businesses have been cora- 'een ced;and not a few houses built, just outside , 'he boundary of the borough. A matter of six- Pence in-the pound may be of no great consequence an exceptional expenditure in a single year; hut when it goes on year after year, it means in the long nui a considerable sum. A penny in the Nund realises in Warrington £540 ; and sixpence rneans £3,240. Assuming that the average of the Tatos can be reduced sixpence during the next ten Years, the saving to the pockets of the ratepayers will be no less than £32,400. It folloks of course chat the Corporate exchequer would receive less that amount; and the real issue is, whether 'with rigid economy—with the practice in a num- ler of things, of a self-denying ordinance—it, ' 'would not be possible to conduct, with efficiency/ the affairs of the borough. As the town increases, the rateable value increases, so that a rate, say of .85- 6d. in the pound means, in the ordinary %Mae of things, a much larger sum at the end of ten years than at the beginning. Whether 'we like it or not, we are called upon to do a great deal for posterity; but there is a reasonable limit to ' ' claims of this kind—just as there is an obligation bing upon the present generation not to saddle 'lPesterity with a monstrous burden of debt. Turning' to the proceedings of the Sanitary Committee, which have for some time excited a good deal of attention, we are glad to note • that •the Chairman, on Tuesday, showed himself pre- Pared to consider matters in a mood of "sweet reasonableness:' He took the wind out of the , Bails of his,adverse critics, and we are not sure that ,he did not take away their breath, by admitt- ing that the results of the work at the Longford dept were "somewhat disappointing;" that in , iact they did not get as much 'finished material as they were entitled to," and that .-"the cost was Inore than.they ought to pay? Councillor Mowas remarked that these were conclusions at which he bad arrived four or five years ago; but, in.view of -the promise of a special meeting to dis- ebas some new sanitary proposals, he did llot press his motion for obtaining cer- tain information. Judging from the observa- tions made •by Alderman CBOSITELD, it would seem that the Chief of the new proposals of the Sanitary • V•orarnittee is to secure the authority of the Town %amid for duplicating some portion of -the I'l9,ellinery at present in use. This of colirse leans further expenditure; and as it means, too, be of the present system, it is of the utmost importance that not Only the members the Town Council, but that the ,ratepayers should have the whole facts of the situation laid before them for some time ere the matter is detided. At present there does not appear to- be itulY member of the Council, except Alderman ~..taaass (the Chairman of the Sanitary ,u°rnmittee) who is possessed of the data requisite T•o form a definite opinion on the subject, 4,r1r1 he, hitherto, has remained discreetly( or in- uiscreetly, silent. It may be, as Alderman Bun- pleads, that it was "simply a joke" when he said he would supply the information asked for when it suited his convenience; but the joke to tatted the facts of the case that ft was not un- t ; brally regarded as "a true 'word spoken in 'itZst." Councillor MONKS suggested that, before 21? special meeting of the Council which is shortly rbe held, a report should be printed giving the 111 formation required. It would be unsatisfactory, tbet to say absurd, for the members of the Coupon • "°' go to ain • • eetmg, and vote upon facts and figures --"7b) se to speak, at their heads, and, so far as

. . they were concerned, wholly undigested. If the proposed scheme is a sOund scheme, its merits will not suffer by the fullest consideration, and, if it is unsound, ample time should be given to discover its defects and to reject it. Alderman BURGESS owes' it to himself and to the Council to see to it that the members make no leap in the dark. He has battled hard and long with the difficult Pro- blem of sanitation; and if, the results as to Long- ford are "somewhat disappointing," it is not be- cause he has failed to display an active and intelli- gent interest in the work which has been done. He believes he is succeeding we trust he will succeed, and we are quite sure that if he will speak out fully and frankly, aild show that he .is on the road to success, he will be frankly and cordially supported by the members of the Council.

Mn. W. J. Fein is the now President of the National vUnion of Elementary Teachers. It is always interesting to hear what teachers have to say for themselves and what suggestions they have to rnake as to improvements in the Education Code. There never yet was a code that was wholly satisfactory to teachers, and it is, perhaps, in the nature of things that there never vill be. The in- terests of Teachers and of the Department are in some respects identical, but there are sornerespeets in which they are not identical; and where there is not an identity of interest there is generally an element of antagonism. . The Department and the Teachers agree in stat- ing that their aim is to give the children of the day the best elementary education which it is possible to give. The question is— how can this be best accomplished? The prin- ciple which has been in operation for some years is—" payment by results"; or piecework as ap- plied to education. But, 0.9 it has been carried out, the system is found to have its defects; and teachers4s a'rule, strongly condemn the twactice. They say that it is more or less demoralising, since it leads to an incessant grind with a view to obtain a large percentage of passes. It is in vain that the Department make prevision for School Inspec- tors 'taking other things into consideration. Mr. POPE says—" So long as her MAJESTY'S Inspectors are allowed to write the results of the percentages system on teachers' certificates, so long must tea- chers make a high percentage the one aim of their existence." It would seem to be his opinion that "payment by results" is a bad system, and that the sooner we get rid of it the better. But as to this we join issue with him. What is needed is that the "results" shall mean everything that goes to ensuring a thoroughly sound education. Gran- i ted . that there is a moral element in teaching which cenritt satisfactorily be brought into per- centages of "results," still we do not see that it Ivould be any improvement to get rid of the per- centage system entirely. There must be inspec- tion to distinguish the well-taught schools from the ill-taught; and if it is 'to be left to her MAJESTY'S Inspector 'to decide, apart from per- centages, on the merits of schools, the next cry will be that too much depends upon the deposi- tion of 'the Inspector, and nothing on "results." Mr. Porn complains that teachers are expected to qualify children for passing who are frequently absent from wheel. But would it be any remedy for absenteeism op the part of the scholar to abolish "payment by results?" Nay, would it not tend to make the teacher indifferent as to these negligent scholars? At present he knows that unless a scholar is kept up to a certain mark in attendance, there is little or no chance of preparing him for passing. This causes the truant, to be looked after, and it ends in his attend- ing school more frequently than he otherwise would. Teachers who Want to be made happy with an all-round.good attendance, should help on in'every way they can the movement in favour of Free Education. There is nothing so much inter- feres with the attendance of children as the "eternal lack of pence" which vexes the souls of parents. We do not see, on this question of passes, that the Department or that School Managers can be expected to go beyond thiN recommendation of the London School Board, namely, that "the teachers be informed that the Board do not set great store by percentages, but rather look to the general tone and character of the school." !Jet percentages count for what they are worth, and. no more. The system has worked ,wonderfully well so far, and will continue to work well, if too much be not expected from those who have a heavy task imposed upon them in the training of the young.

MR.. JOHN MORLEY delivered -a powerful speech at Newcastle, on Wednesday evening, in which he dealt with the Irish Question, the Budget, and the Local Government Bill. He showed that the Liberal party need not fear that their programme it about to be exhausted; for, while the present Administration are being goaded on to travel on the Liberal road, they are disposed to turn aside 'and had by their Tory 'Ways. In speaking of the, Local 'Government Bill, Mr. MORLEY, while acknowledging that it was based on democratic lines, was merciless in pointing out sundry grave defects which we havechad occbsion to notice in these columns. Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH had remarked that the new Tory maxim was "Trust in the people ;" but, asked Mr. MORLEY, " what sort of 'trust in the people is it to insist that the election of the chief constable, for instance, of a county shall be aecided by the nominated magi- strates, and not bir the elective council- lors ? " As to the proposal to introduce the aldermanic element as in Town Councils; he did not hesitate to describe it as a retrograde Step. Mr. MORLEY, in licensing matters, is a local optionist ; he is in favour of "the ratepayers in a sufficiently large area having a decisive voice in the matter .' With regard to compensation to• publicans and brewers, he was somewhat uncer- tain in sound; but he did go the length of saying Pthat it-was, is his opinion, another retrograde step for the Goversment to fteek, for the first time, to "give the possessors of licenses a vested interest in these licenses." But if, he was not emphatic him- self, he quoted a sufficiently emphatic authority; and the quotation is so much to the point that we give it in full. Mr. Mostar said:— I reasemher at St. Peter's and St. Anthony's I told you, what I will take the liberty of telling you again, how I once went and saw a great man, now gathered to his fathers—Carlyle. (Hear, hear.) That great man, that great genius, began to talk upon the question of the publican! and he said, "I cannot understand any of you Parliamentary gentle- meet being in favour of compensation "—(cheers), —and the old man, he was then very near his end, waxed hot in holy lire and struck the arm of his chair, and said. "If one of these men came to me for compensation I would say to him 'go to your father, the Devil.'" (Loud cheers and laughter). We will not add to this judgment beyond slying that if Parliament goes wrong on this question, we shall be alike surprised and disappointed if the nation does not display something of Canivi,E's holy fire.

- - - eouple ,at Clinton, lowa, who bad been en- gaged for eighty-one years, were married lately. They will possibly find that, after all, "pursuit is sweeter than possession;" but let none say that they married in haste to repent at leisure.

Mr'. Chamberlain turfs the Position of the• Liberal Unionists "is now stronger than ever it has been"; but Mr. T; W. Russell, M.P. for South Tyrone, writes:—" If I give up the seat now, it would simply mean the return of a Parnellite by 1,000 majority." Which of these Liberal Unionists is right?

The latest craze among the fashional;le ladies in America, according to a Chicago paper, is to wear a diamond embedded in one of their iront teeth. This looks very much like a Yankee crammer—a brilliant of the first water • but if it be true, the ladies who resort to such a crazy exhibition of their vanity deserve -to lose their teeth, ifnd their diamonds, too. *

William Jenkins, an Ayr carpet weaver, seems to have been having "a wee drop in the On Sunday, he climbed on the wall of Alloway's Auld Haunted Rirk, celebrated as the scene of Burns's Tam o'Shanter, and vigorously rang the bell. . The disturber was next day fined by tho Sheriff in Ayr. Kirk Alloway is roofless, and Jenkins has evidently "a slate off."

It is interesting to observe that, while licensed victuallers,- 'at their various meetings, express themselves as strongly in favour of compensation, they have nothing but hard words for the clauses in the Local Government Bill which give pewer to close public houses on Sundays. There is a good deal of human nature in publicans; they would like plenty of " ha'pence " but no "kicks."

The Home Rule ball is kept rolling. The CA:in- vention of representatives of the Royal Burghs of Scotland, at its annual gathering in Edinburgh, on Tuesday, adopted by 43 Votes to 20 a resolution declaring that Home. Rule should be granted to Scotland, whereby the people of Scotland should have -the sole control of their own national affairs. Patience, patience, we shall have Home Rule all round in the end. .

The Chancellor of the Exchequer was ques- tioned in the House of Commons, yesterday, as to whether he was prepared to abandon, or at any rate modify, the proposed tax on wheels. In re- ply, Mr. Goschen said he saw ,no reason to propose any modification of the tax on the heavier vans; but he did not say whether he would relieve carts, &c. If he does not mind he will be "in for it " ; it's going to be a case of "wheel" or woe with him.

Competition for cups is the order of the day. M. Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division, has presented one to be competed for, at billiards, by meMbers of Conservative Clubs in the Division. Skill of foot and of hand has every encourage- merit. Is it not time that some one presented a cap, or a jug, or a mug, for competition ,amongst the members of the debating societies—gay, for the best speech in favour, of (or against) Free Trade P Intelhience ought to have a look in.

They still appoint Common-Lookers at Newton, but to very little purpose, if, as one speaker re- marked at the Township Meeting, "they had been quietly looking on, while the Lord of the Manor was taking the land." How suggestive is tins of the old rhyme:— We prosecute the man or woman • Who steals the goose from off the Common; But leave the greater felon loose Who steals the Common from the goose.

The other day a policeman, in Vienna, arrested a lady who was stationed at a window, in a very slight costume, and • speaking to some one in the street,. Her appearance was, in the eyes of the. constable, an offence against public propriety. The explanation was that the lady was "dressed for a ball," and perhaps we need not wonder that Robertus was shocked. The judge seems to have been shocked, too, for he sentenced the lady to eighteen houtf imprisonment.

Sir Richard Temple has just issued his "Pales- tine Illustrated. " Referring to his observation of the rising of the moon as he passed through Ajalon, he says :—" The moon was singularly mo- tionless, looking down win the valley. Instantly there rose to memory the text, 'And the moon stood still in the vallay of A.jalon.' " • But what is wit he cirivin at ? Is he offering an, explanation of the mir of Joshua's moon? If this sort of thing god on ,we shall have nothing left in the way of the wonderful. .

Sir Morel' Mackenzia is, it transpires, popular with the masses of Berlin. When he drove out the other day, he met with an enthusiastic recep- tion. The fact that he is about to visit London next week is proof positive that the Emperor is in no serious danger. It is stated that Dr. Norris Wolfenden' of Bolton, left London on Monday afternoon for Berlin, where he will, along with Sir Morel Mackenzie, see the German Emperor. The visit is the outcome, it is alleged, of an in- vitation by His Majesty, when, as Crown Prince, he was attended by Dr. Wolfenden last summer.

At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Wm. Husley, a working-man, was summoned for travel- ling from Edge Hill to Prescot, without having paid his fare. He taleged that he could not open the door at Edge* Hill, to which he had booked, and had no 'wish to get to Prescot. Husley was ordered to pay costs, the Company being satisfied with this course on the defendant's explanation and apology. But why pay anything? If his ex- planation was satisfactory, he ought rather to receive something from the Railway Conipany; it was their carriage door which caused him to lose both his time and his temper.

Councilor Bolton, as a brer, was alone in his glory at the Warrington Town Council, on Tues- day, in asserting that it was discreditable to the Watch Committee to slfirm that the increase of drunkenness amongst females was probably to be accounted for by the off-license system. lie knows, if he has given any attention to the subject, that, durinethe past ten years, the increase in the num- ber of females convicted for drunkenness is over 100 per cent. How does he account for it? If not the off-lieenses, would he have the Committee lay the blame at the doors of the holders of " on"- licenses? In any case Councillor Bolton will find himself on the horns of dilemma.

It is officially stated that the Queen has been pleased to confer the honour of knighthood upon the Judge-Advocate General, the Right Hon. W. T. Marriott, M.P.; and it is also made known that, Her Majesty has forwarded a photograph portrait of herself to Mr. Chamberlain, bearing in her own handwriting the inscription :—"To the Right Hon. j. Chamberlain on his return from Washington. Victoria R." "(Jan such things be, and overcome us like a summer cloud P" And fancy Mr. Mar- riott and Mr. Chamberlain being bracketted with honours. Oh, the humour of it I Still, they are alike in this—they have both rounded on the Liberal party.

The action of the National Association for the Promotion of Technical Education, coupled with the proposal of the Government to legislate on the i matter, s causing leading men in various boroughs to consider what course it may ultimately be ad- visable to take. Thereis we understand, a move- ment on foot in Warrington with a Slew to calling a meeting, at an early date. Seeing that Govern- ment is likely to grant a subsidy, under certain conditions, it is desirable that each town should feel itself in a position to receive, if possible, a portion of the grant. Technical education may mean much, oi it may mean little. There are kw towns, it is to be hoped, which will not, at any rate, go, the length of formally considering the question.
There is only one kap to have good servants; that is, to be worthy of being well served. All nature and all humanity will serve a good master and rebel against an ignoble one.—Ruskia. . . . ,

The members if the juvenile branch spent a pleasant evening in the National Schools on Thursday, when Mr. J. B. Imion gave a magic lantern entertainment. The views comprised some magnificent scenes in America, and the vicar, the' Rev. I. Wright Williams, acted the part of guide ia an entertaining man- ner. . _ _

RUNCORN POLICE Cour.—Yesterday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst, ar young man named James Barge' was charged with having, on, the 27th March, stolen a tin of salmon from the-shop of John Dun- babin, grocer, Weston Point. He pleaded guilty, and in consideration of the fact that he had been remanded in goal ten days, he was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. Cifrust-enuncn, WEsrom POINT.—On Easter Sunday, holy communion was celebrated at tlaiS church at 8 a.m., and at the usual morning service the anthem' "Jesus Christ is risen to-day" was rendered by the choir. At the evening service the anthem "Christ, our passover " was sung. For the first time the choir were robed in surplices. ' The offertorieS for the day 'were devoted to the day school fund. , WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB.—The fifth smoking concert hi connection with this club was held owThursday evening. ' Mr. J. Morrison, president, of the club, occupied the chair, and there was a ea pital attendance. The pro- ceedingssommenced with an able paper on ",Fifty years of Liberal Reform" by Mr. F4lartland, and then songs, " &c., were givefi by Messrs. Morrison' Caldwell, Ilatdow, F. He-yes, W.Duggan, H. B. Shores, &c. . PROPOSED NEW gATHOLIC CHURCH AT DUXCORN..-.., The Rev. Dr. Gastal i has commenced a movement with the object of 'securing funds for the erection of a hew Catholic Church at Runcorn. As a! first step a committee has been formed, and numerous subscriptions have been already received. The present church of St. Edward's is unsuitable for the requirements of the congregation that worship there, both as regards the accommodation and the situation of the edifice. THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A SOLDIER AT WIDNES.— At Widnes Police Court,- on Tuesday, before Mr. John Brock, Daniel Gilmour, a discharged soldier, was again brought up charged with causing grievous bodily harm to Joseph Donovan, with intent to kill and murder him, on the night of Saturday, the 24th March. Dr. Hutchinson stated that the injured man 'was not yet out -of danger, -and he thought it would be fully a fortnight before he would be able to appear, and the prisoner was again re- manded. SINGULAR DROWNING FATALITY AT WESTON.—At the Royal Oak Inn, Weston, on Tuesday, Mr. Worsley held an inquest on the body of John Thomas Ileathcote, a flatman, who lived in Jeff's yard, off Church-street. On Monday afternoon Heathcote was moving the fiat Mary along by means of a boat hook. The hook slipping, he fellinto the water, and as he could not swim, was drowned before aid arrived. .His wife was on the boat and witnessed the occurrence' but could not render any assistance. A verdict of "Accidental Death" was re- turned. • f .

RABIES AT Winiims.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Hignett and James Burrows were each fined as 6d and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled.—Mr. E. K. Muspratt (chairman of the pench) remarked that it would be as well to give the public ivarning that althouethe local order com- pelling dogs to be muzzled or kept under proper control expired en the 31st March, the general order issued by the Privy Council was still in force. By that order dogs need not be muzzled so long as they were kept under proper control.

FAuliwourn TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. In aid of the funds of the Farnworth branch of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society, a concert was held in the Girls' schoolroom on Tuesday night. There was only a moderate attendance. The programme, which had been arranged ' by Mr. A. G. Davies, was of a very entertaining charac- ter. Songs were given by Madame Walker and Miss Wilde, of Liverpool, Miss J. Magness, Miss A. Magness, Miss Eaton, Miss E. Gording, Misses R. Pennington, and H. Heath. The humorous part of the programhie was ably sustained by Mr. Wilson Blackledge, of St. Helens, and Mr. A. G. Davies. Master Jesse Westworth per- formed a violin solo. The duties of accompanist were jointly carried out by Miss J. Magnels, Miss Wilde, and Mr. Blackledge. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT RUNCORN.—George Shaw, an old boatman from Middlewich, was. brought before the Runcorn magistrates yesterday to answer a charge of cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it whilst in an un- fit state. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and P.C.,.Breeze stated that the animal, which was drawing a boat along the Weaver Canal at Weston Point, was walking on three legs. He discovered that the animal had a sprained fet- lock. The defendant said he worked the horse because he did not think it was so bad, and because he wanted to go home. It was 17 years old,4and only worth about 30s, and he would as soon dieNas the horse. Mr. Aplin, inspector of R.S.P.C.A., said the prisoner was a respect- able man, and had dealt with this matter in a straight- forward manner. The Bench, in consequence of this statement, only imposed the small fine of lOs and cost', ss. • FOUND DEAD IN THE MERSEY AT RUNCORN.—Yester- day, at the Burial Board Office, Runcorn, Mr. J. E. Wors- ley, the coroner, held an, inquest on the body hf Joseph Atherton, a fiatman, who had resided at Sankey Bridges, near Warrington. It appeared that Atherton was last, seen alive on the evening of the 7th December, 1887, by a flatman named John Mellor; 'Who resides in Davy-st. Widnes. At that time Atherton was drunk, arid al- though he Was walking in the direction of the river, he told Mellor that he was going to Warrington by the nine o'clock train. On Wednesday afternoon William Henry Robinson was on the river in a boat, and found the body floating opposite the Old Quay Works, and he towed the body to the shore. P.C. Gibson afterwards had it re- moved to the mortuary. A verdict of "Found dead" was returned. The deceased leaves a wife and seven children.

RUNCORN Smoot. BOARD.—The monthly meeting WWI held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev.. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. C. Beckett, E. Irni- son, and G. Moss, clerk.—The Clerk reported that the school fees for the past month amounted to £25 7s 2d, which, was £3 Os 2d in excess of corresponding period last year. The balance in the bank was £l6l 7s 9d. The visitor reported that the total number of scholars on the rolls was 3,164, and the average attendance was 2,628; percentage 83. There was an increase on the rolls of a, and on the average attendanceof 48. During the month 64 parents had been summoned before the Board for breaches of the Education Act, and 15 of these had been summoned before the magistrates and fined. The visi- tors had also served 222 warning notices to people who had not sent their children regularly to school. A VIOLENT SHIP CANAL Linotnniti.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Trotter, who was described as a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with having been drunk at Halton on the 2nd inst., and also with assault- ing P.C. Fryer. On Monday night about 10 dclock, the constable found the prisoner lying on the ground in front of Dr. Carruther's residence. As he was in a state of drunkenness the constable helped him to his lodging's, and was about to leave him at tile back door ,when the prisoner kicked him on the. stomach, and struck him several times on the face with his fist. The constable then took him into custody, and on the way to the police station the prisoner behaved very roughly.—aperin- tendent Hollingworth said he had no wish to be harsh, but he must ask that the police shall be protected from the ruffians that came into the neighbourhood.—Mr. Brundrit said it was a pity that the prisoner, a stranger to the neighbourhood, should be guilty of such conduct. The police must be protected in the execution of their duty. The prisoner was fined ss. and costs for being drunk, and 20s. and costs or a month's hard labour for the assault. • • _

STABBING A WIFE AT WinnEs.—At the Widnes Police Court on Tuesday, John Drought, of 3, Gerrard-street, was brought up on remand charged with stabbing his wife with a knife on the 24th March. Prpsecutrix—who gave her evidence very reluctantly—stated that on the night of the 24th March prisoner asked her to send for two gills of beer. She did so, and after drinking the beer he asked her to send for two more gills. She re- fused, and threw three pennies, which she had in her hand, at him. At this point he jumped up and knocked he down with his fist, and while on the floor he struck her with his fist and kicked her on the side with his clog. He cut her on the left eve with his fist and the wound bled,ptofusely. She shouted "Oh, don't kill me," and M. Carlon, the next door neighbour, came in. She was sure he did not use a knife to her, and she did not tell the police that he (Ed. She told a policeman that she felt herself struck with something sharp, but that she be- lieved it was his pike. He had had his knife out cutting tobacco a ,few minutes before, but had put it back in his pocket. -Prisoner heAl Mused her before, but was a good husband if he kept off drink.. She did not wish to prose- cute him, as there were five little children to support. Corroborative evidence having been given, prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next county Quarter ISessions.

div.p: • A STREEi NUISANCE AT Win/pm—Peter Batterton, • Thomas •Melnerney, and John Mclnerney, young men, were summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, on a charge of obtructipg Marsh- street, on the 25th March. P.S. Clarkson stated that the defendants and twenty or thirty pthers were playing football in Marsh-street. The thoroughfare was completely blocked, and people could not pass along. The police had received complaints by, letter and by word of month about windows being broken through this nuisance. The defendants denied that they were playing with the footballers, but the Bench arrived at a different conclusion, apd ordered each defendant to pay 7s 8d costs. Mr. B. Gaskell, jun., announced that future offenders wmild be severely punished. % Rersrtau, As-rum. Mr. T.. L. Rodgers, the medical superintendent of this institution, in. his annual report, says that during the year 345 , pa tients were admitted, the highest number re- ceived in any one .year since that in which the asylum wad opened for the reception of patients, January Ist; 1851. Fifty-live patients were, die- charged as Tecovered. THE RECTORSHIP OF WARRINGTON. It is rumoured that the Hon. and Rev. Victor Edward Powys, brother of Lord Lilford, has been appointed to the living of Warrington, rendered vacant by the death of the late rector, the Rev. William Quekett The living is said' to be worth about £1,500 a year, and is in the gift of Lord Lilford. Mr. Powys was ,born in 1839. and is a widower with two scuts. SMALLPDX IN THE PRESCOT UNYON.—It Will be Seen from a notice in our advertising coilumns that the Guardians of the Preseot Union are taking ac- tion to prevent the spread of smallpox. They state that smallpox having appeared in the Union, the Guardians consider it desirable that all children and other persons in the distriet who have not been successfully vaccinated should be vaccinated with- Out delay. It is further urgently recommended that all persons not vaccinated since childhood, who are likely to be Exposed to infection, should be re- vaccinated. A list of medical gentlemen in the Union who vaccinate gratuitously is also given. Looar: RAINFALL.--The rainfall for the first quar- ter of the present year is very much short of the average. The amount recorded in the 13 weeks in- cluding the 31st March, at the Warrington Fever Hospital, amounted to 4-37 inches. . The rainfall during the corresponding period of 1887, a similar dry season, was only 4.05 inches. In 1886 it was 7.08 inches, in 1885 it was 6.02 inches, in 1884 .it was 7.42 inches, in 1883 it was 7.30 inches, in 1882 it was 6.05 inches, or an averagiNor the five years of 61. Similar conditions are recorded in other parts .of,England and Ireland, varying from one half the average in the south to one-third in the midland, 'north-western, and south-western districts. The rainfall in March has considerably reduced the de- ficiency throughout the county, though the amount here (1.94 inches) does not reach the aggregate in other districts -(21 inches). " PE:krECETII WESLEYAN SUNDA SCHOOL.—The Wesleyans of Penketh have for three or four years celebrated Good Friday with a tea meeting, and entertainment at, night, the object being to keep the scholars from participating in the sports held at Fidler's Ferry. Tea was on the table at Ave o'clock, when about 150 scholars and adults sat down to tea. After the tables were cleared, Mr. Garnett occupied the chair, and the following pro- gramme was gone through :—Address on India, by Gnanamu; recitation, "Anniversary address," Louisa Glover; general secretary's report, Mr 13, Hobson; financial report of Sunday school, Mr J. Jackson, treasurer; solo, "Christ arose," Miss E. gobson ; sick club report, Mr T. Leeds; flute trio, °Forgive blessed shade," Messrs. Shane, Hobson, and Board- man; library report, Mr A.. Wyan ; violihs and cornet duet, Mr Ames Fildes and Sons (Bowdon); band report, Mr T. Dunabin ; recitation, "My Mother," Edith Marsland; recitation, "Ode to the sun," H. Budden ; duet. M. and Lilly Routledge ; recitation. "Industrious boy," G. Marsland; recita- tion, "All among the flowers," Alice Seed; recita- tion, "Counting the pennies," B, Jackson. There was a crowed meeting. and all seemed to enjoy themselves. The following ladies had charge of the tea arrangements :—Misses Garnett, Wynn, Manley, Routledge, Cross, Moses, &c. During the evening prizes of books were presented to the scholars.

HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The medical officer of health reported that the number of deaths registered during the month amounted to 30, showing an average death rate ot a little over 21 per 1,000 for the twelve months, and, exclusive of three inquest cases, of a fraction over 19 per 1,000 of the estimated population.
