div.head: FINANCE: A NEW RATE.
div.p: FINANCE: A NEW RATE.

The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to ale 158 7d, and accounts amounting to £llO 6s 6d were recommended for pay- ment. It was recommended that the estimates for the year ending 25th March, 1889, amounting to £4,733 be approved, and it was also recommended that a general district rate of 2s in the £ for the year ending March 29th, 1889, be made. With respect to the assessment and laying of the general district .rate for the ensuing year it was recommended that the owner instead of the occupier be riled under the provision of section 211 of the Public Health Act, 1875, where the rateable value of any premise's liable to assessment did not exceed the sum of £10; and that he be assessed on a reduced esti- mate of three-fourths of the net annual value of such property —Mr. Fisher moved. and Mr. Taylor seconded the adoptiort of the minutes, which, after some discus- sion, were passed. THE NIGHTSOU CONTIACTOR.... Mr. Lightburn, as Chairman of the Health Committee, reported that the nightsoil contractor was not doing his work very well. There were now 100 ashpits requiring to be emptied.—Mr. Grica said the contractor had trea- ted the Board in an unfair and dishonourable manner, and it was time the Board took some steps to put an end to the engagement.—Mr. Speakman said it had been in- timated to him that Mr. Field would like to be relieved of his contract. He suggested that a letter should be at once sent to Mr. Field drawing attention to the terms of his agreement, and the serious consequences that would ensue if he did not properly Carry out his conttact. In answer to questions the Secretary said the contract did not expire for two.yea,rs.—The Chairman said Mr. Field had been very unfortunate. He had lost two horses and had a boat sunk. He hoped the Board would give him a little consideration.—The matter was ultimately left in the hands of the Health Committee.
WATERLOO 13EIDOE.

The committee respecting the improvement of this bridge recommended that the expenses of the deputa- tion to Manchester, amounting to Ll I.ls 6d be paid.— Mr. Pritchard moved, and Mr. Lightbum seconded, the confirmation of the minutes, and the proposition was agreed to.

div.head: RUNCORN AND THE LOCAL CiOVERNMENT BILL,
div.p: RUNCORN AND THE LOCAL CiOVERNMENT BILL,

The Chairman submitted a copy of the Local Govern- ment Bill, and asked whether a special committee should be appointed to consider its provisions or should the Bill be referred to the Parliamentary and Legal Comniktee. —The Law Clerk said the Bill, so far as Runcorn Com- missioners a's an urban authority was concerned, would affect this district very little, and the provisions of the Act would not come into force until 1890. There was a provision made for the transfer of the whole of the powers of the Commissioners to the body to be called the District Council for Runcorn. The liabilities and assets wouldle • formally transferred from one body to the other. There was nothing at all in the Bill as it stood which could prejudically affect the district of Runcorn. —ln reply to Mr. Mellor and Mr. Smith, the Law Clerk said the Burial Board would be controlledhy the District Council. It was not proposed to absorb boards of Guardians, and one of the first things done after the for- mation of district councils would be to enlarge the work- houses.—lt was resolved to hold a special meeting of the Board on Monday next to consider the details of the Bill.
There was no other business.

SHOCKING FATALITY AT NEWTON' PAPER WORKS.—A shocking fatality occurred at the paper works of Messrs. Gillespie and Ma,s,m, Mill-lane, Newton, on Wednesday. The deceased was a labourer named John Broadbent, 67 yearsOf age, who resided at Hermitage Green, and who for some time past had been working at one of the cir- cular saws. About eleven o'clock on the forenoon of Wednesday a man named Foley left the deceased for a few minutes, and on his return found him lying dead near the pulleys, round which run the strap for driving the saw. How the deceased met with his death is not defmitely known but from a lacerated wounds on his right hand, and a large scalp wound on the back of his head, it is suppoqed that by some means he was caught by a portion of the machinery and was dragged round, his head coming in contact with some overhanging iron- ' work. ,

LOCAL VESTRY MEETINGS.
WIDNES _ PARISH CHURCH.

The annual meeting of parishioners was held at the National School on Wednesday night. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar, presided, and there was a fair attendance. Mr. Thomas Hughes, the vestry clerk, read the minutes of the last meet- ing, which were adopted.—Mr. H. N. Wharton presented' the accrountiof St. Mary's Church, which showed that the total Income from all sources for church expenses amounted to £123 16s 00. The expenditure amounted to £l3B 16s sd, leaving a deficit of £l5 Os 40. There had been offertories for special objects.—Mr. F. Neil presented the acc3unts of St. Paul's Church. The collections for church expenses realised £75 14s, and the expenditure amounted to £7O 188, 110, leaving a balance in hand of fie 4 15s. The total offertories had amounted to £266 18s 9th, and had been disbursed to the various organisations connected with the church and the diocese, fic. The accounts were adopted.— The Chairman re-appointed Mr. F. Neil Vicar's warden.— On the motion of Mr. W. Treacy, senr., seconded by Mr. J. Dickson, Mr. IL N. Wharton was re-appointed people's war- den.—The Vicar elected the following gentlemen as his sides- men :—L. Kilcross, W. Treacy, P. Hewitt, T. Hughes, F. H. Pankhurst, James Williams, J. Farrant, F. Cave, A. Edwards, William White, James Beatty. t. Brockleban)c.—The follow- ing gentlemen were selected as people's sidemen :—W. Chad- wick, W. Dwerryhouse, William Bruce, D. Brooks, John Hart- land, C. Watson, C. Jones, Thomas Atherton. John Dickson, junr., Henry Beacham, J. Beach, William Arnold.—Messrs. J. B. Imison and L. Kilcross were unanimously appointed lay- representatives, and Mr. T. Hughes was again elected vestry clerk. Messrs. Thomas Hough and Richard Falkner were ap- pointed sidesmen in place of Mr. Enemas and Mr. Hughes.— Mr. Chadwick said that had not the Vicar been abofit to leave the town, It was his intention to propose that it was desirable that St. Mary's Church should be made free and open. Seeing, however, that the control of the parish would change hands before long, he would now give notice that he shouid move such a resolution at a mere convenient period.—The proceed- ings terminated with the usual votes of thanks. ST. AMBROSE, WIDNES.

The annual vestry meeting in Connection with St. Ambrose parish was held on Thursday evening, the new incumbent, the Bev. G. Le Bert. presiding. Ajnougst those present were Messrs. John Valentine, H. Johnson, G. Nell, W. S. Callen- der, Riley, S. Kidd, E. M. Harrison, J. Williams, \V. Hill, 11. Mercer, J. Shuttleworth, Pyle, Burgess, Lee, Latham, and Glover. The churchwardens accounts for the Past year were presented by Mr. Riley, from 'which it appeared that the total Income for the• year was £9B 6s, made up of a balance of £2 16s 2d and offertories £93 9s 10d. The total experiditure had been £B4 18 ICleavlng .a balance in hand of £l2 4s 11d. It was stated that a sum of £250 had been invested in the In- corporated Society for the enlargement and Improvement of churches and chapels, and it was decided that the accounts be paid from the interest oil the fund.—The accounts were then duly passed.—The Chairman said he was now amongst them for weal or woe. He should, for his own part, be iforry to see any change made ruthlessly. He would name Mr. If. joluison as his warsten.—Mr. Joseph Williams was elected as people's warden, in the place of Mr i Valentine, who did not again de- sire to occupy the position.—The following gentlemen were elected sidesmen:—Messrs. .Valentine, Carlisle, Callender, Goff, Hill, Kidd. Edwardson, Lee, Mercer, Minton, Foster, Upward, Riley. Pyle, Geach, Niel, and Smith. Messrs. W. Hill and S. Kidd were re-appointed lay representatives, and Mr. Riley was re-elected treasurer and secretary for the ensu- ing year.

Sutton (Ark). Amongst the numerous audience , were the Rev. W. Bryant, the Rev. J.. °Tindlall, Messrs. H. Coleburn,' Mr. Barker, B. Marwood, J. N. Lello, J. E. Meredith, .T. Johnson, B. Indian), W jimmins, G. Sum- merfield, .L Littler, W. Bate, G. Wood, C.*Poivnall, W. Shaw, ne.—Mr. F. A. Lake submitted the statement of accounts, and I stated that the offertories for church expenses and on account of the stipends of the assistant clergy amounted to £251 is lid, and the offertories fur special purposes, such as Mis- sionary Societies, ace., amounted to £Bl 3s 9d, making a total income of £332 Sc 81(1, the whole of which had been disbursed for various ,purposes.—Mr. Suannerlield explained, the accounts of the Church of St. Michael's and All Angels. The income amounted to £126 13s 7d, and after pay- ing all expenses the sum of £lB 17s 64 was handed over to the Runcorn Curates' Fund.—The accounts were unanimously. approved.—The Chairman appointed Mr. E. Mat-wood as I vicar's warden lot-the ensuing year. Mr. Whittaker was re- I elected people's warden.—The following sidemen were then I elected out .of 13 gentlemen nominated :—W. Bate, John Williams, W., Towns, W, Timmins, George Hewitt, J. E. Meredith, W. Cropper, Thomas Kirkham. The following officers were elected to serve at St. Michael's and All Angels :—Vicar's warden, G. Summerfield ; peo- ples warden, Themes G. JOttes ; sidennen, R. Peacock, T. Blundell, S. Greaves, dames Cropper, S. H. Dawson; and Henry Hill. For Weston: Vicar's warden, Thomas Ford (Cavendish Farm) ; people's warden, Joseph' Tudor; sides- men, James Ford, janr., W. A. Armstrong, and E. Aaron.— Mr. W. Whittaker and Mr. F. A. Lake were elected the lay representatives for the parish.—A vote of thanks was accorded the out-going wardens, and Mr. Sutton, who, after fifteen years of service as parish clerk, had deter- mined to give up the office, was also heartily thanked. Votes of thanks were also accorded to the organ- ists and choirs of the Parish Church, St. Michael's Church, and Weston Church.—Mr. Coleburn complained that the musical services of the Parish Church were of such a char- acter that nineteen-twentieths of the congregation could not take part therein. They wanted more congregational services hi the Parish :Church. The chants and anthems were sung to music which was not understood of the people.—Sonitin- terruption followed, and Mr. Imison said Mr. Colaburn as not receiving fair treatment. Many people had been benefited by a course Mr. Coleburn took at the last vestry, and while he did not pretend to sympathise with either Mr. Colebnrn's objections or arguments, yet he was entitled to a fair hearing.- Mr. Coleburn then proposed the following resolution :—" In consequence.of the difficulty experienced by the majority of the Parish Church congregation in not being able to join in singing smite of the chants and anthems and so forth during divine service, they hope the vicar will take steps to re-arrange the services, and make them thoroughly congregational, so that all can take part therein."—The Chairman referred to the musical education the children received in the day schools, and said that we Should have to.look forward in the future; not to a diminution of music in divine worship, but rather an increase of it. '(Applause.) The people who approved of a musical service would feel ag- grieved if the music were taken away, and as far as he could Judge, the greater number of people who attended the Parish Church liked a musical service. '(Applause.)—The Chair- num then pronounced the Benediction, and the meeting separated.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY.. RUNCORN.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY.. RUNCORN.

The 'annual Easter vestry was 'held on Monday, under the presidency or the Rev. W. Preston, MA., the vicar, and there were present Messrs. Wrririner, W. Hankinson, J. Hutton, J. 11,Salkeld, and .T. Ainsworth.

FtNaNctit. STATEunvr.—Mr, Fisher, the vicar's warden, reported that (hiring the year the income for church expenses amounted to £67 6s 74-d. Forty-four collections had realised £4B 9s 54, and there had been also received £7 17s 2d intkreat on DoCk Bonds, and £9 14s 64 per eentage on pew rents, mak- ing the total previously named. Collections had also bee: made for the Curates' Aid Fund, Church Pastoral Aid Society, amounting to 2,24 12s He thought those present would see that things hod been going on In a pleasant told satisfac- tory ntauner. . . .

Rtnertux OF Watinxxs.—The Chairman having announced his intention of shortly departing on a voyage for the coast ef Africa and South Spain, referred to the work Of the past year. He mentioned with pleasure the erection of the Jubilee wall round the church, and cordially thanked Mr. Brundrit, Mr. E. Timmins, and Mr. Iforsefield for their generosity, in connec- tion therewith. Since the last vestry meeting he had been offered two good positions elsewhere, but he had refused them, as he had not yet taken a dislike to Runcorn. (Hear, hear.) He was very happy there, and it would be something,of pecu- liar character that would tend to make him sever Ids connec- tion with that parish. (Hear, hear.) Runcorn had many attractions for him, and he was very comfortable as things were going on. He hoped next year to do another good work for the parish. it was the jubilee year of Trinity Church. Fifty years ago the church was called into existence, and he hoped they would not permit the jubilee to pass by without do- ing something to commemorate it. The organ was practically useless, and he intended to put it into proper condition. He also wished it to be removed from the gallery, as this would be a great benefit to the choir and to the church. He had already received subscriptions towards this object. Having thanked the organist and choir for their efficient services, the Chairman nominated Mr. W. Fisher as Isis warden for the ensuing year. —Mr. Fisher accepted the position, and said he would have kreal pleasure in doing what he could for Trinity Church.—Mr Rankinson moved, and Mr. J. If. Salkeld seconded, the re- appointment of Mr. J. Buckley as people's warden, and the motion was carried unanimously.—Messrs. W. Hanklnson, J. Foulkes, J. Savage, and R.'lilicross were elected sidesmen, and Messrs. E. Timmins, J. H. Balkeld, J. Meadowetoft, and W. Lea were appointed representatives on the Church Council. Messrs. W. Fisher and W. Hankinson were appointed dele- gates to the ruridemnal couference.—The customary votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: ST. LUKE'S, i'ARNWORTH.
div.p: ST. LUKE'S, i'ARNWORTH.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the chancel of the church. The Key. J. E. Lawton, curate, presided, and there were present Messrs. Kidd, Fletcher, Baker, .T. K. Lea, P. Longton, Taylor. Hamblen, and Palmer.—The Chairman read the accounts, from which it appeared that the total funds for the year amounted to £.93 2s 101, leaving a balance due to the treasurer of a 19s Thd after paying all expenses.—Mr. P. Longtoniwas elected vicar's warden, and the following were elected people's wardens for the following townships :—Bold, Mr. Baker; Cuerdley, Mr. Taylor; Crouton, Mr. Glover. In case Mr. Glover declined to serve, it was resolved that Mr. W. Longton be nominated in his place. The following' sides- men were elected in addition to those already appointed : Messrs. Guest, F. Lea, Alfred Bradshaw, and W. Jones.— Messrs P. Longton and Baker were appointed lay representa- tives, and Mr. Palmer was re-appointed clerk and sexton.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH. The annual vestiry meeting was held on Tuesday night. The vicar, the Rev. J. Lockwood, presided, and there was a fair attendance.—Mr. Thomas Wright was re-elected vicar's war- den, and Mr. Joseph Stokes people's warden. The other offi- cials were also re-elected.—On the proposition of the chair- man, a vote of condolence and sympathy with Lady Brooke and family was passed.—The Chairman stated that the church and other parochial matters were in a satisfactory condition. The Income for the year amquilted to £274, and there was now a balance in hand of 210.—The customary votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. FRODSHAM.

, ...The annual meeting of the parishioners of Frodsisam was held on Monday morning. Present—Rev. A. Grier, senior curate (in the chair), Rev. J. Stevens, /siessrs. C. B. Linaker and John Robinson (churchwardens) ; Messrs. H. Linaker. R. Holland, T. Lewis, T. Davies, John Pollard, T. H. Hitchen, H. Tlley, T. Riley, G. H. Denby, R. Foulkes, IL B. Hey- wood, if. G. Linaker, R. Watson. 8. Davies, W. Noden, J. Forster, G. (Heave, W. Price, and 8. Sharp.—The parochial accounts were submitted and unanimously passed.—The pre- siding Chairman, en behalf of the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. }Nogg, had pleasure in nominating Mr. C. E. Linaker as vicar's war- den.—On the motion of Mr. T. Riley, seconded by Mr. G. H. Denby, Mr. John Robinson was unanimously appointed parishioners' warden.—Mr. C. R. Linaker nominated Messrs. G. Gleave and H. E. Heywood as the vicar's sidesmen, and on the motion of Mr. John Robinson, Messrs. It. Date and R. Watson were appointed parish sislesmen.—Messrs. R. Holland and S. Davies were unanimously appointed auditors.—Messrs. J. Robinson, H. Tiley, and T. H. Ilitchen were appointed unanimously lay representatives.—The Parish Church Tower Restoration Committee reported that they had completed the restoration of the tower, which was re opened on April 17th, 1887. Afteedefraying the whole cost of such restoration they had a smallbalance of funds in hand.—The report was adop- ted.—Mr. H. Lina,ker offered a sum of £5 towarcls•a fund for the purposeef the completion of the carving on the exterior of the church, which was accepted, and Mr. J. Robinson pro- mised to attend to this matter, and endeavour to have the carving domnleted.—Proposed by Mr. R. Foulkes, and so- donded by Mr. John Forster (to test the meeting), that a

notice be posted on the church door that people be requested to keep their seats during the processions. On being put te the meeting, one voted in favour thereof, and six against.— Mr. Foulkes then made the following motions, none of them, however, being seconded :-1. That the clergy and choir do not turn their kacks on the congregation during the recitation • 6 of the Creeds.-2. That the Hymns Ancient and Modern be done away with, and to introduce a sound evangelical hymn book.-5. That this vestry entirely disapproves of... Church pro- cessions.—lt was decided to have a notice put in the porch of the church, to the effect.that all seats are free : books pro- vided for strangers.—On the motion of Mr. C. E. Linaker a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the F,ev. A. Grier for pre- siding. '
THE KENTUCKY MINVRELS AT RUNCORN.

An entertainment was given in the Public Hall, Rwicorn, on Thursday evening, by the Kentucky Minstrels, towards liquidating the debt ow the de- funct gymnasium. Mr. S. Coventry introduced the troupe to the audience, and explained that there was a considerable debt still owing by the Gym- nasium Committee, and the Kentucky Minstrels had kindly volunteered their services to assist in clearing off the debt. The programme contained some first-class songs and choruses, which were very efficiently rendered, the audience testifying their appreciation by frequent outbursts of applause. Many of the item g won well deservetioncores. Mr. • J. Leathwood sang" White wings" and " Little 'sis- ter's gone to sleep rid the other songs were "Sil- ver moonlight," 'Master J. Hampson ; "Kiss me ere the daylight fades." Mr. J. Bir_ kett ; "Down by the river," Mr. S. sher_ lock ; "Take back the heart," Mr. R. Moreton; "Wake, Nicodemus;" Mr. W. J. Millington The comic element was admirably sustained by, four cornermen, Mr. T. WhinyatJ4and A. Riley (bones), and Messrs. Up. Billington and A. Matthews (tam- • bounties). The humorous songs were "Golden Slippers,' Mr. A. Riley; "I'm one of the ticklish ' kind," Mr. J. Whinyates ; "Razors in the air," Mr. D. Billington; "On the banks of the silvery I Thames," Mr. F. Elbrell ; and "Crackpot in the City," Mr. D. Billington. A pianoforte solo was also given by Mr. Clifford ,Le Cousteur. Mr. D. Billington provoked much mirth by a stump ora- tion. The local and topical duet by Messrs. Whin- yates and Billington "I shall never be happy again," fairly brought down the house, the allusions to well-known celebre- ties, including some of the ;prominent local football players, being keenly appreciated. The pro- ceedings concluded with a laughable farce entitled "The country cousin," which was very creditably given, and caused endless fun. Mr. J. Birkett per- - formed the duties of interlocutor, Mr. H. Handley being at the harmonium, and Mr. C. be Couteur presided at the piano. The entertainment was 'thoroughly enjoyed by the large audience present. The jokes and conundrums between the coriermen were of a high order, and created much laughter,. and the songs and choruses w,ere eminently satis- factory. The troupe, which is entirely a local com- bination, fully merited the flattering reception which was accorded.

div.head: FRODSHAM MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: FRODSHAM MUSICAL SOCIETY.

On Thursday evening the 14th concert of this society was given in the Frodsham Town , Hall, when a most interepting and popular programme was gone through. The programme contained items of the most interesting character yet pro- duced by this society. Tne great work of the even- ing was 'a pastoral operetta by Mr. W. H. Birch, en- titled "The merrie men of Sherwood Forest." The characters represented were as follows :—" goad Marian," Miss K. S. Rigby ; • "Robin Hood," Mr. J. Kent; "Little John," Mr. Ben Rigby; "Will Scar- lett," Mr. Curnow. The work is a bright, spirited operetta, and describes the forest days in the olden • time. Each of the soloists had a special song. That - of Robin Hood's was "To arms, ,the trumpet sounds,' being a call of his comrades to release "Will Scarlett," who has been taken captive by the Sheriff of Nottingham. In singing this Mr. Kent showed a fair amount of resolution and attack. The recitative and aria, "Sweet, pretty bird," brow,. for Miss K. S. Rigby a most enthusiastic recelition. The piano and organ were tuned tip to pitch, and,in the short recitative," Sweet Echo," her register Combined two octaves, from C to C, and she • produced a remarkably good swell on the top, B. Mr. Curnow was unfortunately suffering from a severe cold, which greatly affected the production of his solos. He, however, made a bold attack with the recitative" Friends and brother Saxons," and sang with feeling the " MiserereDomine,"which preceded the "Dead March." Mr. Ben Rigby won for him- self hearty applause in the Bacchanalian song "With a Ho! Hi! Ho ! " The favourite of the even- ing was the song and duet "I'll love thee still," in which " Robin Hood" swears devotion to "Maid Marian" inanost affectimate terms, at the Mar- riage Festival. This waif- enthusiastically encored, and was resnonded to by Miss Rigby and Mr. Kent. The work ot the chorus was very creditably per- formed, and gave proof of the careful training of the conductor, Mr. Curnow. The parts of the chorus were evenly balanced, and the united efforts of each added in no small degree to their undoubted suc- cess. They were rewarded by an encore of the finale, being a galonade entitled "We'll trip it mer- rily o'er the lea." This contains three movements of a most attractive style, and there only wanted the natural surroundings of the trysting tree and the forest to make the performance complete. The first part of the programme contained solos by Mr. F. Spencer and Mr. Curnow, several part songs, and the prize glee. with which the society was victori- ous over the Welsh choirs at Chester Eisteddfod in the early part of last month. The trio "0 memory was also very tastily given by Miss K. S. .Rigby, Miss Edith Riley. and Mr. J. Kent. Mr. C. Hibbert presided at the pianoforte and deserves great praise for the way in which he officiated. The hall was well filled, and we understand that the annual re- port will show a substantial balance on the right side.

A MILITARY "HERO" IN Tnounia.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas Rothwell, of Collins Green, one of the Rorke's Drift heroes, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Earlestownonthe previous night.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and added that ever since he was in Africa the tirink had affected him.—The Chairman said he was sorry te see there was such along list of convictions against the prisoner.—Superintendent Weir: He is a pensioner, and the fact is he has to pay away all his pension in- fines.—The prisoner said ever since he was in the Kaffir and Zulu Wars he became drunk if he took half a pint of drink.—Mr. Houghton. : Then I would not take half a pint of drink.—The •Prisoner It is the ruination of Mee—A fine of 5s and # costs was imposed. FOOTBALL AT EaurzsTowN.—The Earlestown club pro- vided an excellent list of matches for their supporters during the Easter holidays. Three well known organis- ations were engaged to visit Earlestown, and the con- tests which took place on the mesnes were all largely attended. On Good Friday the Earlestown team was opposed by the once famous Turton club. The visi- tors played down hill during the first half, and had a breeze in their favour. • Before the change of ends they scored on three occasions while the home team were pointless. In the second period, how- ever, the Earlestomans played in magnificent form; and amid repeated cheers scored no less than five goals. As the visitors failed to score in this half a..highly interest- Mg and exciting_game resulted in a splendid victory for the home team by five goals to three. The victory was a very populacoone.—On Saturday the return match was played with the Farnvrorth Standard Club, and Earles- town won this match by three goals to two.—The well- known Blackburn Park-road team visited Earlestown on Easter Monday, and another splendid game was wit- nessed. Playing with the ground in their favour Earles- town scored twice in the first period. On the change of ends the play was very even and exciting, and each side scored on two occasions, Earlestown thus winning by four goals to two. THE REV. PETER MACK' VzIE AT NIITGROVE.—On Easter Sunday, the Rev. Peter MacKenzie, of Dewsbury, preached the annual sermons in the Nutgrove Wesleyan Chapel. Both in the morning and in the evening there was a large congregation, and the collections, which were in aid of the chapel debt, amounted to £l4 13s 7d. On Monday night the Rev. Peter MacKenzie gave his' lecture on "Queen Esther" to a crowded gathering, in the same place of worship. The chair was occupied by the Mayor. (Alderman D. M`Kechnie), and there were on the platform the Revs. John Pickwell, T. Baines, G. G. Brown, and Mr. J. T. Anderton The Mayor said he was glad to have the opportunity of being present, if it would be any encouragement to the friends in their ',cork. It was About twenty years ago since he first had the opportunity of listening to Mr. MacKenzie, and he felt it to be very stimulating to himself to be there. The Rev. P. MacKenzie then proceeded with his address, and said the subject of his remarks was a lady, one who Was a diamond without a flaw, a rose without a thorn, and a luminary without'a spot on her disc; one of the honoured tribes‘of Benjamin. He narrated Esther's early career, and said she became the wife of King Ahasuerus, but unlike 'many now who are helped on the way, she did not folget her friends. He concluded an impressive discourse, interspersed with interesting narratives. The Rev, J. Pic.kwell moved a vote of thanks to the lecturer, and Mr. Robinson seconded. Mr. Mac- kenzie replied, and moved a vote of thanks to the chair- man. This was seconded by the Rev. T. Bainae, and carried. The Mayer replied, expressed his willingness to ' be a listener on a futeire occasion, and the meeting then closed. The collection amounted to £5 24 3d for khe day, ' in addilion to a cheque given bylheMayor.

RUGBY RIJI.F-S. RUNCORN " A " Tss.fs v. MANCHESTER RANGERS " A " TRAM .—This match was played on the ground of the lat- ter on Saturday. The Rangers l'aid the assistance of several players from other clubs, and had whipped up a strong team, whilst Runcorn was only. moderately' repre- sented. A noisy game ended in a win for the Rangers team by 1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minors, to r try and 4 minors. For Runcorn, Booth had a lot of work to do, and played a sale game throughout. The forwards did not display that combination as they are accustomed to de, and were a lot off colour. For the Rangers, Donald- son, Elliso9, and Meeham played a good game. Teams: —Runcorn: Full back, S. Booth ; three-quarters, Lunt, Crompton, and Pendlebury ; half backs, Hollingsworth and Evans; forwards, Gatley, Abrams, Cox, Raffe, Ford, Whinyates. Grounds, Higgins, and Hampson. Rangers: Full back, Daniels; three-quarters, Ellison, Gra- ham, and Donaldson; half backs, Radcliffe and Meeham; forwards, McDougall, Frost, Unsworth, Pearson. Kinder, Vickers, Urwin, Tyacke, and Pammall. WIDNES V. Osserr.—The return match between these teams was played on Saturday on the. Widnes ground. before about 2,000 spectators. The weather was fine and the turf in good condition. (The home team were without Hughes and Pennington. Webster, the Ossett captain, kicked off at 3-35 up the slope. Hardman re- turned, and smart loose play- fdpwed in the visitors' ter- ritory, the outcome of which was that Kiddie passPd to Parkinson at the quarter, and he ran in and grounded the ball safely over the line. Plumpton failed at the place. Shortly afterwards, when the ball was scrim- maged at the visitors' quarter, 'it was kicked through. Hardman dashed after it, and in a twinkling placed it in position thus securing, the second try, Plumpton again failing to record the major point. This reverse spurred the Yorkshiremen to greater exertions, and for a time the game was contested in the Widnes territory, the visitors adding tvk minors, after which Lee, who played a very plucky game throughout, seethed the ball in front of the home citadel and dropped a fine goal. Ossett were now leading by a goal and two minors to two tries and after changing ends they added two more minors, but a different complexion was put upon the state of affairs when Kiddie made a fair catch in the OsSett half from which he kicked the ball high in the air, and Plumpton, securing it in its descent, dashed through the midst of his opponents and secured a splendid try, but Farrell failed at goal. The heavy Yorkshiremen, by their weight in the scrimmages, again took the ball to the Widnes quarter, and added two dead balls to their score, after which Parkinson made a splendid attempt at a dropped goal, and the ball just falling short, he darted after it, and secured a try beneath the posts. Farrell again took the place, Mad landed a fine goal. The game closed shortly afterwards, Widnes being the victors of a well-contested game, by a goal and three tries to a goal (dropped) and six minors. RUNCORN V. DEWSBURY. Fresh from their great victory over Warrington on Saturday, the Dewsbury team turned up at Runcorn on Monday to play the I.leshire champions, and found worthy foemen. Runcorn won the toss, and Wolsten- holme kicked off for Dewsbury; and, there being no re- turn, some open vr,rk took place in mid-field, of which the home team had the best. Lockwood made an effort to get away., but was brought down by Riley. At. the Dewsbury 2.5 line Runcorn was penalised by a free kick, . but a good return placed the home players in position, and H. Hughes ran through, but was tackled timely, and Hopkins punted to Brazendale, who kicked a dead ball— first blood to Runcorn—and this was quickly followed by a touch-in-goal. Stadden' forged away towards the centre, but Runcorn got the upper hand of some loose play, and Whitby passed to W. Hughes, and he ran in— a grand bit of work—and Brazendale kicked a goal. The home players still forced the pace, notwithstanding a dashing effigt of ThOmson to relieve. Hopkino ran across for au opening, but was dispc&itAsed, and Wain- wright:dashing up, kicked the ball over the line dead. After the drop-out Wainwright ran from the centre un- opposed, and grounded close ta the corner flag, Brazen- dale taking the place to no purpose The wearers of the green gave no quarter, and kept the Yorkshiremen on • the defensive, H. Hughes and Davies being very promi- nent, the latter being tackled by Lockwood when look- ing dangerous. The international then kicked Well up the field, Brazendale getting a free kick, a point gained by Stadden for the other side almost im- mediately, and this latter point secureek. the Tykes' first entry into the, home territory, Ibiltendsle now brought down the house by a short run.and drop into touch in his opponent's half, and W. Hughes dribbled, and, picking up, grounded, and from arl••excellent posi- tion Brazendale directed the ball nicely over the bar. Another dead ball to Runcorn, and then W. Riley passed to H. Hughes, and half-time was announced with the ball in the Dewsbury 25, the points standing two goals, one . try, and five minors for Runcorn to nothing. Without loss of time sidA were reversed, and W. Hughes kicked off, Stadden replying. The first noteworthy move was a run by Cookson into Dewsbury ground. The Yorkshire- men rushed it down the field, and Loekwood in turn tackled Wainwright and Cookson when they were going strongly. A good run by Davies gave the home players an excellent place, and a touchdown was recorded. A grand kick by Lockwood into touch rought play into the Rtincorn 25, and tirom a throw-in Cookson ran to centre, Lockwood puffin' him up, and Stadden kicked over the home line, the ball going dead, and Naylor took a drop a moment afterwards—another minor to Dews- bury, who continued to have a little the best of the argil- • ment, and Stadden making a fair catch, Heeson kicked a goal. Play continued to rage in the Runcorn half, and Lockwood ran into the 25, where Wainwright collared him, and this play led into the opposing 25, but the lines were cleared, and Jackson kicked over the Runcorn line, and another valueless point was the reward. A free kick did not help Dewsbury much, and then W. Riley, Cookson, and H. Hughes passed nicely, but on came tile "Stripes," and after a maul Runcorn had to concede a minor, and shortly after the whistle blew with the score as follows :—Runcorn two goals, one try, and six minors to a goal and four minors. Teams :—Dewsbury : J. Heeson, back ; R. E. Lockwood J. Naylor, and Hopkins, three-quarter-backs; Samp- son and Stadden, half-backs; J. Garforth, Thomson, C. Garforth, Redfearn, Jackson, Taylor, Wolstenholme, Randall, and Boothiman, forwards. Runcorn : J. Bra- zendale, back; T. H. Davies, W. A. Riley. and R. Cook- son, three-quarter-backs ; H. Hughes and Geoege Whitby, half-backs; W. Faulkner, W. Hughes, George Wain- wright, J. Gayter, R. Dolan, P. Riley, F. Hancock, J. Clarke, and W. H. Broady, forwards. WARRINGTON V; HECKMONDWIRE. Sp:endid weather again favoured football enthusiasts
in tie Warrifigton district on Monday, and the ". bill ef

fare" being anether Yorkshire organization, who played • such a desperate game with Elalifax in the Yorkshire Cup, a large number of .people assembled to witness the encounter. The home team differed in one respect from that which figured against Dewsbury, T. Jolley,. taking Nevins' place at back. The visitors—the biggest team that has been seen at Wilderspool this season—were strongly represented, and di±ectly after the advertised time set to kick Off Frank Turner commenced hostilities against a slight breeze. Noble returned; and Barnes I having his kick charged down, matters appeared rather I gloomy for the home team. Jolley however came to the I rescue, and his efforts being aided by Davies, the game was transferred to the Ileckmondwike quarters. Barnes passed to Massey, the latter making a gallant bid for scoring honours; but Wharton held him close to the line. Give-and-take play was the order, until Sutcliffe, 'by a huge punt, changed the venue to the Warrington quarters. Speakman replied by smart work to the half- way flag, and both Jolley and Barnes individuallyhelped to press the Tykes back to their lines. The Warrington skipper was foiled by Sutcliffe, but a smart kick by Jol- ley was well followed up, and the return was prevented. Fair. Turner charged Sutcliffe's kick down, but the ex- Bradford player was again to the fore with some really smart work. The brothers Jolley put in some tall kicks, and from a pack near the visitors'line, Sutcliffe received possession, and punted to the Warrington quarter flag. The visitors followed up smartly, arid Porritt and Noble took the leather over, the first-named being the lucky recipient. The kick at goal failed. A huge drop out was followed well up by Littlewood, the latter prevent- ing the reply. Fair. Turner put, in some strong work, and Davies west° the fore with a really brilliant run. Masseywas awarded a free kick, and again the home team VAS placed in the aggressive. Jolley replied to a hugh kick of Sutcliffe's, and from the latter's effort War- rington conceded a minor. Povey prevented a reply to the drop out, and Ashton put in a grand dribble to the Fieckmondwike lines. Warren was now seen threading his way through the apposing team, but unfortunately grounded the wrong side of the line. Fair. The weather just before the time set for the lack-off showed for rain, but happily it passed off, and when both teams made their appear- ance from the pavilion end,:hearty cheers greeted them. , Barnes having lost the toss, Frank Turner commenced hostilities from the pavilion end, but off-side play neces- sitated a scrimmage at centre. From a line-out Lock- wood obtained possession, but was foiled by Barnes, who relieved neatly to neutral ground; but the Dewsbury men were not to be denied and a strong dribbleby the forwards, headed by Redfern, caused ...Nevins to adopt the saving clause. Fair Turner and Littlewood were prominent after the drop-out, and Massey headed a fine dribble to the Dewsbury quarters, Lockwood saving. Frank Turner dropped out, but a good rush, headed by Thompson and Redfern, placed the home line in jeopardy. Frank Turner relieved by a dribble to quarter flag, but Graham obtaining Possession put in a huge punt to Nevins, and the latter failing to gather the ball, Jackson rushed up and grounded, Heesom landing a goal from the place. Warrington were again pressed after the recommencement, Barnes and Jolley making strenuous efforts to retrieve their position, the latter I eventually running the ball out to quarter flag. War- rington now had a turn. Littlewood broke away from the line-out, and following up smartly, prevented Gra- ham from returning. Jolley further improved by a punt to the Dewsbury quarters, but the visit proved to be of short duration, the, home ttani be forced back by the strong combined play of the Dewsbury men. Half time was immediately afterwards called, with the score—Dewsbury, 2 goals and 3 minors; Warrington, 1 try and 2 minors. On resuming, Ashton charged down the kick-off, and play was for some time confined to cen- tre. Warren here made strong efforts to get away, but was foiled by Graham; but the home forwards succeeded in invading the Dewsbury quarters, where Lockwood, being beautifully served by Graham, made tracks for the home line, and, rounding his opponents in the easiest possible manner, grounded the leather, Heesom failing to improve the point. Exchange kick; by the opposing backs followed the re-start, Warrington having slightly the advantage. pressing the Yorkshiremen back. Warren now got round the pack and put in a short run, and kicked across to Massey, who gathered the ball in fine style, but was unfortunately pushed into touch on the Dewsbury line. A series of scrimmages ensued, Hullah returning to neutral ground. Warrington, however, again pressed, and a good rush, headed by Ashton,Povey, and Fair. Turner, ended in Heesom kicking dead. The drop-out still found play in Dewsbury quarters, Barnes, Warren, Jolley, and Massey putting in some sterling work, the latter player losing the ball just when he seemed to have a chance, Dewsbury saving. From the drop-out Barnes secured possession and `put in a dodgy run, but the visiting forwards went up the field with 'a rush, and Nevins again failino• to return, a minor re- sulted. From the drop-out Warren and Massey were answerable for some good work, and gradually the Tykes were forced to give ground, Lockwood eventually con- ceding a touchdown; but the venue was soon changed, and operations raged for some time after in the Warring- ton twenty-five, where from some loose play Garforth by a flying kick placed another goal to the Dewsbury score. It cannot be denied that the best team won, the Dews- bury men playing well together and showing superior combination, but the game was not of so one-sided a nature as the score would indicate. During the first half, indeed, Warrington had a full share of the game, the combination of the forwards and the tackling of the backs being all that could be desired ; but in the second half both backs and forwards seemed to lose heart, and I did not play with their accustomed dash and spirit. ELTON HALL.-It has often been remarked by foreign- ers travelling in England, that the relations existing be- tween the landowner of large estates and his numerous tenants are almost without exception of the pleasantest. The English farmer takes great pride and thoroughly enjoys seeing the master at the hall riding to hounds across his growing wheat and oat fields, and rushes out crying "Tally-ho" with all the zest of a lover of the sport, even though his crops are seriously damaged thereby. The master and his family in return do not forget the tenant. During the shooting season on large preserved estates, many a brace of game finds its way to the farmer's cottage, and by other numerous little atten- tions the farmer is made to feel that his welfare is not lost sight of by the master at the hall. A notable in- stance of the landowner's thoughtfulness of the require- ments of his tenantry and sympathy with their misfor- tunes was recently illustrated in Ludlow. H. Bullock Webster, Esq., master at Elton Hall, Ludlow, Salop and Hereford, was passing one of his cottages on Sunday, when a dog-cart drov* up bringing the cottager's son, Mr. George Whitton, who had been living on a farm in Radnorshire. Upon inqniry he found the son had been sent home being completely crippled with rheumatism in his legs, so much so that it took three men to help him out of the dog-cart into the cottage. Mr. Webster, with that sympathy which characterises the true English gentleman, followed the mother of the lad into the cot- tage, and learning of his serious condition advised her, before sending for the doctor, to use St. Jacobs Oil, offer- ing to furnish her a bottle from his own supply, which he always kept at the hall, telling her to follow the di- rections carefully. The Oil was applied by the mother, the lad being too feeble to use it himself, with the result of immediate relief from pain, and in three days the lad was able to walk about; and in one week from the &St application walked to Ludlow railway station,which is five miles away, in order to get back to his place in Radnorshire by rail: The mother naturally looks upon St. Jacobs, Oil as a wonderful blessing. It not only cured her son, who was crippled and helpless, in one week, but it saved her a large doctor's bill. She used, we under. stand, but two bottles of this now famous remedy. Mr. Webster not only volunteers to vouch for the truthful- ness of the above statement, but allows his name to be used for reference. The above is but one of the many instances which constantly occur, as showing the in- terest which the English landowner always has in his tenant's welfare, and which is not equalled by any country in the world.

ANOTHER EMBANKMENT.

The waters of that part of the canal which runs through the land at present enclosed by the bend of the river will be provided with embankments as the intended level of the canal will be almost e'ven with the natural surface of the ground here. Throughout the length the embankments will be about ten feet above the waters of the canal, and the southern slcpe of the embankment will, for , the purpose of improving the view from the Thel- wall direction, not be steeper than one in ten feet, and if the Canal Company, are required by Mr. Stanton, this slope will be covered with good soil to a depth of two feet at least, and planted with suitable trees and shrubs. And it is ,further provi- ded that no buildings, except a ferry house, shall at any time be erected by the Company on the south side of the canal between the eastern boundary of the township of Thelwall and the village of Thel- wall, without the consent of Mr. Stanton, or unless that gentleman shall dispose of or apply his land in ale neighbourhood to qommercial purposes.

div.head: CART ROAD.
div.p: A CART ROAD.

Just at the Lymm side of Mr. Stanton's residence there branches off, in a northerly direction, from the road leadimf from Warrington to Lymm, a cart road which, after taking a sharp bend towards the north-west, again resumes its northerly course alongside the Mersey. This roadway, like so many others, will be intersected by the conal, and in this case there does not seem to be any provision for a ferry or other means of crossing. That part of the road which lies to the north of the route of the canal will, it is evident, be cut off from its present connection with Thelwall ' • but to obviate this difficulty there isto be "a good and sufficient" cart- way made along the north bank of the canal, and between the canal and thediverted river, which will give the means of getting on to the cartroad which at present runs from the centre of Thelwall village northwards, and for wbich, as we mentioned last week, there is to be a ferry for the purpose of carry- ing over persons and vehicles. (TO Le continued.)

Addressing a deputation who waited upon him at Birmingham on Wednesday, Mr. Chamberlain spoke in favour of the adoption of the principle of friendly negotiation in the settlement of international differ- ences.

div.p: CHRIST CHURCH, LAiCHFORD.

The annual vestry meeting of this Church was held in the Schoolroom, Wash-lane, on Thursday evening, the Vicar (the Rev. B. B. Prescott) presiding. There were also present Messrs. H. Woods, John ' Lee, William Tinsley, Edward Greanall. junr., John White, John Goxon. Wallace, Gorton, Lowe, Starkey, W. Green, Kirkham and Gen.—The accounts, which were presented by Mr. H. Woods, showed that, the re- ceipts for the past year had been Erpt 5s 6d, and the expendi- ture £lB6 15s 9d; leaving a balance due to the churchwardens of Ell 10s 3to:l.—After the adoption of the accounts, the Vicar nominated as his warden Mr. H. Woods, and Mr. James Lowe was elected people's warden.—Messrs. J. Coxon and Gorton were elected sidesmen, and Messrs. John White and Edward Greenall, jun., were elected lay representatives.—lt was decided that the salaries of the organist and the apparitor should remain the same as last year.—Mr. H. Woods men- tioned that the view of the beautiful window in the east end of the church, given by Captain Reynolds, wairspoiled by the corona In the chancel, and that the corona was inconvenient In other respects. It had been suggested that it should be taken down, and the chancel lighted by standards or pendants.

It was, however, necessary that the consent of the vestry should be got for this proceeding.—Mr. John Lee proposed, and Mr. W. Tinsley seconded, that the consent of the vestry be given, and the proposition was carried unanimously.—Mr. John White said that he hoped that no more standards would be placed in the chancel, as they would be very annoying to people who sat in the body of the church.—On the proposition of Mr. Gorton., seconded by Mr. Wallace, a sub-committee, consisting of the vicar, churchwardens, sidesmen, and Mr. John White, was chosen to consider the best way of lighting the chancel.—The question of new psalters for the choir ' was also brought up, and, after some discussion, Mr. William Tinsley said that if they would order the 'sultans he would be pleased to pay for them.. (Applatise.)—A vote of thanks, proposed by Mr. W. Woods, and seconded by Mr. Lowe, was then accorded the organist and choir for their efficient services during the past year.

The Easter vestry for the township of Southworth-with- Croft was held on Monday morning. The Rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman. presided. Messrs. The ati!!`eal vestry meeting was held in the schoolroom, on Tuesday; th.,,,s vicar in the chair, and there were also present—Messrs ,John Hindley, John Higham, Wyndham Smith, Peter ratrix, It. T. Mr. Jarhes Hindley and Mr. John Ingham were re-elecled war- dens for the ensuing year, and the following gentlemen were appointed sidesmen Messrs Lythgoe, Lowe, W. Smith, and John Holland. Resolutions were come tO,baaring on the chur&yard question, and as to the voluntary contributions towards the expenses of, the year. The death of the Rector of Warrington was referred to with much feeling by the chairman, who also regretted much the loss of Mr. 11609011. MARRIED IN HASTE TO REPENT AT - LEISURE.

- --- Before Mr. John Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Blackburn was summoned for assaulting his wife Sarah. The defendant did not appear.—The Col- plainant said she kept the Albion beer-house in Peel-street. Her husband had been at sea, but OA present he was not doing anything. She married' Ili:fiat:tout 17 months ago, after having only been acquainted with him three weeks as he appeared such a nice decent young fellow. . A week afterwards, , he made her little girl's mouth bleed, and he had behave" • badly to her since. He had given her black eyes el several occasions. He did not get any work to do, anu was driving business from the house. She had a familY and plenty of money when she married him, but now nearly all her money was gone ; and he did not seen; to care. On Saturday the 24th March .he "cursed anti swore" at her and struck her on the head with his fist' On the application of the woman the Bench granted 3 warrant for the apprehension of Blackburne, and hei;o3 brought into court before the rising of the magistrates. Mrs. Blackburne now said she was sorry to say anything against her husband, and if he would say he mas sorl she was willing to forgive him. She had forgiven hinl many a time, of course," but she ought to forgive hitn because she thought well of him. She was a bitliot-ter pered and very hasty as well as he was. They would he very happy together if he would just " shape " a bit.-; Defendent : Did you pick up a poker to strike me.—N°' got a bit of stick. lam sorry to say I ani a great covi: ard or I should have used it.—Gertrude Littlewood, daughter Of the complainant's, proved the assault, an' said the defendent threatened to throw a bucket of wal upon her mother.—Mrs. Blackburne : That was only fun, you know my love.—The defendant said he sorry to appear there. He denied striking his wife. merely pushed her when he was taking the poker EI her.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said the woman been to the police station on many occasions, and he afraid there would be something serious sometime.—, defendant: There will be nothing further done. .1 I going to get work to-morrow.—Mr. Brtmdrit : That what you ought to have done long since. He ought be ashamed of himself to live upon a woman and abc her.—The defendant was fined 20s and costs las ed, or default, a month's hard labour.

div.head: WA"RRINOTON UNION RURAI, SANITARY
div.p: WA"RRINOTON UNION RURAI, SANITARY
AUTHORITY.

• The monthly meeting of this Authority WAS held at the Workhouse yesterday morning. The Itev. G. F. Roberts presided: , and there were also present Messrs. W. Darbyshire, Jolley, Heaton, W Hough- ton, J. Heughton, Hiimpbries, Penniagtoti, Rilshail, Crieening, Z. Armitage; S. Sutton (clerk), Dr Seph- ten (medical, officer); W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Nerfoot (inspector). FENFIMI DRAINAGE; minutes of a nApetiny I of the Penketh Parochial Committee, lield on the 27t1). March, were'readTahttfrOrtrthem it appeared that Mr. Routledge had produced specifications of work to he done in connection with the 'drainage •scheme; and the same were approved: •Tenders for the work prescribed in the specifications which had been received by the clerk' 'Were opened and considered. They were as ,follows : Messrs ay-ce and Randle, • £246 is 3d ; Messrs Hough and Son, £380; Messrs Roberts Brothers, , £266 14s; Messrs Aaron Turner and Sons, £320; Mr Robert Maim bar, £226 ; 'Mr John Taylor, £200; and Mr W. Heaton, £215. After discussion it was decided to recommend to the Rural Sanitary. Authority the acceptance of Mr. Taylor's tender: for £2oo.—The CLERK reported that he •had served the necessary notices as instructed at the last , meeting upon Messrs ,Pilkington, Cook, and Pownall, and produced duplicates of the same. He also read a letter from Messrs Brighouse, Brighouse and Jones, solicitors, Ormskirk, on behalf of Mr: Pilking,ton, objecting to the notice. . The Clerk was instructed to lay the same before.the Rural Sanitary Authority. Mr Routledge was instructed to see Messrs. Pilkington, Cook, and Pownall upon the subject of compensation, for damage.—The,se minutes after some discusSion in which Messrs. Rout• ledge and R. Garnett, who were present on. behalf of the Parochial Committee, took part, were confirmed.

,HOSPITAL ACCOMMODATION.—A letter was read. from the Local Government Board asking as to what the Authority Was doing with regard to the provision of hos- pital accommodation.—The Cpsax said he had written in reply stating that the matter had had the considera- tion of the Authority, who were alive to the importance of the question, and would be prepared to deal with it in a satisfactory manner. He also 'mentioned that the small-pox cases had disappeared, and that in ,case of need the Authority coulrLhaye a portable hospital erec- ted within a few houra.—ln reply to this letter the Local Government Board had sent a further communication stating that they did not consider the arrangement with regard to the portable hospital as efficient. Hence, they regretted that the Sanitary Authority had net seen their way to providing such permanent hospital accommoda- tion as would be available for the immediate isolation of the first cases of infectious diseases.—Mr. PENNINGTON thought it wasmot muqh use that Authority into ac- tion as, after the Local Government 13ill came opera- tion, their sanitary powers would be taken out of their hands. Ultimately •it was agreed that the Local Governtnent Board shonld be informed that the subject would have the Authority's attention. ALLEGED NVISANCES.—Dr. SEPIITON reported that com- plaints had been made of the pollution of Garnett's brook, Latchford, by Messrs. rierpoint and Bryant 's skin yard at Latchford, and he had instructed the inspector to obtain samples of the water above and below the works for analysis. He had also had complaint made by Mr: Wonky, of Winwick, of a nuisaace existing at Long- ford opposite to the Corporation depot, and a few yards on the east side of the Winw*k-road, caused by the de- posit of excreta from the pails from Warrington.—ln- structions were given that steps should be taken ler the abatement of the nuisances in each case, it having been ' previously explained by Mr. Greening that tho nuisance at Longford was not caused by the Corporation, but by 'farmers who had bought raw material from the Corpora- tion.

VOTE OF THANKS.—That being the Ist meeting of the Authority within the period for which the chairman was elected,a cordial vote of thank as passed to Mr. Roberts on the motion of Mr. DARBYSHIRE, seconded by Mr. Z. ARMITAGE, and supported by Mr. GREENING.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT DITTON.
div.p: THE ACCIDENT AT DITTON.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner. on urday held an inquest, at the Blackburne Hotel; Ditton, on the body of James Tomlin aged 13, stepson of Peter Harper, of 55, Oakl. street, 'Widnes. TO MR. SIMPSON. An event of interest to the • Wesleyans of 111 corn was celebrated on Tuesday evenings years had elapsed since Mr, John Simpson .

connected with Brunswick Wesleyan Siinday Schl and it was determined to mark this unique jubi in a suitable manner. Subscriptions to the* monial to Mr. Simpson's life of christian usefulo flowed in very freely, and the:money was expendeLii in obtaining a massive gold medal ad a beautr and faithful portrait of J 111•. Simpson. On the 0, verse of the medal is the following iuscriptiofl,e, "Presented to John Simpson, Esq., on his coroP,II, tion of 60 years' connection with the BrunsWle Wesleyan Sunday School, by the teachers a1,1,e Scholars at present or formerly- connected with School, as a token of their esteem and appreciatA, of his valuable services. Runcorn, January 11' 1838." On the reverse side is a capitairepresentrc lion of the front of Brunswick School. A simll3,, inScription wait placed upen the handsome frali7. of the portrait. (Hear, hear.)—Mr J: Unsworth relateo ho the idea of the testimonial to Mr. Simpson origin?: ted with the teacherk' meeting and said when their w. tendon became known sutnekptions flowed in freelY,', —Mr. T: Simister sincerely congratulated Mr. SiMPse'l upon having completed fifty years of what they felt 114, been a work of faith and a labour of love. The prosper'" bf the school was largely owing to Mr. Simpson's intlueneel. Mr. Simister then handed Mr. Simpson the gold medo' ' and at the same time Mr. Unsw.Orth uncovered the Pf trait, the audience rising to their feet •simultaneou and enthusiastically cheering Mr. Simpson for a considcl; able time.—b reply Mr. Simpsonrthanked all of tho'd Who had taken part in this matter most heartily 0e most sincerely for their very great 'kindness, , which ',.' , fully appreciated. Mr. Simpson, having given some ticulars of his early history,:related sonic reminisce"c.,' of the old ' school, and the teatters and sciwt lags, and described how. he ,became supeirintendent Mill Brow,"and then at Brunswick. From the 23rd ALigi 1857, when he became superintendent at BninsWict 'Schliol, to the 6th September, 1862, he was only absetto. three Sundays—(applause)—and for more than 35 he had never once been late. (Applause.) Twenty-±t years ago the teachers 'and friends in connection wia, Brunswick Sunday School presented him with a han some silver cup, and at the centenary of Sunday scho°,', the representatives of the Nonconformist Sunday scho°' in the town presented him with a silver medal. OW ,plause.) He should treasure these mementos of his 0,11; nection with Sunday SchooLs, and that portrait whiL,, , had just been uncovered would be something for friends to look at when they could not have the pleastij of viewing the medals. In conclusion, Mr. Simpson st that as long as he lived and had health and strength should never feel disposed to sever his connection v4,t,;, Brunswick Sunday School, (Applause.)—Mr. J. Norman; and rd.,' Dunbavand paid their tribute of praise to Mr. for his self-sacrificing labours, and the meeting CC" eluded.

div.head: BOAT' ladE‘ ON THE MERSEY.
div.p: BOAT' ladE‘ ON THE MERSEY.

The nineteenth annual yacht vice in connection with the Warrington (Bank Quay). Sailing Club took place on the Mersey on Saturday ,in line weather. A large number of persons assenibled on the bank of the river, on the Lanbashire sine, to witness the finish of the race, and the presence of a number of shownien, and other itinerant caterers of public amusement, gave the place the appearance of a fair ground. The course was from Runcorn, round a boat moored at; Six Acre, near Walton Arches, and•thence to the west end of Thewlis's wall. The competing boats were :—Gipsy, Captain John Leigh; Florence, Captain William Warburton; Mischief, Captain T. Swift; and May Fly, Captain James Davison. The boats made an exc'ellent start from Runcorn, under the management of Mr. John Rathbone, who perforined the duties 'of starter in a very satisfactory manner. May Fly and Aliscilief were the first to leave the starting point, and, under a stiff breeze from the north-east, they kept well together, and made an exciting race, up to Hough- ton Marsh point. Florence joined in the race five minutes later, and Gipsy brought up the rear five , minutes after Florence. There was plenloy of water to move in, and thus there was every prospect of an excellent contest. In a short time it became evi- dent that Gipsy was gradually diminishing the distance betive6n the lroit and the ones precedifig her, and even- tually she succeeded in passing Florence near Richmond Island, and went on . in hot pursuit ,of the re- maining boats. By, this time The wind had abated considerably, making progress Slower, and the spectators, many of Whom! had been waiting some time, began to feel doubtful whether any. of the boats would succeed in reaching the winning post. Their fears in this direction were heightened on account of what little wind remained being dead again tile peting craft. The Gipsy. however, could be seen to be steadily coming up, "hand over hand," and she passed the other boats at the entrance of the Bank Quay reach. Her excellent sailing qualities, combined with' the skill .of her captain, enabled her to make an easy *in. 'Gipsy was the only boat that sailed the entire course—round the buoy at Six Acre, and back to the end of Thewlis'i wall—.and she therefOre gained the first prize, £3 15s. The remaining boats finished in the' following order May Fly, prize £2 15s; -3, Mischief, prize £2 ; and 4, , Florence, prize , £l. Mr. :James Leigh was judge, Mr. C. C. Naylor secretary, Mr. J. Whit- field treasurer; and • Mr. W. ;Melia- •number• taker.— On,Monday the members of the Upper 'Mersey Sailing Club lield their first annual race, an event which in future it is intended to establish as an Easter Monday fixture. Five boats competed, and a:4 there were five prizes each competitor obtained a reward. The course was from Fidler's Ferry to Ma.ndock Bay, near Arpley Station. The contest lasted two hours, and was watched by a considerable number of spectators. From the start Torn Bowling took the lead, and maintained it with com- parative ease for the whole of the distance, eventually winning a runaway race by half an hour from the second boat. The other boats kept well together for the greater part of the time, but Primrose took the lead when three- quarters of the distance, and sailed in second The fol- lowing was the order at the finish :—Tom Bowling (Cap- tain John Harris), 1 ; Primrose (Captain Samuel Spencer), 2; Deerfoot (Captain T. Skelhorn), 3; Reaper (Captain James Leslie), 4; Jane (Captain Henry Lloyd), 5. The officials were:' Judge, Mr. James Ash- urst ; starter, Mr. James Green; secretary, Mr. John Harris; and treasure, Mr. Thomas Armstrong,

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Pre.sta ilOard of Guar- dians was held at anion Workhoute, Whiston, on Ttturs day week, when Mr. J. Fisher presided, and them:were also present—Messrs. W. Middlehurst, J. Griffith, J. Whalley, W. Swift, T. Eatock, .T. lluckley, E. Syder, J. Burchall, W. G. Ashton, J. Leatherbarrow, C. B. John- son, W. Tyrer, J. Musson, J.Ranson, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.—"The Master reported that there were 528 inmates in the house this week, 554 last week, grid 492 in the corresponding week of last year. There had been 71 vagrants relieved during the past week, against 68 in the corresponding week of last year.—The Clerk said the master would like the Hoard to allow him more help in the office. He had, been pay- ing a lad for eighteen months out of his own pocket.— The matter was referred to the Visiting dnd Finance Committees. _

THE VACANCY AT RAINFORD.—The LOCAL Government Board wrote- intimating that they had, issued orders authorising the special election of a guardian for the township of Rainford. VACCINATION 'OFFICER FOR lIITYTON. A communica- tion was received from the Local Government Board, asking if the guardians had appOinted a successor to Mr. J. Pendleton, vaccination officer, for the Huyton district, and if so they desired the particulars of the appointment. —The Clerk said forms had been filled up and sent to the Local Government Board. SmAt.Lrox.—The Clerk said that as smallpox had made its appearance in the Union, the master would like dis- cretionary power to stop visiting in the Workhouse in the event of the spread of the disease.—Mr. Leatherbar- row moved, and Mr. Graves seconded that the power the master asked for be given.—Carried.—The Clerk after+ wards stated that he had received a letter from one of the medical officers of the Union, reporting a case of smallpox, and oh receipt of that letter he had issued notices inviting attention to the desirability of vaccina- tion or re-vaccination, as the case might be. THE L.ATE MR.. JOSEPH JACESON.—A lettA3t VMS read from Mr. Hugh H. Jackson, of St. Helens, acknowledg- ing, on behalf of his mother, the receipt of the letter of condolence and sympathy from the Guardians on the death of his father. THE Drynanow or A PAUPER—The Clerk read the fol- lowing letter from the Widnes Local Board :—" Dear Sir, —The annexed is a copy of the recorded minutes after the interview with your deputation on Menday last. If in order please confirm.—Yours, &c., J. B. ALLEN, clerk. —'Fever Hospital Pauper Cases. The following was agreed to as a definition of a pauper for the year ending the 35th March, 1888 :—All tramps and all in receipt of relief (money or kind) immediately prior to the removal to the hogpifal. Resolved, that the Widnes cases under the foregoing definition be received upon the Guardians undertaking to pay 3s per day for each case, and to pro- vide medical attendance."—The Clerk said that was the outcome of a visit to the Widnes Local Board, and he would recommend that they accept the terms.—Mr. Eatock prpposed that the terms be accepted. He thought it was very fair.—The Chairman said the Board had met them very courteously, and gave every attention to what they had to say.—Mr. Buckley seconded the mo- tion, which was carried. This was all the business.

Sir,—l am forced to the conclusion that , when "Cadmus" read my two letters, he was either standing on his head, or was suffering from moral blindness, he has so entirely mystified, not to say falsified, my opinions. To bandy further words with him is to thrash a dead dos., for no matter what I write he will twist it round to his way of thinking, which is about as wide of my own ideas as an unscrupulous advocate can care to go. His conceited -views of his logical strength are simply lamentable; and I think the most charitable construction is the best to put on what he has subscribed to your columns, and I give him the benefit of it, and say that he is the living representation and illustration of that verse which runs thus:

That fellow—he is gravel blind, ADA ne'er has seen the skies; For nature, when she made his head, Forgot to dot his eyes! Farewell, " Cadmus !" And don't write any more letters until your moral vision has improved, and when you can tell (when you will tell) black from white. Up to now, you either cannot or will not. BELLEROPHON. Warrington, April 4, 1888.

LIBERALISM IN THE NEWTON DIVLSION. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me a little space to air what is felt here to be a considerable grievance, namely, that while the Conservative party were qualetly allowed to hold their round of pablic meetings without any comment from your contemporary here, the moment the Liberals began their round, a series of snarling par- agraphs appeared in its columns, to which a writer signing himself "Nil Desper:andum " replied. Now it seems, however, that there is a change in the tactics owing to pressure on their space; and, as the matter is in a sense so very trivial and may be forgotten before room can be found, it may be as well to say at once that it is a pity the writer in the last issue should have gone out of his way to show the poverty of the Haydock meet- ing while professing such friendliness. It is, however, all of a piece with his jibing of the Liberal party in the Newton Division, and can serve no good purpose except perhaps to open the eyes of its readers more ,clearly to see who are their fair-weather friends. If it be really true that the Liberal party is sick, it is only in accor- dance with the fable that the Tory ass should come to give him a kick, but he is not so far gone as to mistake his braying for anything more serious. But, beside all that, it is not true ; there is good hope of his speedy recovery from his passing lethargy. Exception was taken to the way in which an ima.gin- ary meeting was treated as a real meeting, and the 3oke was thought so immense as to be worthy of figuring in the "Liverpool Courier," and when the real meeting was held no reporter was present. If he had been, he would have found, as in Haydock, that not a tithe of ,those called dame, because they couldn't, and yet the meeting in Newton was in other respects very satisfac- tory. And so it was in Haydock, that while the first meeting was but small, the reporter for himself, and without pandering to any perverted taste, should have said so, or held his peace for ever. The adjourned meeting which took place on the 27th ult, .was both business-like and satisfactory. I don't, of course, know what meaning he attached to the word "influential," which, without being asked he used; but this I know that it is through the combined efforts of "ordinary voters, reporters, and registration agents," who are also voters, that elections are won, in despite of the malign influences to which "Nil Desperandum " had referred, in his series of letters now cut short, I suppose. But these influences will soon lose their power to do fur- ther misclgef either in Newton, Haydock, or elsewhere. But neither did the übiquitous reporter attend that meet- ing either ; I suppose he was so little in touch that he knew of neither. Who is this that affects to sneer at reporters, registration agents, and ordinary voters. Some superior person, doubtless! But let him and all whom it may concern know that such lowly persons are as much a necessary evil as he is. Ay! and if this new Local Government Bill of the Tory-Whigs should pass into law, there will, and must be more of the latter, and their status will be better than ever. Some good people, who ought to know better than to expect it, wish the Government to introduce manhood suffrage, and do away with registration altogether, as they vainly think it will, while the Government are on another,and quite opposite tack, and have given 'us in- stead an extension of the municipal suffrage to females in counties. How qtfietly we are taking this projected -extension of the franchise_ to female householders .in the counties. And why? Bocause there is a consciousness m all that there is no valid argument against it. This of itself will bring grist to the mill. If there is to be man- hood suffrage, there must also be womanhooi suffrage now or the old inequality will subsist, but we are yet a little way off that consummation. Consider what may have been the intention of the Legislature in the recent enactments for lodgers, and how easily that good inten- tion was frustrated by the simple device of the rating clause, "And after that we shan't need them." Indeed, then how about the franchise in America? Does every one record his vote wherever he likes and why.never.he likes? Is he registered? and if so, by whom, when and where and why? Perhaps some of your readers will en- lighten us on the subject. The idea is beautiful in its simplicity, but how does it work out in practice? Having some regard for your space, I reserve what further I have to say for another opportunity. Thank- ing you for the present privilege, I am, yours truly, BONNE ESPERANCE.

RUNAWAY Honsn.--On Saturday evening last, as Mr. Worsley, one of Mr. Brown's shop assistants, was about to urgiarness a horse near to Mr. John Leigh's yard, the animal bolted and made direct for one of Mr. J. Warbur- ton's windows. Mr. Worsley was, however, able to swerve the horse round, but at the same time the board- ing over the cellar immediately under the window (and which extends the whole width of the footpath) gave way. Still more startled by this incident, the animal rushed round Mr. Ferris's corner, with the cart behind him, up Pepper-street, where he was captured opposite Mr. Holt's. Fortunately, no one was injured, and it is stated that the horse was also unhurt. _ _ _
