Mairs WEDDINGS.—On Tuesday, the weddg of Mr. Hugh Harrison to Miss Sarah Wood Brazendale, fourth daugh- ter of Mr. William Brazendale, was celebrated at the Parish Church, Lyntn, by the Rev. G.. W. Guest, assisted by the Rev: E. W. Lomax. The bride wore a dress of silver grey cashmere and silk, and the brides- maids, Miss Harriet Brazendale, sister, and Miss Ball. of Eccles, cousin of the bride, wore dresses of the rittane colour, but a little darker in ' shade. Mr. George Fair- dough and Mrjrank Brazendale performed the office of best men. The bride was given away by her father. Before the ceremony Mr. Blackmore played the March Militant, on the organ, and after the ceremony rendered Xendelssohn's Wedding March. • After the breakfast the

newly-niarried pair were driven to Warrington, from whence they travelled by train to Llandudno, where the honeymoon will be spent. Among many other valuable presents received by the bride the teachers of the Parish Church Sunday School presented her with a beautiful silver cake basket and knife, on the former of which was engraved, "Presented to Miss Sarah Wood Brazendale, by the teachers of the Parish Church Sunday Schools, Lymm, on her marnage, April 3rd, 1886." An illumin- ated address and a family Bible were also presented by the pupils of her school.—The wedding of Mr. George Littleton Dewhurst, eldest son of Mr. G. Z. Dewhurst, of Oughtrington Park, to Miss Davidson, daughter of the late Archibald Davidson, sheriff of Midlothian, was solemnised at the Cathedral in Edinburgh, on Wednes- day last.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
(Continued from page 6.)
LOWER WALTON.

This week a number of men have been put to work on the/ canal near Morley Common, the Company having come into possession of land .from Acton Grange to Lower *Walton. Near to the Common about 100 men are busy makir

ing the preliminary cutting, soil and rock being con- veyed in waggons underneath the archways of the two railways at Acton Grange to the embankment by the Old Quay Canal. As no embankments are to be made in the vicinity of Morley Common, some million tons of earth will have to be disposed of in this manner, the distance being from one and a half to two miles.. A per- ceptible change has already been effected, and ft cutting some 200 yards in length has been made near to Lower Walton. Holes have been sunk for the purpose of pump- ing up the surface and spring water. A portable engine and other machinery have been got on the field adjoining the foot-road, leading from Walton Arches to opposite Mr. Crosfield's, Walton Lea. Sheds have been ppt up and other preparations are in progress for the purpose of facilitating the work. Near Acton Grange twelve workmen's dwellings have been erected. They are of wood, with brick fireplaces and chimneys. A number of these dwellings are likewise to be erected on the other side the railways in the field near Ball's Wharf, where already a large engine-shed capable of holding eight loeomotives has been built. Fresh material is continually arriving at Ball's Wharf, which is already covered with a variety of plant, con- sisting of machinery, waggons, wheels, barrows, timber, and other articles. In the cutting near to what was formerly Bellhouse-lane, the men have resumed work after the Easter holidays, and a large number of new hands have been successful in getting a job on the canal. MOORE.

Near to Bob's Bridge trunks and other portions of large trees have been unearthed at a depth of two or three feet below the surface. The "American" navvy is doing good work; the cutting is growing larger every day. The German navvy has made a deep cutting about half a mile in length; and at the bottom there is a swift run- ning current of water. Two more of these wonders are to be got to work shortly; one to be used on Frodsham marshes, and the other at Barton, near Manchester. A number of the directors passed along this section on Thursday and inspected the works from Acton Grange to Runcorn. A large number of people from Warring- ton and surrounding villages continue daily to view the progress of the work.

div.head: -15E-ATH OF A NAVVY,
div.p: -15E-ATH OF A NAVVY,

One of the workmen employ6d at Bob's Bridge was taken ill very suddenly, and expired at his lodgings, in Moore, after a few hour's suffering. He was interred at Daresbury Church on Friday. The deceased, whose name was George Barnes, was a stranger to the district. The coffin and expenses of funeral were provided by the Company and by his fellow-workmen. It is stated that inflammation was the cause of deaths THELWALL. .

At Thelwall the work is still being pushed ahead with great vigour. Steam navvies are now in operation, and locomotives are constantly busy drawing waggons laden with "spoil" from the intended bed of the canal. One row of navvies' huts is now rapidly approaching com- pletion, and another row has been begun with. Another largewooden building being rapidlyerected neart,o Morris Brook, and evidently intended as a shed for the locomo- tives, and indeed the whole scene is now of the busiest description.

div.head: RIXTON.
div.p: RIXTON.

Work was resumed on Tuesday after the Easter holi- days, and steady prpgress is being made. Two addi- tional engines have arrived at Irlam station, and have been conveyed by road to the scene of operations. They are named the Norton and the Didsbury. Portions of another steam navvy have arrived, with several wagon loads of pipes for draining purposes. The works during the,holidays were barricaded off, and the public were not allowed upon the ground.

WIFE DESERTION AT WARRINGTON. AN EX-COUNCILLOR BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. At Warrington Borough Police Court on Thurs- day, before Major Litton and Alderman Webster, James Cave Whittle, described as a mining engineer, and Who was formerly a member of the Town Council. was brought up in custody on a charge of having neglected to maintain his wife, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians, stated that about eight weeks ago the prisoner left the town, leaving his wife in a destitute condition and without means of support. On Thursday week she sent fOr him, and on going to the house he found that everything had been sold, he believed for rent, and Mrs Whittle was turned into the street. A neighbour took her in, as she was in a_pitiable condition, having nothing but the clothes she stood in. She was admitted to the Workhouse on Monday. Inquiries 'were then made as to the 'whereabouts of the prisoner, who had left the town, but ore'Wed- nesday he came back to Warrington, and was apprehended.—Prisoner alleged that his wife was addicted to intemperance, and he could not live with her. He made her an offer some time ago of 12s a week, but she refused to accept any sum, nd expressed her intention to remain with him. She tore up every letter that came to the house ad- dressed to him, and had also destroyed his letter- book, and in consequence of this his business was ruined. He had also been in ill-health. Half the time he had been away he was confined to bed. He denied that his wife was in want of the necessaries of life, as she had unlimited credit from trades- pecple in the town, and he believed there were now several pounds owing for food which had been ordered during his absence from home. He wanted to get rid of his wife, and the only way he could find, peace was by leaving the town. He was al- most entirely without any income, and he was at a loss to know how he was to contribute to his wife's maintenance. She was an able-bodied woman, and could take the place of a ser- vant. Ultimately the case was adjourned un- til yesterday morning, prisoner being admit- ted to bail. Yesterday he was represented by Mr. A. Browne, who said that Mrs. Whittle had practically had utilimited credit at four shops in the town. Mr. Whittle had only an income of about £3O a year. and had been almost ruined in business by his wife's conduct. He was willing to pay what was due to the Guardians-14s 64—and enter into some arrangement. Ultimately the parties retired, and on their return into court it was stated that an arrangement had been made, whereby the husband agreed to pay to a third party 6d a week towards his wife's maintenace for the next three months, and to again appear before the magistrates at the end of that period. He was then bound over to so appear in hic own recognisances of £lO, and Mr. Wright acted as a surety in the same amount, it be- ing understood that the proceedings would be with- drawn at the end of the three months if the promise' to pay 6s a week had been kept. At the Borough Court on Thursday, a man named William Allen was charged with having neglected -to maintain his.wife and five children, who had be- come chargeable to the common fund of the Union. Previous to last October prisoner's wife obtained re- lief from the Board. of Guardians. Prisoner was ordered to pay 128 64 per week towards her main- tenance, but after promising repeatedly to do so, had failed. He was sent to prison. He had since again neglected to maintain his family. The mag- istrates sent him to prison for a month:

ASHAMED OF HIMSELF.—Before Colonel George MeCor- quodale, and Messrs. R. Houghton T. J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, John Kelly, of Collins Green, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the 11th March. Mrs. Kelly appeared, and in reply to the Bench who asked why her husband had not appeared, he said he was ashamed to come.—The Chairman: But he will have to come.—Mrs. Kelly said her husband told her he was guilty.—The case was adjourned for the defendant to attend at the next court. Local. Fmtuns.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, Joseph Appleton, a baker and flour dealer I at St. Helens, appeared on hislpublic examination The statement of affairs showed total liabilities £929 lOs 10d, and assets £2113 16s 3d, leavink a deficiency of £712 14s 7d. ,In reply to questions by the official receiver, the debtor stated that he commenced,bUsiness in Baldwin- street, St. Helens, in 1882, and did 's. good business ; but two years later he moved to Warrington New-road,being then, as he estimated, worth a clear £4OO. After that he began to go wrong. The debtor was also examined by Mr. H. L. Riley, on behalf of Mr. France, the petitioning creditor, and an adjournment was taken. .

WYC1.121,11 COCIEHRDGE MISSION SELECT CLASS or MALES.—On Good Friday a tea party, kindly given by Mr. John Plituiton„ was held in the above place. About 130 persons sat down to tea, presi- ded over by the Misses Reynolds Hill,. Lilley, Dan- nett, and others. Afterwards an entertainment.took I place, Mr. George Jackson presiding. Songs were given by Messrs. W. Jackson, T. Gallop, J. Astley, J. IMuskett, and a reading by Mr. Joseph Phcenix. At Ithe conclusion of the entertainment a presentation consisting of a large portrait of all, the members of the select class was made to Mr. J. Plinston by Mr. John Hampson, one of the scholars. In the course of his speech he commented on the many services which Mr. Plinston had rendered to the cause of religion at Cockhedge, and to his untiring energies as, teacher of the select class. Messrs. Willett, M us- kett, and Blease also made a few remarks. Mr. Plinston, in replying, assured,the scholars that his interest in the class was as great as ever, and that in the future he trusted they would :have as many successful gatherings as they had had in the past. Mr. Walter Daniels proposed a vote of thanks to all who had so kindly assisted at the tea. This was seconded by Mr. Joseph Smith, and replied to. Games were indulged in after till about 10-30, all dispersing after having thoroughly enjoyed themselves. RASTER SIJNDAY AT Sr. MART'S (8.C.) CHAPEL. —The services at Buttermarket-street (R.C.) Church on Easter Sunday were of more than an ordinary character. Masses were said at eight, nine, and ten o'clock in the morning; the solemn service com- mencing at eleven o'clock, when the officiating priest (Father Sumner) entered the church attended by acolytes, and proceeded down the middle aisle, blessing the assembled congregatiozi with holy water. The priest then retired to-robe for the Mass, and in a few moments the procession entered the church headed by cross bearer, incense bearer, and acolytes, followed by Father Flanigan as deacon, Father Browne sub-deadon, the Superior of St, Mary's, Father Sumner, 0.8.11., as celebrant of the Mass, walking last. The Gospel was sung by Father Flanigan, with organ accompaniment, his flue tiinor voice 'being heard to great advantage. The music selected was Mozart's "Twelfth Mass," which was rendered in an efficient manner by the choir. A sermon was preached,by Father Flanigan, who took for his text, "This is the day which the Lord bath made,; let us be glad, and rejoice therein." Psalm cxvii., verse 24. At the conclusion of the morning service the "Hallelujah Chorus" was played on the new organ, as the largkcongregation left the church. In the evening the vespers were sung 'in English, and the sermon preached by Father Browne, after which the high altar was lighted up with a great. number of candies and adorned with flowers and plants. Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament was given by Father Sumner, assisted by Father Flani- gan and Father Browne. During the Benediction service the choir gave selections. THE DEATH FROM BITRNS,Mr. W. T. Hushand, deputy-coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an inquest at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-street, on Tuesday, touching ,the death of a child, named Frances Smith, two years of age, who was ad- mitted into the Warrington Infirmary on Wednes- day evening, suffering from severe burns.—Theevid- ence ot the child's mother, the wife of a labourer at Acton Grange, was to the effect that on Wednes- day morning she went with her husband to visit some relatives at Frodsham, leaving the child in charge of its brother, seven years old, and a next door neighbour, Mrs. Whalley. On retutninghome, about nine o'clock in the evening, she heard that Ithe child had met with an accident, and had, been itaken to the Infirmary. • There was a fire burning in the grate when she left, and Mrs. Whalley had promised to keep it up for her. A fender was placed 1 before the fire, but no guard.—Elizabeth Whalley said that the deceased child Was playing with her brother, and other children during the after- noon. About six o'clock the little boy came running to the window with his sis- ter in his arms, her clothing being on fire. She extinguished the ,fiames, and found that the child was badly burned about the body, legs, and arm. The appearances seemed to indicate that the child had seated herself on a hot cinder. After applying the usual remedies, she took the child to the Infirmary at Warrington. It expired three hours after admittance.—The Coroner said that he understood that the police knew nothing of the death until 24 hours afterwards. It was in conse- quence of the delay in informing the police that the inquest had not been held earlier. He could not help thinking that the doctm was rather lax in allowing 24 hours to pass before sending word of the death to the police. He hoped the inspector would be able to make some arrangement with the Infirmary authorities, whereby earlier notice of deathr might in future be given.—lnspector Cox promised tq make the Coroner's wishes known in the proper tivarter.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

hospitality. , THE ASSACILT ON A POLICEMAN AT GRAPPEN- HALL.—At the -Quarter Sessions, at Chester, on Thursday, Anthony Callaghan (27), Martin Giblin (20), John Moran (27), and Michael Gaffeney (25), labourers, were indicted for unlawfully assauiting Police-constable Joseph Millington, at Grappenball, on the 24th March last, whilst he was in the exe- cution of his duty. ' Mr. Banks, instructed by Mr. A. Browne, Warrington, appeared' for the defence. ' Prisoners were fpund guilty of common assault, and being sentenced only to one day's imprisonment, they were discharged. LAWN MOWERS Repaired at Garland's. Warrington and Earlestown.—Advt. SUDDEN DEATH AT SANKRY DRIDGES.--A very sudden death occurred on Wednesday morning at Sankey Bridges. A platelayer named Thomas Worsley, 39 years of age, who lives at Bank Quay, went to work as usual early in the morning. About • ight o'clock he and another man named Toft were returning to breakfast, walking along the line, and when near GateiVorth-crossing Worsley suddenly fell down dead. The body was at once removed to the house where the deceased had lived. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquiry res- cting.the death at the Patten Arms Hotel, Wilson Patten-street, yesterday afternoon. Evidence was given to the effect th at on the morning in . question deceased was walking on the-line with a companion when he suddenly fell, as though in a fit, and died in a few minutes afterwards. Just prior to his death he appeared ,to be in his usual health. The jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural

CEES;fS."• - THB BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINOTOIt. —For the week ending Saturday, March 31st, The mean temperature was 371 Fahren- heit, and therefore two degrees warmer than the preceding week. The maximum temperature, 52 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 30th lust, and the minimum temperature,. 23 Fahrenheit, on the 25th inst. The rainfall measured •34in. The general direction of the wind was N.B. During the week. which., was the 13th of the current year, 35 births tad 20 deaths Were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 215 per thousand, -against 25,, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 31.9 the corresponding week of last year. The ' deaths included 2 from whooping cough, 1 from syphilis, 5 from tubercular disease, 1 from cancer, Sfrom brain disease, 3 from lung disease, 1 from heart disease. Nine cases of. scarlatina, 2 of 'typhoid fever, and 17 of whooping cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament. —JOHN H. GoRNALL. Medical Officer of Health.

Annum.. --- On Wednesday, at the County Petty Sessions, Georgeleltiert Caldwell, farmer, Rixton, appealed against an assessment made in respect of property at Raton. of which he is the owner. Mr. H. B. White appeared in sup- port of the:appeal, and Mr. T. C. Sutton: (Clerk to the Board of Guardians) represented the Assessment Committee. Mr. Sutton raised several technical objections, two of which were held to be fetal. The first was that insufficient notice of theintention to appeal had been given, and the second' watt that too long a period had elapsed between the time when the rate was made ii October last, and the time when notice of appeal' was given. Mr.. White said he was not aware Putt the rate was_made so long ago. He could not defeat Mr. Setton's objections. but he might venture to express a hope that the Assessment Committee would look into the matter and dear -with it on a fair basis,' because it was a case where a man did not wish to pay more than he ought ; and had-the appeal been heard, he was in a position to prove that the actual rental of the farm, was its actual value, and, therefore, the appel- lant ought not to be assessed above it. Tfie anpeal was accordingly dismissed. • PRIMROSE LEA.GLIE MEETING- AT' Tuir..WALL.— On Monday evening a tea party andentertainment was held in the Temperance Hall, Thelwall, in con- nection with the Lymin Habitation of the Primrose League. PRESENTATIONS TO MISS WILETNEON'.-0/1 Tues- day evening, a meeting of the congregation of St. Paul's • Church was held for the purpose of making several presentationf to Miss Blanche Wilkinson. only daughter of the Vicar, on the occasion of her approaching marriage to the Rev. G. D. Wray, Vicar of St. Peter's Church. The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) occupied the chair, and there were also present Miss Wilkinson, Mrs Wilkinson, Rev S. Wilkinson, Rev G. D. Wray, and Messrs D. W. Finney, Thomas Morris, W. Lawless, T. Jolley, J. Smethurq, J. Lawless, D. Jones, and others. The Chairman said that they had met together upon a very important occasion, namely, to make several presentations to Nisi; Wilkinson from the congre- gation,lchoir, and Sunday school of St. Paul's. He had great pleasure in making a presentation on bog • half of the congregation., His Worship then went onto-speak in the highest terms of Miss Wilkinson and' concluded by presenting her on behalf of th); congregation with a silver tray, silver coffee pot, egg boiler, Ash knives, &c. Mr. Joseph Lawless then presented Miss Wilkinson with a case of silver fish knives and forks on behalf of the Sunday school, and Mr D. W. Finney presented her with a case of silver teaspoons., sugar tongs, &c.. Mr J. J. Lythgoe with a bible, prayer bookoi,nd hymn book on behelf of the choir, and Miss Smetherst with a scent 'vase on behalf of Miss Wilkinson's Sunday school class. Miss Wilkinson suitably replied, and the proceedings shortly afterwards terminated. ST. ALBAN'S (R•C.) CATIREH, BEWSEY STREET.— The eleven o'clock service at St. Alban's, Bewsey- street. on Easter Sunday, was remarkable for the fact that it included the singing of Gounod's fine " Messe Solennelle." Heretofore the best efforts of local- choirs appear to have been limited to the more commonly known masses hy Haydn and Mozart. The credit of this new departure is said to be due to the present presiding clergyman of the mission, Father O'Hare, and his late colleague, the Rev. Dr. Saunders, who a few weeks ago was re- moved to another missionary sphere. Dr. Saunders is himself a fine musician and tenor singer. The Bewset-street choir must, it is presumed, have im- pressed Dr. Saunders with the belief that they were equal to attempting some good music out of the ordinary beaten track, for it is said he made them a Christmas Presant of-this Gounod's mass in the hope that-they would work it up for Easter. This the choir did, and succeeded remarkably well in their efforts. The music of this mass, given in its best form, is exquisite; but the rendering of it is diffi- cult, especially, for the organist. Mr. Caldwell, the organist at St. Alban's (at one time a pupil of Mr. Pyne, of Manchester), is a player of exceptional ability., to which fact must be attributed a good deal of the success with which the choir acquitted itself. Mr. Caldwell, too, is supported by singers who possess good. voices, and some 6f whom are themselves good instrumental players. They have an energetic conductor in Mr. Whitehead, and Mr. Littlewood, who has attached himself to the choir, and who took the tenor music of the mass, dimlay- ea a voice of remarkable range and sweetnest. • THE ILLEGAL ENCROACHMENT ON GRAPPENITALT,LANE.. . We are glad to be in a position this week to fur- nish our readers with the opinion of a Warrington solicitor as to the encroachments upon Grappenhall- lane. It is as we suspected; the landlord has a right to deal with his own land; but not with laid by the way side which has been dedicated to the public. The prevalent idea that a landlord has a title in all cases to enclose land to within fifteen feet of the centre of a current way is shcrivn to be a prevalent fallacy. lt will be interesting to see what action is taken in the matter by tbe Duresbury Highway Board, whicir meets next Thursday. We need hardly add that the solicitor who, writes us may be regarded .as an authority on the subiect that is disclosed by his opinion itself, which is as follows : I have been requested by a gentleman residing in 'this road to state the law noon this question . and I I have pleasure.in doing so: The landlord liae no' more right to emlose an inch. of Tend on the.side. of a public road than the public have to set back the landlord's fenqe. It is generally believed by- land- lords and their agents that they have a rightto en, close a road Up to 15 feet of the centre of it,. and this idea arises from the construction placedlupon an Act of Parliament, 5 and (Mai. IV., ch. 5, which imposes a penalty on any person who shoun croach by making any building, hedge, &c., on any carriageway or cartway within a distance of' 15 feet from the centre thereof. it has been deciiiod that a highway under this Act is.' that part which is repaired by stones or other materials, and that in order to support a conviction Under this Act, two things must occur, namely,.the encroachment must' be within /5 feet from the centre off the road, and it must be upon the highway, i.e., the paved part.. Now, in order to meet these decisions the 27 and. 28 viii., chap. 101 was passed, and that provided thrt it should' not be lawful to encroach on the sides of any carriageway or cartway within 15 feet from the centre thereof, "notwithstanding that the whole space of 15 feet has not been re- paired with stones or other materials." .A person is not liable. to the penalty under these Acts provided he does not encroach beyond the distance of 15 feet from the centre pf the road; and it has been assumed front this that an adjoining owner may lawfully enclosesup to the 15 feet,but this is not the case. All the land lying between the fences is ,part of the highway, and' this includes the slopes or strips of land Tying along the metalled part of the road, land any person who encloses such land, though he may leave the 15 feet untoucted, is liable to.be indicted for a nuisance at common law, and alsolo summary proceedings before the magi-. strates for obstructing the free passage of the high- way under sand 6' William IV., chapter 15: If the road is a disturnpiked road, the enclosure to with- in 25 feet of the centre is an offence punishable summarily by-virtue of 3 George IV., chapter 216. I regard it as the.euty of the Highway Board to institute proceedings against the owner. They have three courses open. to them, either (1) to sum- mon the offenderbefore the magistrates and have him dealt with summarily for an obstruction; or (2) to indict him.; or 0). to commence an action against him foran injunction. Personally, I hope that some steps will be taken in the matter, as these encroachments have. been going on in and around the Borough • for many years. They are made under the plausible pretence of a "public im- provement," and the improvement consists of the substitution of a wire fence or paling for grassy slopes and green hedges, and the acquisition by the landlord of thousands of yards of land which he has no right to take.

• The • House of Cenuuuns reassembled after the. Easter vacation, and the Speaker took the chairat threee'clock. There was a very-small attendance of menibers, THE ESTIMATESI—The House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, On the-vote of £2.9,260 for the maintenance of the Royal palaces, and after Dr. Hunter, had ineffectually attempted a count out, Mr. LAsoucnium moved the reduction of the vote by £6OO •as a, protest against the expenditure on palaces not • in. the occupation ,of Her Majesty.— On-a division, Mt. Labouchere's amendment was rejected • try 77 votes to 37tand• the vote was agreed to.. The vote of £1,500 for Marlborough House was agreed to;, so was the-vote for £77,0000 for the Royal parks, but not until Mr.Labouchere had complained of the great expense of the Ranges and the House had divided. The voto of £183,000 on account of the Survey was agreedlo,, After other- business progress was reported, and the- House adjourned at 12-Z, • HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FRIDAY.. The. The attendance of members was small. • QtresTioNs.—The'Chancellor of the Exchequer saki the question whether, one horse ought to be exempted in. the case of doctors and ministera of religion was receng the most careful consideration of the Government.—ln reply to Mr. Pickersgill‘ and Mr. 'Kelly, the Chancellor of the Exchequer- said he'was iluite prepared to listen to all remonstrances that might be addressed tAT.him• on the subject of-the-horse and wheel taxes, but at present he saw no reason for modifying the decision at which, the Government had arrived to impose these, taxes.—The Home Secretary, in reply to Mr. Pickersgill; said that he hoped to be able this session to introduce a ,bill to repeal the " whippinr, " 'provisions of the 7th and Bth George

Pilkington's collieries, he had both legs broken and his baclOnjured. He had since been at- tended by Drs. Gaskell and Greig, but notwithstanding every attention he died as stated. BREACH OF THE PEACE: ALLEGED "KNUCKLE DATERS." —At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas Hall and James Pilling, young men residing at Haydock, were charged with committing a breach a the peace by fightibg together in the yard of the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, on the night of the 16th ult. Delendants pleaded guilty, and Hall alleged that Pilling struck him without provocation. He said Pilling wore a pair of "knuckle' dusters," consisting of an non band round each finger, and closed tdgether in the palm of the hand. He carried them about with him in his pockets, and if anyone spoke a word to him he.used them.—The defend- ant Pilling denied this assertion.—Hall said the "knuckle dusters" were enough to kill anybody, and when he was struck with them by Pilling he only defended hirh- self.—in reply to the Bench, the constable in the case said he did not see any "knuckle dusters" in Piffing's possession and Hall had river complained to him about Ahem.—Tl;6 Bench ordered both defendants to be bound oTer to keep the peace for ebrononths.

THE EAsTER HOLIDAYS. - The Easter holidays have passed very quietly at Earlestown and Newton. Both on Good Friday and Easter Monday rain fell in the ear Her part of the day, but in the afternoon the weather was much brighter. The days were observed as general holidays, and all laborious work was At a standstill.

A meeting of the Cabinet was held at the ioreign Office at 12-30 on Friday, Lord Salisbury presiding. Arthur Orton, alias Thomas Castro, the Tichborne claimant, arrived at Queenstown on Friday evening from New York.

yesterday, at the conference of representativei of Local Boards and other sanitary authorities from all parts of England and Wales, held in Leeds, general approval was given to the Local Government Bill. • THE QUEINB AT FLORENCE.—The Queen will remain at Florence undo the 20th inst. and possibly longer. The King and Queen of Italy left on Friday. Previous to their departurethe Queen, Princess Beatrice, and her husband paid their Royal Highnesses a visit, Ruins Orr.—At Lerwick, on , Thursday; a butcher named Mackay was lined £5, under the. It is stated that attempts will be made to.hold thenrat all hazards, andl that the people will 04 'be dispersed by force. A TRAGBDY is BOILYMII.A.—A telegram from'. Mery reports that according to intelligence received' there ' from Bokhara, the' Amber's Prime Minister has, been 'murdered by a native'. The act has caused great excitement among the. people. The murderer and an accomplice have been put to death by being:Hurled • from the top of a tower 180)feet is height. FATAL ACCIDENT' ON &rano/11137.—0n Thursday 'even. iinY while the. One. named Joseph Christie was killed instantly, while the other was so badly injured that he. is not expected to re- ; cover.

div.head: TERRIBLE PIT ACCIDENT NEAR ' WIGAN.-FIVE • , MEN KILLED:
div.p: TERRIBLE PIT ACCIDENT NEAR ' WIGAN.-FIVE • , MEN KILLED:

At noon yesterday, a shocking accident happened at I the Douglas Bank Colliery, Woodhouse-lane, Wigan, Five mentwere engaged sinking a pit down to the Arley Mine:. Three men, named Thomas Morris, Edward Wa,tkin, and Patrick Keefe, were deseendinw the shaft in what is known as a hoppit, a strong 'iron bucket. From what can be.ascertained, the bucket became entangled, and precipitated the men a distance of NG yards. In addition to the three who were in the hoppit,o W. Barnes and Barnard llogan, two labourers, engaged at the sump hole, were also killed. An exploring party was imme- diately gob together, and they descended to bring up the ' mutilated remains of the unfortunate fell'ows,. who were terribly mangled. For some time the utmost excitement prevailed, a.report having been circulated that there was an explosion:. Some hundreds of people • rushed to the pit brovi, The.boclies were removed to the,. Woodhouse Inn, there to 'await an inquest. Three of the men resided .at Standish Lower Grounds; the others 'lived in Wigan. The collierybelongs to the Ross Bridge and Douglas Bank Collieries, Limited..
RUMOURED RESIGNATION OF PRINCE BISMARCK.
A CRISIS.

Reports are current in terlin that Prince Bismarck has tendered his resignation. Nothing is definitely known, except that some difficulty has arisen, presumably about the matrimonial alliance of Prince Alexander of Batten- berg, the late Bulgarian ruler, with Princess Victoria of Prussia.,

BERtuc to-day's morning papers pro- minently discuss the rumours that Prince Bismarck threatens to resign, and all agree in treating theramours very sceptically: The " National Zeitung" professes to have certain knowledge that the endeavours of Prince Alexander_to obtaiir the hand of Princess Victoria are without rult, inVhat therefore no actual reason for the Chancellor's resignation exists. BERLIN, FRIDAY Arraincomv.=—The crisis Continues/It is not known with certainty whether Prince Bismarck will persist in hie resignation. It is generally• thought that he is making use of the Battenberg marriage pro- ject to ascertain whether his influence is as strong as previously.

'He was fined 2s 6d %' costs.

SAD FATALITIY: A LOCAL " CELVBIrrY " ThrowNse•-- he Mary M'Call, an old womaot letter known amongt, working classes at St. Helens as "North Mary," Wa' found drowned ith Watery-lane, Eccleston, on Thursdg morning. Deceased had been re.widow for many years' during which Hi-nether means of subsistence were vet! preca”ous. She was in receipt of parish relief, and t/cipated in the Wiadle and other doles. Whenever ?' was possible she obtained work on farms, arid lived Is various 4 places, incliiding Ecclesnm-street and Greer bank. CM Wednesday morning the deceased went the house of Mrs. Sarah Harrison, widow,.in Wateri; lane, anchsked if she could hive liedgings, as she ha' obtained farm work at Windle MS. Mrs. Harrison" gave her consent, and expected deceased there at nigW; , She did not come, however, and about eight o'clock nOw , morning a letter-carrier employed at the St. Helens Peg Office and another youngman observed her dead bodi in a ditch, orpool of water, about twenty yardt-frr Harrison's he,trse. • It appearsthat deceased went tre' Seven Stars Ilan, at Eccleston, and procured sixper worth of whisky in a bottle,. and left about half-past She was not again seen alive: It is stated that the pl 'where the body was found iS a dangerous one. Half width of the lane is taken up by a ditch, which ' forms a pool form or five yards wide. There is no I .tection whatever, and the water varies from 12 to inches in depths There are marks where deceased b walked along the side for some little distance, and had then fallen iirhead first. When found her head, shoulders were ered, but her body and legs svek quite dry. The body was taken to the Royal Oak W await an inquest.
